title: Establishing Structural Execution Boundaries for Irreversible AI Actions: The WRS Framework

detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence systems increasingly transition from decision support to autonomous execution, contemporary AI governance frameworks face a critical structural gap. Existing approaches—ranging from alignment and constitutional constraints to risk scoring and human-in-the-loop oversight—largely assume that execution is permissible once a decision has been produced. This assumption becomes insufficient in systems where execution can trigger irreversible physical, kinetic, or systemic consequences.

This paper introduces the World Reliability Ruleset (WRS), a veto-based execution boundary framework designed to govern execution itself rather than decision quality or optimization outcomes. WRS formalizes execution as a binary authorization state governed by a default-block posture: execution is permitted if and only if all non-negotiable constraints are satisfied. Any single violation is sufficient to trigger an absolute veto, making WRS a non-compensatory and non-probabilistic governance mechanism.

Unlike alignment-centric or principle-based models, WRS does not evaluate intent, confidence, or risk gradients. Instead, it defines a deterministic execution boundary that remains independent of the decision engine’s intelligence level, preventing increases in reasoning capability from diluting execution safety boundaries. WRS is applicable across advanced AI systems, including AGI and prospective ASI, as well as non-AI automated systems with irreversible consequences.

WRS anchors accountability at the execution boundary by coupling veto events to verifiable binary audit logs, reducing responsibility diffusion and post-hoc rationalization. Positioned as a domain-agnostic execution primitive, WRS complements judgment-layer architectures such as the Linda Energy Reliability Architecture (LERA) while remaining independently deployable. Together, they support a layered governance model in which epistemic exploration may scale without bound, while kinetic manifestation remains strictly constrained by structurally enforced physical permissibility.

This work offers a structural alternative to probabilistic AI safety approaches by introducing a non-compensatory execution-permissibility primitive, providing a governance framework that prioritizes execution authority over decision quality.

title: Do the Largest Components Determine the Index Performance? Evidence from a Concentrated Portfolio Strategy in the Brazilian Stock Market

detail.title: Do the Largest Components Determine the Index Performance? Evidence from a Concentrated Portfolio Strategy in the Brazilian Stock Market
detail.abstract:
This article investigates whether a simple active strategy based on selecting the largest components of a broad market index can outperform passive replication of the index itself in terms of risk-adjusted performance. Using daily data from the Brazilian stock market between January 2022 and December 2024, we compare the BRAX11 ETF — a proxy for the IBrX-100 — with concentrated portfolios composed of the top 20, 10, and 5 highest-weighted assets in the index, with normalized weights.

Performance is evaluated using the Sharpe, Treynor, and Sortino ratios, as well as volatility, beta, and cumulative return trajectories. The 20-asset portfolio presents a Sharpe ratio of 0.393669 compared to -0.271263 for BRAX11, with a beta of 0.522, indicating lower market sensitivity and higher risk-return efficiency. To assess the statistical significance of the observed differences, we apply the Circular Block Bootstrap method under the imposed null hypothesis (H0), using 20,000 resamples and block sizes of 10, following the approach of Olivier Ledoit and Michael Wolf (2008). 

The results indicate that all three strategies exhibit statistically significant differences in the Sharpe ratio relative to the benchmark (p-values of 0.0023, 0.0050, and 0.0172, respectively). The findings suggest that, in emerging markets characterized by high concentration in capitalization-weighted indices, a parsimonious selection of the main components can generate consistent efficiency gains without resorting to complex active management models.

detail.abstract: Papers 1-3 establish that fiscal monetisation generates predictable currency instability in frontier economies, that development finance institutions can screen for this risk, and that operational protocols exist to act on the signal. This paper completes the causal chain by documenting a consistent real-economy deterioration pattern that follows three-condition crisis episodes, using World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) and UNCTAD FDI statistics for Ghana, Turkey, Egypt, and Zambia, with South Africa as a control. Within an annual-data window aligned to the crisis timing established in Paper 2, the crisis period is associated with lower gross fixed capital formation intensity (NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS), tighter private-sector credit conditions as proxied by domestic credit to the private sector (FS.AST.PRVT.GD.ZS), and weaker and/or more volatile foreign direct investment inflows (BX.KLT.DINV.CD.WD), with country-specific exceptions driven by state-led capital expenditure and distressed-asset transactions. The aim is not formal causal identification, but operational pattern documentation: the same upstream monetary-instability signal that predicts currency crises also flags a deterioration in the investment, credit, and external-capital environment in which DFI projects must execute.

title: Soil Heavy Metals in a Typical Coal Mining Cluster of Northern China: Pollution, Source Apportionment, and Eco-Health Risks​
affiliations: Inner Mongolia Agricultural University, Inner Mongolia University of Finance and Economics, Inner Mongolia University of Finance and Economics, Inner Mongolia University of Finance and Economics, Inner Mongolia Agricultural University and Inner Mongolia Agricultural University

detail.title: Soil Heavy Metals in a Typical Coal Mining Cluster of Northern China: Pollution, Source Apportionment, and Eco-Health Risks​
detail.abstract: Coal mining and associated anthropogenic activities significantly perturb the soil environment, leading to pronounced spatial heterogeneity in heavy metal accumulation and ecological risks within and around mining areas. To address knowledge gaps in spatial pollution patterns, dominant sources, and risk contribution mechanisms, this study investigates surface soils from a typical mining area in Tongchuan Town, Ordos City. By integrating Enrichment Factors, the Potential Ecological Risk Index, soil fertility evaluation, Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) source apportionment, and human health risk assessment, we characterize heavy metal distribution patterns, source structures, and risk–response relationships. The results indicate relatively low heavy metal concentrations and strong soil alkalinity, with overall pollution risks remaining controllable. Soil fertility shows a “low organic matter, nitrogen-deficient, and potassium-deficient” profile. Heavy metal accumulation is mainly nil-to-low enrichment, although local Cd concentrations exceed screening values for agricultural land. Ecological risks are most prominent for Cd and Hg; over 60% of the study area exhibits moderate-to-high integrated potential ecological risk, with high-risk zones concentrated in coal mining clusters. PMF results show that industrial and transportation sources contribute 44.09%, followed by natural sources (34.06%), coal mining (16.35%), and agricultural activities (5.50%). Although health risks are generally within acceptable limits, hand-to-mouth ingestion is the dominant exposure route (>90%). Non-carcinogenic risk is primarily driven by Cr and As, whereas As contributes most to carcinogenic risk. Accordingly, source reduction and exposure-pathway management should prioritize industrial/transportation emissions and mining activities, with particular attention to As, Cr, Hg, and Cd.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the canonical rule specification of the World Reliability Ruleset (WRS), providing the operational definition of the execution-boundary framework introduced in “Establishing Structural Execution Boundaries for Irreversible AI Actions: The WRS Framework.” While the framework paper establishes the conceptual rationale for execution governance in systems capable of producing irreversible consequences, this specification formalizes the rule structure required to operationalize that boundary.

WRS governs execution rather than decision quality. It adopts a veto-based logic grounded in the Default Block Principle, under which execution remains blocked unless all non-negotiable constraints are satisfied. Any single violation results in an absolute veto. This non-compensatory structure prevents probabilistic reasoning, optimization trade-offs, or administrative authorization from overriding execution boundaries once irreversible physical or systemic risks are present.

The specification formalizes the core ruleset (WRS-C), domain-specific subsets (WRS-D), and the deterministic scenario-mapping logic used to identify execution conditions involving irreversible consequences. It further defines responsibility anchoring requirements that bind execution authorization to auditable human accountability.

Designed to remain invariant under increases in system intelligence, WRS functions as a domain-agnostic execution governance primitive applicable to AI and automated systems operating in safety-critical environments. The framework therefore introduces a structural mechanism for preventing irreversible consequences while ensuring structural responsibility attribution at the point of execution.

title: From Signal to Decision: A Practitioner Protocol and Institutional Reform Agenda for Integrating Monetary Leading Indicators into DFI Currency Risk Management

detail.title: From Signal to Decision: A Practitioner Protocol and Institutional Reform Agenda for Integrating Monetary Leading Indicators into DFI Currency Risk Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not appliable

declarations.funderStatement: Not appliable

contentType.other: Part of a working paper series

detail.abstract:
The three-condition monetary leading-indicator framework can be deployed within existing DFI institutional structures using publicly available data. The principal barrier to adoption is not technical but institutional: four structural governance failures that this paper identifies and addresses through specific, feasibility-rated reforms.

Papers 1 and 2 establish that the framework detects frontier-market currency risk 6 to 20 months before sovereign ratings reflect it, and that unhedged DFI local-currency portfolios lose 37 to 69 percent of USD-equivalent principal value in full-signal episodes — losses that are illustrative but directionally robust across four crisis cases. This paper operationalises those findings in two parts.

Part I sets out a complete practitioner protocol: a five-variable country-entry screen producing Green/Amber/Red classifications; a 10-point Monetary Stress Score calibrating deal-level risk; a three-covenant design toolkit with objective trigger definitions; an active monitoring dashboard with three escalation protocols; and reversal conditions for re-entry into suspended markets. Part II diagnoses why DFI systems do not already contain this layer — identifying four structural barriers in mandate design, incentive architecture, information asymmetry, and credit committee composition — and proposes nine targeted reforms across policy, operational, and governance levels, none of which requires new data infrastructure or additional capital expenditure.

detail.abstract:
The three-condition monetary leading-indicator framework developed in Paper 1 generalises across frontier-market currency episodes. Applied to Ghana (2022), Turkey (2021–2023), Egypt (2022–2024), and Zambia (2019–2020), it identifies elevated crisis risk 6 to 20 months before sovereign rating agency downgrades, while generating no signal for South Africa — a result that supports the framework's discriminatory power.

Development finance institutions typically rely on sovereign credit ratings as the primary input into country-risk decisions. This paper establishes that such ratings are lagging indicators of the monetary stress that drives local-currency depreciation, creating a structural window in which DFI portfolios accumulate unpriced currency tail risk. Across the four crisis episodes, rating downgrades followed the framework's first signal by 6 to 20 months. A stylised simulation of an unhedged five-year local-currency facility across these markets yields illustrative USD-equivalent principal losses of 37 to 69 percent; realised losses would depend on hedging strategy, portfolio construction, and covenant design.

title: Foreclosed: AI, the Absent Industrialisation Window, and the Case for a New African Development Finance Architecture

detail.title: Foreclosed: AI, the Absent Industrialisation Window, and the Case for a New African Development Finance Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable

declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract:
Africa's demographic stock is accumulating faster than its economies can absorb it into stable, productivity-raising work. The sequence that powered every prior development success — low-cost labour, export-oriented capital, productivity gains, and structural transformation — is being dismantled by AI and robotics before much of Africa has accessed it. This paper argues that the resulting derailment is not a cyclical setback but a structural rupture, and that responding to it requires a different development finance architecture — not a faster version of the old one.

Three alternative pathways remain open, but each operates within a narrowing window. First, Africa can become AI training infrastructure by monetising the continent's linguistic diversity and currently under-captured data surplus. Second, Africa can become a climate-AI R&D geography, converting climate vulnerability into a structural position inside global climate technology value chains, with explicit rules determining who owns the resulting IP. Third, Africa can scale AI-augmented professional services exports, leveraging a durable cost differential before full substitution erodes it.

On the labour side, the BPO and digital services window compresses fastest: Africa's ITES/BPO base is about 1 million workers today, and routine tasks face meaningful near-term displacement risk. The manufacturing entry point is also narrowing as automation erodes the labour-cost advantage that historically underwrote late industrialisation. A third channel — AI-driven supply chain optimisation increasing commodity price volatility — is advanced as a structural risk hypothesis rather than an established empirical finding; the direct evidence at African producer scale does not yet exist.

None of these pathways can be financed at the required scale unless the upstream binding constraint is addressed: frontier-market currency risk remains materially underpriced, and that weakens the willingness of DFIs and private partners to commit long-tenor capital where local-cost execution dominates. The financing implication is therefore institutional as much as analytical. What is required is not a narrow technical framework grafted onto existing practice, but a broader syndication architecture in which African DFIs, climate funds, concessional partners, and private investors share risk more deliberately and price currency exposure with greater discipline at appraisal and structuring stage.

The paper therefore proposes a four-component institutional architecture — (i) a continental AI-economy diagnostic function, (ii) a pan-African data infrastructure facility, (iii) a climate-AI blended finance window with IP-sharing provisions built in at design stage, and (iv) a structured syndication platform for frontier-market investments that embeds currency awareness, tenor discipline, and risk-sharing from the outset. The package is executable within existing balance sheet capacity and does not require new treaty architecture. The window is narrow: the response must be operational within three years and scaled within five.

title: M3 Money Supply as a Leading Indicator of Currency Crisis in Dollarised Frontier Economies: Evidence from Zimbabwe, 2016-2024

detail.title: M3 Money Supply as a Leading Indicator of Currency Crisis in Dollarised Frontier Economies: Evidence from Zimbabwe, 2016-2024

declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

keywords: fiscal theory of the price level

contentType.other: Part of a working paper series

detail.abstract: Broad money supply growth under fiscal dominance is a statistically robust leading indicator of currency depreciation, and Zimbabwe's 2016–2024 experience offers unusually strong empirical validation of this relationship. Using quarterly data on M3 and the Old Mutual Implied Rate (OMIR) as a proxy for the parallel market exchange rate, we estimate four specifications. The levels specification produces an R² of 0.973 (p<0.001), while the first-differences specification produces an R² of 0.705 (p<0.001). A projection constructed in August 2022 using only contemporaneously available data estimated an official rate of ZWL 3,180:USD 1 by December 2023; the subsequent trajectory — reaching ZWL 30,000:USD 1 by April 2024 before currency abandonment — confirms directional and order-of-magnitude validity while illustrating acceleration driven by confidence effects. The April 2024 introduction of the Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG) currency, which lost 50 percent of its official value within six months despite gold backing, provides additional validation of the monetisation mechanism predicted by the fiscal theory of the price level. The paper proposes a three-condition diagnostic framework for frontier-market currency risk assessment grounded in observable monetary and market signals.

title: The Economic Impact of the Arts on the Health and Wellbeing of Children and Young People: A Systematic Review
affiliations: Bangor University, Edge Hill University, King’s College London, University College London, Bangor University - Bangor University and Edge Hill University

detail.title: The Economic Impact of the Arts on the Health and Wellbeing of Children and Young People: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract:
Background: Demand for services to improve health and wellbeing is rising among children and young people, driven by increasing health complaints. Arts engagement is effective across multiple health outcomes and used in public health as a preventive intervention, however the economic benefits from the arts are rarely reported. We aimed to systematically review evidence on the economic impacts of the arts on the health and wellbeing of children and young people and to assess reporting quality.

Methods: Literature published after January 2005 was identified through searches of CINAHL, Embase.com, MEDLINE, PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, Google, Google Scholar, and Semantic Scholar. Articles were screened by three independent reviewers against eligibility criteria. Studies were included if at least 80% of the population were between ages 5 – 24, involved a recognised arts modality that was not combined with non-arts activities, and reported economic outcomes. Checklists specific to study designs were completed to assess reporting quality. Findings were grouped by arts modality and synthesised through a narrative approach. We used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guideline.

Results: Searches produced 11,610 articles, with 14 meeting the inclusion criteria. There was substantial heterogeneity in study designs, intervention details, outcomes, and valuation methods. Benefits from arts programmes outweighed investment, evidenced through economic modelling (£122 million – £800 million society-wide impacts), cost-utility analysis (95% probability of cost-effectiveness using $50,000 willingness-to-pay threshold), benefit-cost ratios (returning 5.89 – 32 per monetary unit invested), social return on investment ratios (returning 1.98 – 7 per monetary unit invested), comparisons between groups (467 – 6,705 monetary units in healthcare savings), and qualitative data. The reporting quality in 11 studies was strong, and the findings aligned with those from less well-reported studies.

Conclusions: The findings provided support for investing in the arts to improve health and wellbeing of children and young people. Discussion of review limitations highlighted evidence from high-income countries only, and potentially eligible studies excluded due to vague abstracts. Future research and arts programme evaluations should consider using standardised measures appropriate for short- and long-term economic evaluations of both wellbeing and well-becoming for young people across their life-course.

title: Universal Capital Endowment at Birth in Italy: A Life-Cycle Financial Infrastructure for Social Stability and Intergenerational Cohesion

detail.title: Universal Capital Endowment at Birth in Italy: A Life-Cycle Financial Infrastructure for Social Stability and Intergenerational Cohesion

publicationDetails.detailsText: Università Cattaneo Working Papers, No. 20, 2026 DOI: 10.25428/2532-554X/20 ISSN: 2532-554X

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a universal capital endowment granted at birth as a structural response to two interrelated transformations in advanced economies: a persistent long-run decline in labor's share of national income, and accelerating demographic contraction. Both trends jointly undermine the sustainability of traditional welfare systems and weaken the economic position of younger cohorts, who enter adulthood with limited balance sheets, high exposure to labor market risk, and effectively no access to capital income.

The proposal — termed the Youth Capital Endowment (YCE) — assigns an initial grant of €10,000 to every newborn, invested immediately in a globally diversified passive equity portfolio benchmarked to the MSCI All Country World Index and held in a legally segregated, individually owned account. Withdrawals are permitted only at three predefined life stages (ages 18, 21, and 28), aligned with major early-life transitions. The endowment is financed through a small structural levy of 0.08 percent on existing household financial assets, generating approximately €4.2 billion annually against a program cost of €3.5–4.0 billion — a near-breakeven structure with a marginal surplus feeding an initial stabilization reserve.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it frames the YCE not as a redistributive transfer but as pre-distributive financial infrastructure — analogous to public education or healthcare — that modifies initial conditions rather than correcting outcomes ex post. Second, it develops a detailed quantitative architecture: under a 6 percent real return baseline, an initial €10,000 endowment grows to approximately €29,000 by age 18, €34,000 by age 21, and €51,000 by age 28, with total real payouts across the three tranches exceeding €37,000. At system level, continuous operation over 20 years generates assets under management of €136–156 billion. Third, the paper introduces a CDC-inspired collective smoothing mechanism — the Stabilization Reserve — designed to mitigate cohort-specific sequence-of-returns risk (the "Birth Year Lottery") without creating guaranteed returns, nominal floors, or contingent public liabilities. The mechanism is fiscally neutral by construction: fund solvency is anchored strictly to net asset value, eliminating any public backstop requirement.

The governance architecture prioritizes insulation from political interference through legal asset segregation, a strict passive investment mandate, independent oversight, and structural rather than discretionary funding. The Italian institutional context — in particular INPS as custodial administrator — is analyzed in detail, though the core architecture is designed to be portable across advanced economies.

detail.abstract: This essay examines the behavioral dimension of institutional stabilization in Iranian universities following political transition. Iranian universities enter such transitions shaped by decades of institutional deformation that have distorted professional incentive structures, creating negative risk asymmetry-a condition in which the perceived personal risks associated with principled professional action exceed those associated with opportunistic alignment or passive silence. Uncertainty about authority, accountability, and the institutional rules governing universities during transition becomes particularly complex as it interacts with these inherited distortions. Drawing on institutional economics, the analysis distinguishes between institutions as rule systems and universities as organizations operating within those rules. When negative risk asymmetry becomes widespread, it can produce an institutional fear equilibrium in which individuals adopt defensive strategies that minimize personal exposure. Over time, such behavioral mechanisms can weaken professional standards, reshape informal norms, and generate incentive drift that undermines institutional performance even when formal governance structures appear stable. The essay then examines how institutional responses can address these dynamics. Institutional arrangements that protect professional behavior, stabilize governance incentives, and signal the credibility of institutional rules can reduce uncertainty and rebalance professional risk. By aligning individual incentives with professional norms, such arrangements can help stabilize universities during political transition while laying the foundations for durable institutional capacity in a post-transition higher education system.

detail.abstract: Classic power indexes, such as the Shapley-Shubik and Banzhaf power indexes, assume each coalition of voters is equally likely. Modern power indexes, such as the Shapley-Owen Value (SOV), limit potential coalitions to those that can form in a map of voter preferences. We refine SOVs by limiting coalitions to those that form from the trajectories of observed votes, which we call vote-specific SOVs (vs-SOVs). We present a computer algorithm for computing vs-SOVs that can be applied to various voting thresholds, weighted voting, and bloc voting. Vs-SOVs also can be applied to subsets of votes, such as issue categories, and they allow for the examination of counterfactuals. To illustrate the usefulness of vs-SOVs, we reexamine a major work on pivotal voters at the U.S. Constitutional Convention of 1787. We find that delegate power varied significantly by issue area, refuting the notion that Roger Sherman was most likely to pivot any vote.

title: Prudent Person Rule Disclosure and Pension Fund Performance: Information From Annual Reports
affiliations: , Ghent University and De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: Prudent Person Rule Disclosure and Pension Fund Performance: Information From Annual Reports
detail.abstract: The Prudent Person Rule is a central part of trust investment law for pension funds. We examine its relationship with pension fund performance by constructing fund-level disclosure indices that capture the degree of attention devoted to four Prudent Person dimensions in annual reports: Investment Policy, Risk Management, Governance, and Sustainability. To construct them, we create a machine-learning assisted lexicon based on 2,052 Dutch pension fund annual reports for 2003-2023. Over the sample period, our disclosure indices increase in all dimensions except Investment Policy. Better-funded pension funds disclose less across all dimensions, while larger ones tend to disclose more on Sustainability. We find a statistically significant negative association between Sustainability and next-year benchmark outperformance. We further show that this effect stems from exclusion-related terms, consistent with the view that greater sustainability disclosure is associated with stricter investment constraints and lower performance.

title: Conjecture of Inflation, Real Price, and Involution Index
affiliations: NEOMA Business School

detail.title: Conjecture of Inflation, Real Price, and Involution Index
detail.abstract: To provide explanations for the controversies surrounding inflation, we propose the Market-Specific Inflation Rate and Structural Inflation Rate rooted in the framework of structural inflation. Furthermore, we introduce a conjecture regarding the new formula for Real Price, which may be derived from the principles of the Harmonic Weighted Mean. This framework allows us to elucidate the Giffen Paradox. Building upon this theoretical framework, we develop a Dynamic Supply and Demand Function. This equation effectively addresses the debates surrounding Veblen Goods and offers insights into the auction process. Additionally, we propose the Involution Index as a quantitative measure of the variation in the disparity between supply and demand in the labor market, thereby gauging the degree of involution.

detail.abstract:
This essay responds directly to the fourth risk category in Dario Amodei's "The Adolescence of Technology" (2026): economic disruption through AI-driven displacement and wealth concentration. It argues that the structural shift from labor to capital income — documented across advanced economies for three decades — is about to accelerate sharply, and that income transfers alone are insufficient to address it. The proposal is a Universal Capital Endowment at Birth: every newborn receives a minimum grant of $20,000, invested immediately in a globally diversified passive equity fund and held in a legally segregated account until three predefined life-stage withdrawals at ages 18, 21, and 28.

The essay's central contribution is a novel funding mechanism: rather than a broad-based financial levy, the endowment is financed through three instruments targeting the primary economic beneficiaries of the AI transition — a levy on AI-attributable corporate profits, a capital gains surcharge on AI-intensive equity appreciation, and a displacement contribution recapturing payroll tax savings from AI-driven workforce substitution. This mechanism is self-calibrating: it generates more revenue precisely when displacement is most severe. The $20,000 figure represents a minimum floor equivalent to approximately 8 basis points of US household financial assets; the architecture is designed to scale as AI-generated fiscal capacity grows.

The proposal draws on and extends the author's companion working paper (Università Cattaneo Working Papers, No. 20, 2026), which develops the full technical architecture, empirical foundations, and a CDC-inspired stabilization mechanism for mitigating cohort-specific sequence-of-returns risk.

title: Colonial Mimicry and the Irony of Identity - A Study of Karma by Khushwant Singh by Jai Prakash Acharya

detail.title: Colonial Mimicry and the Irony of Identity - A Study of Karma by Khushwant Singh by Jai Prakash Acharya
detail.abstract: Colonial Mimicry and the Irony of Identity - A Study of Karma by Khushwant Singh by Jai Prakash Acharya. This paper provides a comprehensive critical analysis of Khushwant Singh’s seminal short story, Karma, through a post-colonial lens. By examining the stark dichotomy between Sir Mohan Lal—a "Mimic Man" suffering from profound cultural homelessness—and his wife, Lady Lal, the study explores themes of identity, colonial mimicry, and the caustic reality of the British Raj. The narrative is analysed as a poignant critique of the "colonial hangover" that continues to influence the Indian psyche. Sir Mohan Lal’s meticulous erasure of his roots and his subsequent humiliation at the hands of British soldiers serve as a literal and metaphorical manifestation of his karma, proving that affectation is no shield against systemic prejudice. Furthermore, this study bridges the historical context of the story with contemporary Indian perspectives, critiquing the modern tendency to prioritise foreign interests and global validation over indigenous authenticity. The paper concludes that true progress lies in recognising one's heritage rather than "aping" Western standards.

detail.abstract: This paper constructs a comprehensive dataset of Japanese equity total returns, real short-term interest rates, and inflation from 1924 to 2024 and studies how financial market efficiency evolves with economic development. Using a GLS-based time-varying VAR, we estimate a joint degree of market inefficiency that captures return predictability and show that efficiency improves over the long run but temporarily deteriorates around major macro-financial regime changes. To interpret these medium-run episodes, we build a monetary endogenous growth model with financial intermediation and borrowing constraints. A relaxation of financial constraints shifts the balanced growth path and slows convergence, generating transitional dynamics that make equity returns more predictable. We then generate pseudo data from the model, add noise, and apply the same time-varying VAR procedure; the estimated inefficiency measure rises during the transition and fades as the economy approaches the new steady state.

title: The U.S. Is Betting the Economy on 'Scaling' AI: Where Is the Intelligence When One Needs It?
affiliations: Delft University of Technology - Department of Economics

detail.title: The U.S. Is Betting the Economy on 'Scaling' AI: Where Is the Intelligence When One Needs It?

publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The AI industry is betting that 'scaling', i.e., adding more and more data, GPUs, compute infrastructure and dollars, will lead to machine superintelligence or Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)-which in turn will lead to exponential growth of output, productivity and profits for the industry and the larger American economy. Focusing on AGI and generic LLMs, the point of this paper is plain: AI's 'scaling' strategy must fail and the AI data-center investment bubble will pop. The paper identifies four bottlenecks: (1) the planned $5 trillion investment in data center infrastructure (during 2026-2030) is not going to pay off; AI revenues will not increase enough and AI inference cost continue to rise faster than revenues; (2) AI firms will have to resort to hyperscale borrowing from banks and investment-grade bond markets to fund their capex; this hyperscale borrowing will create a ticking time bomb on the balance sheets of AI firms, because the core capital expenditure on specialized GPUs and server risks becoming economically obsolete within two or three years; (3) it will be impossible to build the projected data center infrastructure

title: Participatory Democracy as a Pathway Towards Sustainable Development
affiliations: Waseda University

detail.title: Participatory Democracy as a Pathway Towards Sustainable Development
detail.abstract: Participatory democracy is essential for democratic life. The literature on its implications for income inequality draws controversial conclusions, and studies evaluating its effects on legal justice are scant. This study analyses these consequences by adopting a dynamic panel-data model with 119 countries from 1982 to 2022, and describes them using country-income levels. The results suggest that, even at all country-income levels, participatory democracy is likely to tackle inequality and promote legal justice by reducing corruption in the public sector and bolstering regulatory enforcement. To provide further evidence in the Asia-Pacific region, comparative case studies of Indonesia and the Philippines are performed using a synthetic control method (SCM) with control units of 24 Asia-Pacific countries. The SCM results confirm the results of the dynamic panel-data model. These findings underscore the need to promote participatory democracy to achieve sustainable development, particularly by addressing Goals 10 and 16.

title: Formal Sector Hiring Behavior in a Developing Country: Evidence from Structured Interviews

detail.title: Formal Sector Hiring Behavior in a Developing Country: Evidence from Structured Interviews
detail.abstract: This paper empirically presents new evidence for the hiring behavior of managers with emphasis on a developing country, Pakistan. Pakistani economy characterized with a large informal sector, this study, though, is conducted for formal sector private firms, the evidence suggests footprints of informality in its formal labor market as well. The lack of formal labor market institutions leads to greater incidence of informal hiring channels such as hiring through referrals and already received CVs. Use of formal hiring strategies remained significantly less than reported for developed countries and are mainly used for white collar employees. The informal hiring strategies consequently results in frequent wage negotiations, mostly based on the firm's wage internal wage structure. A stark difference to the preceding literature is the significantly shorter vacancy duration that may also be attributed to the stronger dependence on informal hiring methods. Explaining formal-informal labor market linkages, firms have reported frequent hiring from the informal sector, mainly because of relevant experience, and technical education.

title: KGER-PP: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Reasoning for Process Planning based on Large Language Models
affiliations: Chongqing University and

detail.title: KGER-PP: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Reasoning for Process Planning based on Large Language Models
detail.abstract: As manufacturing systems become more complex and dynamic, process planning must adapt to address the increased complexity, uncertainty, and demand for real-time decision-making. Knowledge graph can be used to store and process multi-modal complex process knowledge and support large-scale, dynamic manufacturing environments in form of process knowledge graph (PKG). However, the complex characteristics of PKG schemas and structures remain significant challenges for their effective utilisation in real-world manufacturing scenarios. Therefore, we propose the Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Reasoning framework for Process Planning (KGER-PP), integrating PKG with Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance process knowledge reasoning. Firstly, a process planning semantic parsing module is introduced to transform natural language questions related to process planning into executable structured representations. Secondly, a structural and semantic enhancement method (StSeEM) is designed to generate knowledge-rich rationales that bridge the interpretability gap in answer generation by integrating structured information at the initial embedding stage and exploiting semantic knowledge via the chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Thirdly, a graph-guided tuning method is proposed to align explicit reasoning paths with textual representations with a multi-modal future fusion mechanism, mitigating LLMs' hallucination risks through enforced factuality constraints. Finally, experimental results show that the proposed KGER-PP framework achieves the best performance in knowledge-intensive reasoning rationale generation tasks and outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in process knowledge reasoning research. The code of our work is available at https://github.com/WenWph/KGER-PP.git

detail.abstract: The meta-crisis literature has correctly identified complexity, multiscale causality, and accelerating interdependence as drivers of systemic breakdown. Yet these accounts founder on a critical constraint: systems cannot diagnose themselves accurately when moral blame dominates perception. When organizations, institutions, or societies interpret failure through frameworks of culpability-bad actors, incompetence, moral decay-information flow degrades, coordination fails, and adaptive capacity collapses. This paper introduces The Most Compassionate Story as a metatheory for the meta-crisis. It reframes breakdown not as a failure of intent, intelligence, or values, but as a loss of relational coherence across nested systems. By removing moral blame while preserving responsibility, this framework restores the conditions under which mission-critical information can surface, responsibility can be taken without defensive collapse, and systems can reorganize to better serve their stated purposes. Crucially, this is not therapeutic comfort or moral relativism. It is a functional necessity-one supported by decades of research on organizational learning, defensive routines, psychological safety, and systems dynamics. Where other meta-crisis theories diagnose the problem, this metatheory provides the interpretive conditions necessary for intervention.

detail.abstract: Large-scale inter-basin river diversion projects are increasingly promoted in India as solutions to regional water scarcity. However, their long-term compatibility with climate commitments, biodiversity conservation, and social equity remains insufficiently examined. This paper presents an integrated Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and lifecycle climate impact assessment of two proposed inter-basin river diversion projects in Karnataka: the Bedti–Varada and Aghanashini–Vedavati schemes. Using conservative assumptions aligned with peer‑reviewed literature and government data, the study estimates total locked‑in emissions of approximately 30.09 MtCO₂e over the 2027–2070 lifecycle, primarily driven by operational energy demand, construction materials, and irreversible forest loss in the Western Ghats. Beyond emissions, the analysis evaluates biodiversity impacts within a UNESCO World Heritage landscape and a Ramsar‑designated estuary, alongside livelihood risks affecting over 3,200 fishing families. The projects are assessed against India’s Long‑Term Low Emissions Development Strategy (LTLEDS) and Net Zero 2070 pathway, revealing structural incompatibility due to LULUCF degradation, rising electricity demand, and climate‑induced hydrological uncertainty by mid‑century. The paper further demonstrates that demand‑side and nature‑based alternatives—such as drip irrigation, crop diversification, and decentralized rainwater harvesting—can deliver comparable water security at less than 1% of the carbon footprint and a fraction of the capital cost. The findings suggest that proceeding without comprehensive climate and ESG integration risks creating stranded assets, undermining international environmental commitments, and exacerbating long‑term water insecurity. The paper concludes by proposing a decision framework prioritizing climate‑aligned, low‑carbon alternatives and institutionalizing project‑level carbon accounting in Indian infrastructure planning.

title: Patterns and Gains of Export Diversification in Pakistan
affiliations: State Bank of Pakistan

detail.title: Patterns and Gains of Export Diversification in Pakistan
detail.abstract: This paper explores Pakistan's export dynamics with a focus on diversification strategies including market and product diversification and specialization and their impact on export performance. Generally, the export sector of Pakistan relies on labor-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather, which caused multiple challenges in achieving sustainable export growth. This study finds that the diversification in both product and market portfolios remained limited over the past decade which suggests a persistent concentration risk. However, individual firms exhibit a gradual trend towards diversification, albeit within existing product and market options, which may constrain overall export expansion. The analysis underscores the critical role of market experience in facilitating product diversification, enabling exporters to navigate consumer preferences, business environment, and distribution networks effectively. Conversely, high transport costs emerge as a significant barrier to new product introduction, particularly affecting smaller exporters. Importer status also plays a crucial role in influencing product diversification decisions. Examining market diversification, the study highlights the positive impact of past product experience and government support programs, while acknowledging the challenge of establishing clear causality due to potential endogeneity. Overall, diversified firms achieve higher export values, that emphasizes the importance of expanding market reach over merely diversifying product lines. This work provides insights for policymakers seeking to foster export resilience through targeted interventions in trade facilitation, infrastructure development, and supportive export policies.

title: From Reform to Abolition Stage-6 Institutional Collapse in U.S. Immigration Enforcement

detail.title: From Reform to Abolition Stage-6 Institutional Collapse in U.S. Immigration Enforcement

declarations.funderStatement: Just me, one guy, pushing through the noise into clarity.

detail.abstract:
Debates over U.S. immigration enforcement are commonly framed as contests between reform and restriction. Yet in recent years, institutional behavior surrounding Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) increasingly exhibits a pattern in which reform language persists while operational behavior trends toward delegitimation and functional nullification. This paper argues that the relevant shift is not ideological but structural: once institutional legitimacy is withdrawn, reform ceases to operate as a stabilizing mechanism and becomes rhetorical residue.

Using a cross-institutional diagnostic framework, the paper examines political actions, media narrative posture, cultural spillover, and academic framing to identify what is termed a Stage-6 institutional collapse condition—a state in which enforcement is treated as presumptively illegitimate, reform proposals become non-compliable, and neutral institutions begin behaving defensively in anticipation of moral sanction. The analysis introduces a behavioral tool—the Non-Compliance Reform Test (NCRT)—to distinguish reforms that constrain institutions within legitimacy from proposals that would structurally eliminate their function.

The paper does not evaluate the morality, legality, or efficacy of immigration enforcement policy. Nor does it advocate for or against abolition. Its purpose is diagnostic: to map when institutional behavior has crossed from reform logic into post-reform dynamics. ICE is treated as a high-clarity case through which broader patterns of late-stage institutional delegitimation may be observed across contemporary governance domains.

title: Enabling Effective Communication: Metaverse Simulation for Accessible Job Applications for Women with Visual Impairments
affiliations: Universidad De San Martin De Porres, Universidad De San Martin De Porres, Universidad De San Martin De Porres, Universidad De San Martin De Porres, Universidad De San Martin De Porres, Universidad De San Martin De Porres, Universidad De San Martin De Porres, University of Missouri and University of Missouri

detail.title: Enabling Effective Communication: Metaverse Simulation for Accessible Job Applications for Women with Visual Impairments
detail.abstract: Introduction: Women with visual impairments (VI) continue to face persistent discrimination and structural barriers to employment, reflected in high inactivity rates and limited access to equitable recruitment processes. Negative employer perceptions, inaccessible information, ineffective communication practices, and poorly adapted physical environments contribute to systematic exclusion. Methodology: A four-stage methodological framework was implemented. First, a multidimensional contextual analysis was conducted, considering age and educational level. Second, statistical analyses were performed to identify significant associations. Third, a metaverse-based process model was designed to support accessible information management and effective communication. Finally, a functional simulation was developed. Results: The findings reveal statistically significant associations between age and optimism about the future, as well as moderate-to-high effect sizes related to perceptions of inclusion and attitudes towards technology. Educational level shows a strong association with self-perceived personal value and satisfaction with institutional support. A comparative analysis with generative AI tools indicates that the proposed metaverse model offers a more comprehensive set of accessibility and communication functionalities for job applications and interviews. Discussion: The results underscore the need for structured dialogue protocols, mobility assistance mechanisms, and proactive workplace design strategies. While generative AI tools provide partial support, the metaverse-based approach enables an integrated simulation of recruitment, mobility, and workplace accessibility. Conclusions: This study presents a novel technology-driven framework that promotes both technological and cultural awareness to reduce communicational, physical, and procedural barriers in employment contexts. The proposed model provides a robust foundation for future inclusive recruitment initiatives.

title: Pricing and Production Without The Invisible Hand
affiliations: Yale University,  and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Pricing and Production Without The Invisible Hand
detail.abstract: Modern theories of the business cycle do not allow for the simultaneous rational choice of both prices and quantities, instead assuming that an "invisible hand" determines one of these variables to clear markets. In this paper, we develop a macroeconomic framework in which both prices and quantities are chosen directly by firms, and exchange is both voluntary and efficient. Because of uncertainty about demand and productivity, individual product markets can be in excess supply or rationed. The absence of market-clearing changes pricing and production in qualitatively important ways: markups are no longer determined solely by the elasticity of demand, and higher uncertainty reduces production and increases markups. In equilibrium, production in rationed markets has a negative aggregate demand externality on demand in slack markets. Differently from New Keynesian economies, monetary shocks propagate by reducing economic slack, raising aggregate labor productivity and consumption, while uncertainty shocks act as stagflationary cost-push shocks. We integrate our theory of disequilibrium in a dynamic, rational-expectations "New Old Keynesian Model" and demonstrate its implications for the business cycle.

detail.title: Evaluating How Wireless Emergency Alerts Support Information Processing: An Experimental Study of Young Adults in South Korea
detail.abstract: Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEAs) are one of disaster response infrastructure to facilitate risk communication and enhance community resilience. By providing real-time hazardous information, WEAs enable individuals to make critical safety decisions during emergencies.  Here, the COVID-19 pandemic has significantly altered public risk perceptions and expectations regarding the reliability and utility of these systems. This study examined the effectiveness of current WEA systems through the lens of human information processing, focusing on their role in emergency management. In an experiment, a total of 39 participants were exposed to simulated disaster scenarios (COVID-19 and Avian Influenza) to assess the WEA system’s impact on cognitive and emotional aspects. Results indicate that while current WEA designs effectively provide essential information for disaster response, their impact is mediated by specific stages of information processing. Situation awareness was observed as the most significant predictor of WEA effectiveness, suggesting that resilience in emergency management is deeply rooted in the cognitive clarity provided to the end-user. These findings provide insights for designing resilient emergency alert systems that can adapt to evolving public expectations.

title: Risk Management: From Portfolio Strategy to Value-creating Systems Strategy
affiliations: George Mason University - Interdisciplinary Center for Economic Science, Swedbank and Independent

detail.title: Risk Management: From Portfolio Strategy to Value-creating Systems Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper is concerned with those actions of business firms which are aimed at managing the business and economic risks and uncertainties. The standard example of risk management is finance and insurance but these only capture a small fraction of the business risk faced by a company in a competitive market. These "standard" risks are often dealt with through specialized activities but here what the firms do to manage their total "market access risks" is discussed. The analysis goes beyond, but includes, and builds on, insurable and financial risks to include risks in the firm's customer's processes, the use of IT in this process, and the economic system. The issues explored are: understanding the "new business logic" and its risk; how offerings have become service offerings; management of risk and uncertainty in a more systemic way. A new "risk map" is presented as a tool to analyze the management of risk in a "systemic" context argued to be more relevant to today's risk management challenges. This new, broader scope has new demands on knowledge and systems for effective management. As a conclusion, five historic steps are identified, tied to the new risk map, which show the gradual build-up of the product offering to a service offering and its actions to manage, and ultimately price, the risk management in the offering.

detail.abstract: Early 2026 marks a structural break: intelligence has become a metered commodity, while human intent, verification capacity, and energy throughput emerge as binding constraints. This paper develops the Intent Theory of Value (ITV), a macroeconomic framework for an economy where synthetic cognition is abundant but accountable decision capacity is scarce. Four empirical pillars motivate the model: wage inversion and heterogeneous task complexity make substitution operational yet smooth in aggregate; elastic substitution in the execution composite implies endogenous expansion of cognition as its price falls; frontier compute markets remain concentrated because quality competition requires large sunk costs; and verification capital prevents a lemons collapse. Output is modeled with a nested CES in which intent and execution are highly complementary, and energy binds synthetic execution through powered compute. Intent is measured via rational inattention rather than nominal spending. The labor market follows a search-and-matching structure to capture displacement frictions. Public finance respects Diamond-Mirrlees production efficiency by taxing value added and inelastic inputs, financing a Universal Basic Yield (UBY) whose income effects are modeled explicitly. Internationally, a spatial-equilibrium lens explains compute havens and verification bottlenecks. The result is a tractable macro framework with testable predictions for the post-AGI economy.

title: Decision Compression and Escalation Risk in AI-Enabled Military Command and Control: An Operational Analysis of the ERAM Framework

detail.title: Decision Compression and Escalation Risk in AI-Enabled Military Command and Control: An Operational Analysis of the ERAM Framework

detail.abstract:
Advances in AI-enabled military command and control (C2) systems are compressing operational decision timelines to the point where the time available to detect, classify, and respond to threats (TavailT_{avail}​) approaches or falls below the time required for system processing and meaningful human verification (TreqT_{req}​). This paper defines decision compression as the condition Tavail<TreqT_{avail} < T_{req}​ and argues that such temporal divergence systematically increases the risk of inadvertent escalation in tightly coupled, complex military systems.

To operationalize this risk, the paper introduces the Escalation Risk Assessment Model (ERAM), which estimates the probability of unintended engagement (PEP_E​) as a bounded function of temporal coupling (KK), interaction complexity (XX), ambiguity rate (λ\rho), and architectural robustness (RR). The framework is grounded in physics-based constraints on engagement timelines, including radar horizon geometry and interceptor fly-out dynamics, and is evaluated through sensitivity analysis and fully worked operational examples.

Application of ERAM to missile defense and autonomous engagement scenarios shows that escalation risk rises sharply under high coupling and low robustness, even absent operator error or malicious intent. The analysis further demonstrates that run-time assurance and supervisory control architectures can substantially mitigate this risk by increasing system robustness without sacrificing operational tempo.

title: Drivers of Technological Co-Evolution in Modular Systems of Products and Processes
affiliations: National Research Council of Italy (CNR)

detail.title: Drivers of Technological Co-Evolution in Modular Systems of Products and Processes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE

declarations.funderStatement: no funding for this study

detail.abstract:
Goal :This study investigates the mechanisms driving technological change in complex systems. It examines how the evolution of embedded subsystems shapes the overall trajectory and tempo of a host technology.

Background: Drawing on the theory of technological parasitism, the research conceptualizes modular host systems—such as smartphones—as evolving through dynamic, co‑evolutionary interactions with their subsystems. These interactions shift from parasitic dependence to mutualistic and eventually symbiotic integration. Central to this framework is the role of subsystems as temporal pacemakers that dictate system‑wide innovation rhythms.

Methods: The study utilizes a longitudinal, mixed‑methods design, combining an 18‑year case study of the iPhone (2007–2025) with time‑series regression and log‑log hedonic pricing models. The dataset tracks subsystem performance trajectories and price‑performance dynamics across multiple technological generations.

Results: The research identifies three key phenomena:

  1. Temporal Precedence: Subsystem advances (notably Bluetooth protocol upgrades) consistently precede host‑system releases. Integration lags have shrunk significantly, moving from a three-year window to just one.
  2. Differential Evolutionary Pressure: While camera resolution exhibits rapid exponential improvement, it remains a secondary driver of total system evolution.
  3. Economic Pacemakers: Battery life exerts the strongest economic influence; a 1% performance gain predicts a 0.3% rise in nominal price, whereas display and camera improvements show weaker correlations.

Discussion: The findings reveal that subsystems evolve at heterogeneous speeds and exert unequal systemic leverage. Their evolutionary tempo serves as a leading indicator for host-system transitions, highlighting the asynchronous dynamics inherent in modular architectures.

Implications & Originality: This research advances evolutionary theories of modular innovation by establishing subsystem evolution as a governing mechanism of system-level change.

  • For Strategists: It provides new design rules for forecasting technological generations.
  • For R&D: It assists in prioritization by identifying which subsystems function as strategic pacemakers in complex innovations.

title: Access to Finance -Credit Augmented Per Capita Income: A Framework for Measuring Economic Wellbeing
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY), Stony Brook

detail.title: Access to Finance -Credit Augmented Per Capita Income: A Framework for Measuring Economic Wellbeing
detail.abstract: Traditional measures of per capita income, including GDP per capita and PPP-adjusted variants, fail to account for a critical dimension of economic capacity: access to financing and financial infrastructure. This paper proposes a novel framework-Credit-Augmented Per Capita Income (CAPCI)-which adjusts nominal income by a Finance Access Multiplier (FAM) derived from household debt-to-income ratios and financial inclusion metrics. Using data from the World Bank, IMF, and academic sources, we demonstrate that finance access effectively allows individuals in developed economies to "pull future earnings into the present," creating a temporal arbitrage effect that dramatically amplifies economic capacity relative to counterparts in developing regions. Our illustrative calculations suggest that the true economic disparity between developed economies (e.g., USA) and developing regions (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa) is approximately 74% greater than nominal per capita income figures suggest—rising from a 53× nominal gap to approximately 92× when finance access is properly factored in with a credit discount coefficient. This finding has significant implications for understanding the relevance and imperative for financial inclusion and its relation to global inequality and designing development policy initiatives to incentivize growth. A Critical Distinction: Household Finance vs. Sovereign Debt. It is essential to distinguish the framework proposed here from advocacy for increased sovereign borrowing. Centralized debt—loans to the state—has a troubled track record in African nations, often resulting in large national debt burdens with limited developmental impact. Our framework is fundamentally different: we advocate for empowerment of individuals, households, and communities through access to personal and business financing infrastructure. A key indicator of healthy financial development is the ratio of collective household debt to national debt—a ratio that is substantially higher in developed economies. When households can access mortgages, business loans, entrepreneurship capital, and consumer finance, economic capacity is distributed and multiplied at the grassroots level, rather than concentrated in state apparatus. This distributed (decentralized) approach to financial empowerment represents a fundamentally different path to development than sovereign borrowing.

title: Training Frontline Health Workers in LMICs to Reduce Contraceptive Stock-outs: Evidence from Indonesia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest

detail.abstract: Frontline health workers are an indispensable asset in the healthcare ecosystem of low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). They not only provide clinical care to patients but also frequently shoulder non-clinical responsibilities such as inventory management. However, many lack the necessary skills to effectively manage inventories, leading to the pervasive problem of health commodity stock-outs. To address this problem, several LMICs have launched training programs aimed at enhancing the inventory management skills and capabilities of frontline health workers. Leveraging fine-grained data over a five-year period (2015-2019) from approximately 17,000 health facilities across Indonesia-where the public health supply chain operates as a hybrid push-pull model-we evaluate the impact of a large-scale inventory management training program on contraceptive stock-outs. Applying difference-in-differences estimations, we find that the training program is associated with a significant reduction in stock-outs (i.e., 6.52 percentage-points or approximately 30%). Our numerical calculations suggest that the training program prevents, on average, more than 800 unintended pregnancies and saves 4.25 maternal and newborn lives per 100,000 women of reproductive age within the catchment area of a treated health facility. A counterfactual benefit-cost analysis shows that onsite delivery of the training program (i.e., on-the-job within a facility) yields operational and public health benefits that significantly exceed those achieved through offsite delivery (i.e., outside the facility in a classroom). Our research highlights the practicality and scalability of human-capital-focused interventions in improving health commodity availability and public health outcomes in LMICs.

title: Matching Technology, Fleet Size, and Passenger Wait in Ride-Hailing Markets
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Operations and Information Management and University of California, Riverside (UCR) - A. Gary Anderson Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Matching Technology, Fleet Size, and Passenger Wait in Ride-Hailing Markets
detail.abstract: This paper studies how matching technology shapes the distribution of passenger waiting times in ride-hailing markets. We study two canonical matching technologies—street-hailing and central dispatch—and develop tractable approximations for the entire distribution of passenger wait under each. To arrive at our approximations, we model a city as a square grid of identical locations where passengers arrive randomly and drivers are uniformly distributed. With street-hailing, drivers search for passengers without information about their locations and move according to a random walk; with central dispatch, the platform assigns arriving passengers to nearby idle drivers and directs them along shortest paths to pickup locations. Within this framework, we derive a novel approximation for the distribution of passenger wait under street-hailing and extend a well-established approximation for central dispatch to the grid setting. We validate both approximations using extensive simulation. The resulting approximations are closed-form and interpretable, allowing platforms to define a variety of performance metrics and develop strategies for achieving them. This affords platforms greater flexibility than analytical approaches that characterize only average wait or rely on computationally intensive simulation. Moreover, our approximations allow for nuanced comparison of the two matching technologies considered. While central dispatch achieves lower average wait with fewer drivers, comparing distributions reveals a short-wait advantage of street-hailing: when mean wait is held fixed, street-hailing produces more frequent shorter-than-average waits. We discuss the implications for platform matching technology choices and ride-hailing market equilibria.

detail.abstract: Bee Natural Uganda, Ltd. (BNU) is the largest producer of quality honey and honey products in Uganda, selling 61 tonnes of honey in 2012 with an average growth in sales of 20% per year. BNU's unique business model follows their honey from the hives of smallholder farmers trained by BNU to a state of the art processing facility in Arua, West Nile, Uganda. The company attributes its success to this model, which allows employees to continue checking the quality of their product at every step leading to the sale of BNU's products. In a highly competitive honey market, this consistency in quality has set BNU high above their competition. As Bee Natural Uganda looks to the future, management must develop a strategy to overcome the challenges associated with continued growth and unmet demand in Uganda and the East Africa region.
