detail.title: Vertical Integration and Executive Compensation Arrangements
detail.abstract: This paper examines how a firm's degree of vertical integration influences the design of executive performance measurement systems. Building on the theory of the "metering problem" in team production (Alchian and Demsetz 1972), we argue that operating across vertically related product markets reduces contracting frictions with supply chain partners, lowers noise in financial performance, and increases the informativeness of accounting metrics. Consistent with this view, we find that both the sensitivity of executive pay to accounting earnings and the reliance on accounting-based measures in compensation contracts increase with vertical integration. These effects are stronger when firms have weaker bargaining power relative to supply chain partners and when adjacent vertical markets exhibit lower earnings volatility. We also find that vertical integration substitutes for other performance measures and shifts board functions toward a more advisory role. Overall, our findings highlight vertical integration as a governance mechanism that complements accounting-based incentives.

title: The Shift to Digital Payments: Effects on Spending, Saving and Investment Behaviour
affiliations: BRCM College of Business Administration and B.R.C.M. College of Business Administration

detail.title: The Shift to Digital Payments: Effects on Spending, Saving and Investment Behaviour

publicationDetails.detailsText: VNSGU Journal of Management and Administration

detail.abstract:
Emerging technology in the payment system in India, the shift to Digital payments, is of significant importance to individuals as well as the economy. Digital payments accelerated the rate of financial inclusion in the economy, leading to smoother and more transparent transactions, which reduces the chances of tax evasion, also reducing cash dependency. Digital payments not only equip an individual with the ease and convenience of making a payment but also the highest possible level of security to an individual. 

The modes of digital payments have evolved in the 1980s from plastic money, i.e. credit and debit cards, to improvised and online versions like NEFT, RTGS, online banking and some of the world’s most secure systems like UPI with a user-friendly interface in India. Digital payments, being of such convenience and use to an individual, also changed the financial behaviour of an individual, given the less friction and the security. This paper attempts to study a relation between the usage of digital payments and Spending, Saving and Investment Behaviour. The findings and conclusion of the paper are based on the survey of 200 respondents in Surat city.

title: Regulatory Stringency and Industry Performance: Evidence from RegData U.S. 6.0
affiliations: and Stanford University - Hoover Institution

detail.title: Regulatory Stringency and Industry Performance: Evidence from RegData U.S. 6.0
detail.abstract: This paper studies the economic incidence of broad federal regulation across U.S. industries using RegData U.S. 6.0. We measure regulatory stringency using binding language densityexpected regulatory restrictions per 1,000 words-constructed from the text of the Code of Federal Regulations and mapped to NAICS industries using supervised relevance weights. Using the 1970-2025 regulatory panel, we document three stylized facts: (1) binding density evolves through many small year-to-year adjustments and a recent plateauing in 2025; (2) short-run changes are across industries rather than concentrated in a small set of sectors; and (3) annual changes are weakly related to baseline industry size and productivity. We also validate the normalized measure by showing that treated industries exhibit clear and persistent increases in binding density around major legislative events. Linking within-industry variation in binding density to Bureau of Economic Analysis measures of real output and real value added for three-digit NAICS industries over 1998-2024, we find that a one-unit increase in restrictions per 1,000 words is associated with approximately a 0.7 percent decline in real output and a 1.2 percent decline in real value added. The relationship persists in distributedlag specifications and is robust across alternative functional forms. These findings suggest that normalized regulatory text captures economically meaningful shifts in the regulatory environment and provides a scalable framework for studying their economic effects.

title: How to (and How Not to) Increase Free-Shipping Thresholds: Evidence from Online Retail
affiliations: McGill University - Desautels Faculty of Management, , McGill University - Desautels Faculty of Management and McGill University

detail.title: How to (and How Not to) Increase Free-Shipping Thresholds: Evidence from Online Retail
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Contingent free shipping (CFS) policies are widely used by e-commerce platforms to encourage larger cart values, yet platforms increasingly struggle with how to adjust these thresholds in response to rising fulfillment costs. This paper examines how increasing the CFS threshold affects consumer behavior and derives conditions under which such an increase is optimal for the platform. Methodology: Using detailed transaction and clickstream data from a North American online grocery platform, we analyze a threshold increase from $80 to $100 by employing a difference-in-differences design. Results: We find that raising the CFS threshold results in a 19.4% decline in consumer spending, driven primarily by a reduction in average cart value and, to a lesser extent, a decline in purchase frequency. Consumers also purchase fewer distinct products, shift to lower-priced items, and reduce their share of spending on popular products. We identify two mechanisms underlying these responses. First, the original threshold serves as a reference point, making the new threshold feel less attainable and weakening top-up behavior. Second, consumers with high search effort face disproportionate difficulty reaching the higher threshold and are more likely to reduce or abandon their basket. Managerial implications: To assess the implications for optimal policy design, we develop a stylized analytical model that captures both cost-and demand-side factors associated with increasing the CFS threshold. We find that it is optimal to increase the CFS threshold only when the average cart value is sufficiently close to the original threshold. This result aligns closely with our empirical findings and remains robust to extensions that incorporate consumer heterogeneity.

title: To Disclose or not to Disclose? Reputational incentives and ESG Disclosure in Private Family Firms
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Accounting, China Europe International Business School - Accounting & Finance Department, , Bocconi University and Bocconi University

detail.title: To Disclose or not to Disclose? Reputational incentives and ESG Disclosure in Private Family Firms
detail.abstract: This study examines how reputation linked to family identity affects voluntary ESG disclosure in private family firms, focusing on eponymous firms-those named after their founders or controlling families. Drawing on legitimacy theory, we argue that when family and firm identities are closely aligned, ESG disclosure serves to protect and signal legitimacy to external stakeholders. Using a sample of 2,769 Italian private family firms from 2013 to 2021, we find that eponymous firms are significantly more likely to publish ESG reports. The effect is stronger when reputational exposure is higher, including cases of rarer surnames, greater press visibility, and more positive prior media sentiment. Eponymous firms also report more substantive ESG actions-particularly in social and environmental domains-and exhibit lower realized environmental impact, suggesting that disclosure reflects genuine engagement rather than symbolic reporting. Robustness tests address alternative governance, visibility, reporting standardization, and selection explanations. Overall, the evidence indicates that owner identity, reputation, and legitimacy concerns jointly shape voluntary ESG disclosure and sustainability outcomes in private family firms.

title: From Ideal to Non-Ideal AI Ethics: Towards Adaptive Governance Through Checks and Balances

detail.title: From Ideal to Non-Ideal AI Ethics: Towards Adaptive Governance Through Checks and Balances

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: The author is employed as a PhD researcher at Copenhagen Business School. This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Governance of AI is frequently articulated through high-level normative principles intended to guide diverse applications and jurisdictions. While such "ideal theoretical" approaches offer conceptual clarity, their reliance on abstraction can obscure the institutional, political, and technological conditions under which AI systems are developed and deployed. This risks a detachment between principles and practice, resulting in vague guidance and limited compliance. In contrast, the non-ideal approach defended here emphasizes feasibility, context sensitivity, empirical grounding, and the problem of non-compliance, proposing a model of governance rooted in the diverse realities of AI development and deployment. Here, governance is conceived as an institutional system of mutual constraints, in which principles, sectoral integration, and stakeholder engagement function as checks on one another. However, such a non-ideal approach faces challenges arising from uncertainty within a rapidly evolving socio-technical landscape. The proposed solution entails an adaptive framework operating through a polycentric system of checks and balances, enabling the real-time identification of emerging risks and techno-moral shifts amid the rapid deployment of generative and frontier AI systems. In doing so, this framework both generates epistemically relevant moral data and functions as a dynamic governance mechanism capable of co-evolving with changing institutional, technological, and moral conditions across diverse contexts of AI deployment.

title: Reflexive Valuation Operator Theory (RVOT): A Unified Framework for Endogenous Pricing, Return Predictability, and Intermediary-Driven Equilibrium
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Reflexive Valuation Operator Theory (RVOT): A Unified Framework for Endogenous Pricing, Return Predictability, and Intermediary-Driven Equilibrium
detail.abstract: We develop Reflexive Valuation Operator Theory (RVOT), a framework in which asset prices are fixed points of a valuation operator that augments the classical stochastic discount factor (SDF) recursion with a pressure distortion driven by intermediary balance-sheet constraints and institutional flows. The central design choice-anchoring the distortion to an exogenous benchmark P ⋆ t rather than the endogenous price-delivers exact cancellation in the contraction comparison, yielding a sharp payout-discipline condition for equilibrium existence and uniqueness. The empirically operative result is localized: uniqueness holds on any bounded valuation set M K with θ K > 0; as θ K ↓ 0 the model transitions from uniqueness to multiplicity to rational bubble feasibility, with the non-contractive boundary characterized by Schauder's theorem. The theory delivers five main results beyond existence: a closed-form return decomposition into fundamental, SDF, payout, and pressure channels; a predictability threshold linking pressure mean reversion to long-horizon R 2 ; a rational bubble characterization via an augmented transversality condition; cross-asset spillover dynamics governed by a pressure Jacobian; and a nonlinear BSDE continuous-time limit with closed-form pricing PDE. We further provide a second-order welfare wedge from pressure-induced pecuniary externalities, and GMM and sieve estimators with asymptotic theory and a replicable empirical blueprint for U.S. equity data. Classical SDF pricing is nested as the zero-pressure special case.

title: Entry Mode, Risk Governance Intensity, and Project Failure: Evidence from Multinational Construction Firms
affiliations: University of Waterloo - School of Planning, University of Waterloo - School of Planning, University of Waterloo - School of Planning and University of Waterloo - School of Planning

detail.title: Entry Mode, Risk Governance Intensity, and Project Failure: Evidence from Multinational Construction Firms
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how entry mode and risk governance intensity jointly influence project failure in multinational construction firms. Using 214 overseas projects from 21 firms across 19 host countries between 2011 and 2022, we classify entry modes into wholly owned subsidiaries, joint ventures, and consortium-based contracts. A hierarchical panel-survival framework is developed to model the time to project failure, defined as severe cost overruns above 30%, contract termination, or unresolved payment disputes. Governance intensity is measured using a composite index that captures frequency of on-site risk reviews, budget monitoring, and compliance audits. The results show that joint ventures reduce project failure hazard by 17.4% relative to wholly owned subsidiaries, but only when governance intensity is above the sample median. For projects with weak governance, joint ventures display a 12.8% higher hazard due to coordination and accountability issues. Consortium-based contracts show the highest baseline hazard but experience a 21.3% reduction when coupled with integrated risk-compliance dashboards. Sensitivity analyses with shared frailty models and alternative failure thresholds confirm the robustness of the estimates. The study provides granular evidence on how multinational firms can align entry mode choices with risk governance strategies to reduce project failure in cross-border environments.

title: Spatial Optimization for Medication for Opioid use Disorder Facilities: Modeling Treatment Expansion
affiliations: University of Alabama and University of Alabama

detail.title: Spatial Optimization for Medication for Opioid use Disorder Facilities: Modeling Treatment Expansion
detail.abstract: Opioid and polydrug overdose deaths have increased drastically in the US, largely driven by the COVID-19 pandemic and the increasing toxicity of the drug supply. Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) with FDA approved methadone or buprenorphine is considered the most effective treatment for opioid use disorder. However, there is a scarcity of MOUD provider availability in the US. Recent research has found that a staggering 97% of buprenorphine providers across community types in the US are at their patient capacity limit. This work operationalizes location science in the context of opioid treatment resource allocation by applying the Maximum Covering Location Problem (MCLP) to optimize coverage of scarce MOUD resources, using Alabama as a case study. Further, to ensure the allocation of MOUD resources across urban, suburban, and rural community types, a novel variation of the Multiple Type-MCLP optimization problem is presented to incorporate facility types. This work provides a road map to begin improving access to buprenorphine via data-driven intervention planning. Further, research findings demonstrate a comparable amount of coverage can be achieved when facilities are strategically distributed outside of urban areas. This result is important given that suburban and rural communities have experienced a disproportionate burden of opioid overdoses, while these same communities predominantly have low or no accessibility to treatment resources. These coordinated treatment allocation efforts can contribute to omitting treatment availability as an overarching constraint in curbing the opioid overdose epidemic.

title: Managerial Competence in International Projects in Medicine, Mental Health, and Developmental Neuropsychology: A Consensus-Assisted Literature Review
affiliations: Bogomolets National Medical University and Pylyp Orlyk International Classical University

detail.title: Managerial Competence in International Projects in Medicine, Mental Health, and Developmental Neuropsychology: A Consensus-Assisted Literature Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is theoretical in nature and does not involve human participants or personal data. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Managerial competence in international projects spanning medicine, mental health, developmental neuropsychology, and adjacent pharmaceutical systems has become a decisive determinant of implementation quality, ethical robustness, and sustainability. The contemporary project environment is defined by intensified interdisciplinarity, expanded digital infrastructures, growing dependence on distributed teams, and increasing scrutiny of governance, data quality, and mental health in the workplace. Against this background, the present review synthesises literature on the competence profile required of managers coordinating complex international initiatives across health-related domains. The review was conducted using an AI-assisted search workflow via Consensus, followed by staged screening and relevance-based selection. A broad search corpus (n = 1000 identified records) was reduced through screening (n = 797), eligibility assessment (n = 280), and final inclusion of the 20 most relevant publications. The included works comprise conceptual and empirical studies, scoping reviews, mapping reviews, practice-oriented reviews, and conference abstracts, with evidence drawn not only from health and mental health settings but also from adjacent project-intensive sectors where managerial mental health and governance have been modelled in detail. The synthesis identifies a multi-domain competence architecture comprising foundational (scientific literacy, ethics, diversity and interculturality, systems thinking, reflective practice), functional (assessment, intervention coordination, consultation, advocacy), and operational-strategic (governance, stakeholder alignment, uncertainty management, digital/AI literacy, quality and risk management, communication architecture, and organisational climate stewardship) components. The findings further indicate that managerial competence is not reducible to generic project management skills; rather, it is an integrative capacity to govern interfaces across disciplinary, cultural, regulatory, technological, and psychosocial domains. Digital transformation and AI/LLM uptake are altering competence requirements, but the literature simultaneously highlights persistent risks associated with data governance, over-reliance on automated tools, and insufficient human-centred design. Major barriers include the absence of internationally harmonised competence standards, uneven evidence across subfields (especially developmental neuropsychology management and digital ethics implementation), and the under-theorisation of burnout prevention for project leaders in large, matrixed programmes. The article concludes by proposing an integrated competence framework and a set of research priorities for standard-setting, measurement development, and intervention studies. This synthesis is designed for Scopus-oriented scholarly use and may serve as a conceptual foundation for subsequent empirical and psychometric studies of managerial readiness in international health projects.

detail.abstract: In financial credit modeling it is common to transform variables from their raw state into weight of evidence (WOE) transformations for binary problems such as probability modeling. One advantage of using WOE is that it handles missing value, outliers, and categorical variables. It also reduces noise and provides an intuitive way of comparing the variables' predictive power as well as producing directional relationships. In this paper the examples and explanations will be from a finance credit modeling perspective. Instead of the common terms of "event" and "nonevent" for modeling a binary outcome, the term "bad" will be used for the event of a loan default and the term "good" will be used for non-defaulted loan. WOE is used in many industries however this paper is using finance to create a more tangible example.

title: Selling the Haggle
affiliations: , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management,  and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Selling the Haggle
detail.abstract: Price haggling is widely viewed as a source of friction in retail markets: customers bear bargaining costs, and firms face operational complexity. This logic has motivated some firms to adopt fixed pricing. We show that in markets organized around personal selling, eliminating negotiation can backfire. Using lead and transaction data from a major automaker in China that introduced a one-price policy for one model while retaining negotiation for all others at the same dealerships, we find that the policy reduced sales of the targeted model and shifted demand toward models where negotiation remained available. Notably, although the fixed price was below the prior average negotiated price at most dealerships, the pattern persists within this subgroup. We argue that the process of negotiation serves as an effective deal closing tool for the salesperson. When this instrument is removed for one product, salespeople become less equipped to convert leads into sales and may redirect customers toward products for which negotiation remains available. Consistent with this mechanism, demand switching is larger among salespeople who relied more heavily on price discussion prior to the policy. These findings suggest that, beyond negotiation outcomes external to the firm (such as customer disutility, price dispersion, or surplus extraction), an internal organizational factor also matters when evaluating pricing regimes: the salesforce, whose ability to haggle often serves as the instrument that closes the deal.

detail.abstract: The GOD Formula presents a theoretical model of societal evolution wherein future outcomes emerge as exponential functions of human and technological potential, balanced by moral and equitable stabilizers. The core equation proposes: This model posits that societal collapse occurs not from technological advancement itself, but from imbalances in moral frameworks (Virtue) and systemic fairness (Equity). Empirical validation draws from post-2001 U.S. religious decline patterns, deaths of despair epidemiology, and historical empire collapse studies. Data show Christian identi cation declined from 78% (2007) to 62% (2023-24), while deaths of despair increased 2.5-fold from 1999 to 2021, reaching fth leading cause of death status[1][2]. Historical analysis reveals inequality patterns preceding major empire collapses, with Gini coe cients correlating with political instability[3]. The formula implies that advancing technology requires proportional scaling of virtue-based ethics and equity-based rights protections to prevent systemic failure.

title: Developmental Uncertainty: When Coordination Demands Enable Occupational Mobility Across Status Boundaries
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - College of Engineering and

detail.title: Developmental Uncertainty: When Coordination Demands Enable Occupational Mobility Across Status Boundaries
detail.abstract: Organizations struggle to develop professional talent while workers without credentials struggle to obtain it-a structural mismatch with consequences for firms, workers, and the economy. Nonprofessionals increasingly work alongside professionals in technology development, but prior work is pessimistic about implications for skill development: status boundaries are defended, knowledge is hoarded, and inclusion efforts tend toward extraction rather than development. We theorize a striking exception. In a three-year field study of an AI-enabled robotics vendor, nonprofessional "drivers" who joined during high-uncertainty phases built substantial technical skills-76% advanced to professional roles, with 19% moving into positions typically requiring credentials they lacked. Workers who joined later, with identical job design, had far more limited development. Drawing on contingency theory, we identify developmental uncertainty: uncertainty drives cross-boundary coordination that enables skill transfer and occupational mobility across status boundaries. As uncertainty is consumed and encoded into automation, coordination demands decline, boundaries harden, and the developmental window closes. We draw on 145 interviews, 17 months of observation, and 29 million records of human-robot interaction to document this process. The findings offer rare leverage on the talent mismatch problem-but only for those who recognize the window while it remains open.

title: Standardizing Laboratory Data for Interoperability: Challenges and Lessons Learned from LOINC Implementation in Singapore

detail.title: Standardizing Laboratory Data for Interoperability: Challenges and Lessons Learned from LOINC Implementation in Singapore
detail.abstract: Background: Standardization of laboratory test data is crucial for ensuring interoperability, clinical decision support and allows comparability of results across systems or over time. In Singapore, the segregation of healthcare clusters created challenges for national data integration due to diverse healthcare information systems across different clusters. In line with a national directive emphasizing interoperability, Synapxe undertook the implementation of Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes (LOINC) to standardize laboratory test data across multiple Public Healthcare Institutions (PHIs) in Singapore. Methods: A phased implementation approach was adopted, with individual PHIs implementing separate deployments rather than a coordinated national rollout. Mapping was performed collaboratively by laboratory medical technologists, informatics specialists, and consulting clinicians to ensure clinical and operational accuracy. Training sessions were conducted, emphasizing accurate coding and maintenance of data quality. Laboratory data was collected from 14 PHIs and mapped systematically. The LOINC-mapped data was integrated successfully into healthcare systems, and validation activities ensured all existing data flows remained unaffected. Results: As of March 2025, all 14 PHIs are LOINC-live with a collective 90.1% of laboratory tests mapped. Key challenges included limited human resources due to competing demands from the COVID-19 pandemic response and concurrent EMR system upgrades, organizational resistance and knowledge gaps among laboratory and informatics staff, and technical complexities in laboratory-to-electronic health record interfacing. To address these challenges, targeted interventions such as deployment of semi-automated tools, proactive stakeholder communication, and interdisciplinary training were employed. Some lessons learned from the implementation journey included the importance of early stakeholder engagement for establishment of clear roles and pre-emptive data quality checks. Conclusion: LOINC implementation in Singapore led to improved data consistency, regulatory compliance, and readiness for secondary uses such as clinical analytics and disease surveillance. The experiences and lessons outlined in this paper provide valuable insights for healthcare institutions embarking on similar laboratory data standardization initiatives.

title: Design and Implementation of an Intelligent Mineral Prospecting System Integrating Large Language Models: GoldMiner-AI
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU)

detail.title: Design and Implementation of an Intelligent Mineral Prospecting System Integrating Large Language Models: GoldMiner-AI
detail.abstract: Current intelligent mineral prospecting faces systemic challenges: fragmented data sources, disconnected analytical workflows, poorly organized knowledge, and a lack of automated, reproducible, and traceable processes at the system level. To overcome these limitations, we present GoldMiner-AI, an end-to-end intelligent system engineered for mineral exploration tasks. The system leverages a RuoYi-Cloud-Plus microservice architecture and a collaborative multi-database framework (PostGIS, Neo4j, Milvus, MySQL) to unify the management of multi-source, heterogeneous geoscientific data spanning geological maps, geochemical and geophysical surveys, drilling logs, field observations, and textual reports. Its intelligent core integrates two key components: the KAR-Graph anomaly identification framework and the deep learning model for multi-source feature fusion. Coupled with a mineral-systems knowledge graph and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), this architecture supports a domain-tailored large language model (LLM). This design establishes a closed-loop intelligent workflow that integrates anomaly detection, target delineation, knowledge-aided reasoning, and interactive Q&A. Validation experiments in representative ore districts (Youjiang Basin and southern Qin-Hang metallogenic belt) demonstrate that: (1) It effectively identifies Carlin-type gold-related Au-As-Sb-Hg anomalous assemblages and extracts diagnostic geochemical fingerprints of ore-forming processes; (2) Through multi-source data fusion, it accurately predicts the spatial distribution of Pb-Zn mineralization zones; and (3) The domain-specific LLM mitigates the “hallucination” common in general-purpose models, significantly improving the accuracy of geoscientific knowledge retrieval and Q&A. Collectively, GoldMiner-AI provides a reproducible, scalable, and production-ready platform that advances mineral exploration toward fully intelligent and systematic workflows.

title: CausLab: LLM-driven Multi-agent Bayesian Framework for Causal Discovery and Inference
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, Faculty of Business and Economics, Students, The University of Hong Kong, Tencent Weixin Group and Tencent Weixin Group

detail.title: CausLab: LLM-driven Multi-agent Bayesian Framework for Causal Discovery and Inference
detail.abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), known as A/B tests in industry, reliably estimate treatment effects. However, uncovering causal mechanisms underlying observed lifts and transferring those insights to guide future product decisions remain major challenges at scale. We propose CausLab, an LLM-driven multi-agent Bayesian framework for joint causal discovery and causal inference from longitudinal experimentation data. CausLab accounts for temporal drift and heterogeneous treatment effects across user groups by partitioning experiments both by user subgroup and over time. Earlier experiments form a prior dataset, from which an LLM-based reasoning agent extracts, clusters, and filters a compact set of interpretable causal factors for each subgroup. Using more recent experiments, a Bayesian inference module supported by an LLMbased evaluation agent updates beliefs about factor contributions and enables treatment-effect inference for new interventions. We evaluate CausLab on large-scale real-world WeChat experiments. Compared with baseline methods, CausLab improves estimation accuracy for causal inference on new treatments by 39.0% and increases downstream click prediction AUC by 10.23% by incorporating the discovered causal factors as additional user features.

title: Strengthening Continuity of Care during Infectious Disease Emergencies: An ISO 22301–based Business Continuity Maturity Roadmap with Digital and AI Enablers
affiliations: Shaqra University

detail.title: Strengthening Continuity of Care during Infectious Disease Emergencies: An ISO 22301–based Business Continuity Maturity Roadmap with Digital and AI Enablers
detail.abstract:
Background: Continuity of care during infectious disease emergencies depends on resilient operations, digital infrastructure, and prepared staff, yet BCMS implementation is often fragmented. 

Methods: We developed an ISO 22301–aligned BCMS framework integrating evidence synthesis, a five-level maturity model, tiered critical-service recovery targets (RTO/RPO), and a 36-month implementation roadmap with digital enablement and optional AI modules. The framework was implemented in 12 healthcare organizations and evaluated using incident/downtime logs, recovery metrics, staff readiness surveys, ISO 22301 clause-fulfillment audits, and a cost-of-disruption model.
 
Results: Mean total downtime incidents decreased by 53% (40–62%), with a 67% reduction in Tier-1 critical disruptions. RPO achievement improved from 51% to 93%; downtime procedure compliance from 46% to 83%; and staff readiness from 51% to 93%. ISO 22301 fulfillment rose from 31% to 87%, while high-severity audit findings fell by 83%. BCMS maturity increased from 1.8 to 3.3 (1–5). Modeled payback was 19 months (14–24) with a 3-year ROI of 271% (127–412%). 

Conclusions: A staged, metrics-anchored ISO 22301 approach can reduce disruptions, improve recovery performance, and strengthen preparedness; prospective studies should evaluate AI-assisted risk forecasting and response orchestration.

title: Identification of Functional Components and Usability Requirements of a Digital Twin– Enabled Smart Care System in Long-Term Care Settings: A Formative Mixed-Methods Study
affiliations: Seoul National University - Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Kyungbok University, Seoul National University - Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Seoul National University - Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Seoul National University - Seoul National University Bundang Hospital and Seoul National University College of Medicine

detail.title: Identification of Functional Components and Usability Requirements of a Digital Twin– Enabled Smart Care System in Long-Term Care Settings: A Formative Mixed-Methods Study
detail.abstract:
Background: Long-term care (LTC) systems face growing pressures from population ageing, workforce shortages, and increasing care complexity. Digital twin–enabled smart care systems have been proposed as integrated information architectures to support continuous monitoring and workflow coordination in LTC settings. 
Objective: The objective of this study is to identify functional components and usability requirements of a digital twin–enabled smart care system in LTC environments and to assess perceived usefulness among frontline professionals. 
Methods: This formative mixed-methods study involved a retrospective secondary analysis of advisory interview data collected during system development. Nineteen LTC professionals (physicians, registered nurses, nursing assistants, and care workers) from facilities in Seoul, Gyeonggi-do, and Gangwon-do completed a structured questionnaire (five-point Likert scales) and provided open-ended responses. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. 
Results: All participants agreed that the system would benefit both residents and care providers. Workload redistribution was most frequently endorsed (100%), followed by improved health management (89%) and workflow effectiveness (79%). Real-time physiological monitoring received the highest usefulness rating (mean 4.80 ± 0.42). Fall incident alerts (4.90 ± 0.23) and fall-risk alerts (4.80 ± 0.37) were prioritized. Qualitative findings highlighted five themes: workflow redistribution, proactive risk management, usability requirements, technical reliability and cost concerns, and tensions between standardized monitoring and individualized care.
Conclusions: LTC professionals prioritized safety-oriented monitoring, alert functions, and EMR interoperability within a digital twin–enabled architecture. Perceived benefits were contingent on workflow integration, usability, and reliability. These findings provide actionable design guidance for implementing interoperable smart care systems in LTC settings.

title: Effectiveness Of E-Services On Hr Administrations: A Study Based On Sri Lanka Army Central Human Resources Management System (CHRMS)

detail.abstract: Central Human Resources Management System (CHRMS) is one such tool powered by ICT and used in e-Government implementations for Personnel Management or Human Resource Management in any organization. From the perspective of military organizations, commonly known as Armed Forces, Human Resources Management is of utmost importance, while ensuring legal confidentiality and security becomes a massive operation due to its organizational structure and strength. There are many new technologies available as IT applications to easy of administrative activities more efficient. In the Sri Lankan Army as a major Armed Force on the island, personnel management is one of the key activities that is used to maintain proper administration among various internal establishments with several procedures. In the Sri Lankan Army, CHRMS is the primary software system that aids military administrations in HR management. By evaluating CHRMS, it can be found the effectiveness of e-services on HR administrations whether the Army is satisfied or not with the CHRMS. It was anticipated that the existing manual system in the Sri Lankan Army should be extensively adopted and used efficiently if it is to provide the projected benefits to the organization as e-services. This research is based on the deductive approach and concentrates on quantitative approaches in the appropriate stages. For data collection, use multi-methods such as interviews, questionnaires, and document reviews. This research identified there are 7 prominent factors (Top management support, User training and technical support, ICT infrastructure, System usefulness, System user-friendliness, User’s computer self-efficacy, and User’s change reluctance) related to the effectiveness of e-services on military HR administrations and surveyed to identify the actual impact due to the said factors in the context of the Sri Lanka Army. The collected facts were used to perform an analysis of the effectiveness of e-services on military HR administrations using CHRMS in the Sri Lankan Army. The findings highlighted that all seven factors are influenced by the effectiveness of e-services on military HR administration using CHRMS in the Sri Lanka Army, as hypothesized. Keywords: media, communication, information, technology, e-government, e-services.

detail.title: Enhancing Disaster Management and Emergency Response in the Utility Sector through Information Systems: A Case Study of the Maldives
detail.abstract:
The increasing frequency and severity of natural and technological disasters underscore the urgent need for effective disaster management and emergency response strategies, particularly in Small Island Developing States (SIDS) such as the Maldives. This study examines the role of Information Systems (IS) in enhancing disaster preparedness, response, and resilience within the utility sector, focusing on electricity and water services in the Greater Malé Region. These sectors are critical for ensuring continuity of essential services during crises, and their disruption can severely hinder immediate response and long-term recovery.

Using a qualitative approach, data was collected through semi-structured interviews with senior stakeholders from key utilities. The findings highlight systemic challenges, including fragmented coordination among agencies, limited integration of disaster data, and inadequate utilization of real-time information for decision-making. The study demonstrates that integrated IS can significantly strengthen situational awareness, streamline inter-agency communication, and support more efficient emergency operations. The adoption of digital platforms for data sharing and monitoring enhances both organisational preparedness and public service continuity.

This research contributes to knowledge on disaster risk reduction by showing how IS can be leveraged to build resilience in critical utility infrastructure. As the first empirical study of IS integration in Maldivian utility disaster management, this research provides practical recommendations for policymakers and utility providers, with transferable insights for other SIDS facing similar vulnerabilities.

title: Technological adoption in green practices as a mediator between green supply chain practices and operational performance: evidence from the agro-processing and food industry
affiliations: American International University-Bangladesh and Westcliff University

detail.title: Technological adoption in green practices as a mediator between green supply chain practices and operational performance: evidence from the agro-processing and food industry

publicationDetails.detailsText: Brazilian Journal of Operations & Production Management, volume 22, issue 4, 2025[10.14488/BJOPM.2695.2025]

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This study investigates the mediating role of Technological Adoption in Green Practices (TAGP) in strengthening the relationship between Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM) practices, Green Procurement (GP), Eco-Friendly Packaging (EFP), Waste Management Efficiency (WME), and Supplier Environmental Collaboration (SEC) and Operational Performance (OP) in Bangladesh’s agro-processing and food industry. It aims to identify how technology integration enhances the effectiveness of sustainable practices and overall operational efficiency.

Design/methodology/approach: A quantitative research approach was employed, collecting data through structured questionnaires distributed to 325 agro-processing firms in Bangladesh. After screening, 243 valid responses were analyzed using SmartPLS for Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). This method allowed for the evaluation of both measurement and structural models, assessing direct and mediated relationships among GSCM practices, TAGP, and OP.

Findings: EFP and SEC had significant positive effects on OP. Technological Adoption in Green Practices also demonstrated a significant direct influence on OP. Mediation analysis confirmed TAGP as a significant mediator in all four green practices performance relationships, revealing that technology integration is vital to transforming green initiatives into measurable operational outcomes.

Practical implications: The study offers valuable insights for managers and policymakers, emphasizing the necessity of technological investment to optimize green initiatives and improve performance within the agro-processing sector.

Social implications: Promoting sustainable and tech-enabled practices can contribute to environmental conservation and resource efficiency, benefiting both society and the economy.

Originality/value: This study uniquely integrates TOE, RBV, and NRBV frameworks to empirically demonstrate the pivotal role of technology in enhancing green supply chain performance in a developing country context.

title: Estimating Visual Attribute Effects in Advertising from Observational Data: A Deepfake-Informed Double Machine Learning Approach
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business and Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Estimating Visual Attribute Effects in Advertising from Observational Data: A Deepfake-Informed Double Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: Digital advertising increasingly relies on visual content, yet marketers lack rigorous methods for understanding how specific visual attributes causally affect consumer engagement. This paper addresses a fundamental methodological challenge: estimating causal effects when the treatment, such as a model's skin tone, is an attribute embedded within the image itself. Standard approaches like Double Machine Learning (DML) fail in this setting because vision encoders entangle treatment information with confounding variables, producing severely biased estimates. We develop DICE-DML (Deepfake-Informed Control Encoder for Double Machine Learning), a framework that leverages generative AI to disentangle treatment from confounders. The approach combines three mechanisms: (1) deepfake-generated image pairs that isolate treatment variation; (2) DICE-Diff adversarial learning on paired difference vectors, where background signals cancel to reveal pure treatment fingerprints; and (3) orthogonal projection that geometrically removes treatment-axis components. In simulations with known ground truth, DICE-DML reduces root mean squared error by 73-97% compared to standard DML, with the strongest improvement (97.5%) at the null effect point, demonstrating robust Type I error control. Applying DICE-DML to 232,089 Instagram influencer posts, we estimate the causal effect of skin tone on engagement. Standard DML produces diagnostically invalid results (negative outcome 𝑅 2), while DICE-DML achieves valid confounding control (𝑅 2 = 0.63) and estimates a marginally significant negative effect of darker skin tone (-522 likes; 𝑝 = 0.062), substantially smaller than the biased standard estimate. Our framework provides a principled approach for causal inference with visual data when treatments and confounders coexist within images.

title: Adoption of AI tools in Higher Education, Exploring the Role of AI Anxiety: A hybrid PLS-SEM & ANN Approach
affiliations: ITM sls Baroda University and University of Kashmir

detail.title: Adoption of AI tools in Higher Education, Exploring the Role of AI Anxiety: A hybrid PLS-SEM & ANN Approach
detail.abstract: The use of AI tools for academic content creation and research in higher education is a complex process influenced by a range of personal and environmental factors. This is true, despite potential advantages. The purpose of this study is to identify the factors that influence behavioural intentions regarding the use and subsequent adoption among faculty in higher education. The UTAUT2 (Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2) served as the underlying theory in this research. Along with the variables proposed in the UTAUT2 framework, which include performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value and habit, AI anxiety was introduced as a novel predictor variable in the research framework. The sample consisted of 376 faculty members from higher education institutions across India. A hybrid PLS (partial least squares) structural equation modelling and ANN (artificial neural network) approach was utilised in this research. The results of this study posited that performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, facilitating conditions, and price value have a significant and positive effect on attitude towards the adoption of artificial intelligence tools among faculty in higher education. Furthermore, a positive attitude towards artificial intelligence tools significantly influences behavioural intention. Additionally, the hybrid assessment using PLS-SEM and ANN demonstrated similarity in predicting behavioural intentions through performance expectancy & facilitating conditions. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI, specifically in higher education and managerial practice.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Fair Loop Initiative, a paradigm shift that defines AI development as industrial-scale resource extraction rather than ""learning."" By introducing the Know Your Data (KYD) protocol and the Polluted Data Doctrine, it establishes a framework where data flows are transparent, the burden of proof rests with the extractor, and value is redistributed via Shapley-value based micro-payments. The model aims to ensure cultural sustainability without stifling technological progress by treating data as a finite, ownable resource under resource law rather than traditional copyright.

title: Demand for a Public AI Option
affiliations: University of Notre Dame - Mendoza College of Business and Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Demand for a Public AI Option
detail.abstract: As governments increasingly debate public or government-backed AI services, understanding how such services reshape markets has become more important. Because revealed-preference data is not yet available for large-scale consumer-facing public AI, we leverage a discrete choice experiment with 4,215 market-eligible U.S. adults to provide an ex-ante evaluation of public option entry. We find that public option availability compresses incumbent residual valuations and increases private-sector price sensitivity. These patterns are consistent with a salient-benchmark interpretation rather than a uniform taste for government. Counterfactual simulations illustrate partial-equilibrium trade-offs between competitive pressure and take-up under varying user fees.

title: Smart Prediction of House Cost Price Using AI and Machine Learning
affiliations: , ,  and

detail.title: Smart Prediction of House Cost Price Using AI and Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Predicting home costs with accuracy has become a central requirement in the areas of real estate management, investment decision making and policy making. Traditionally, valuation methods include the manual appraisal and linear model-based techniques that, in almost all cases, are not designed to identify the complex nonlinear relationships between variables such as location, property size, amenities and market movements. This study addresses the above issues by generating housing price predictions using a data-driven intelligent framework that takes advantage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques, which have the potential to be more accurate and interpretable. The suggested model combines various regression-based and ensemble learning methods—such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and Artificial Neural Networks—to capture the complex interdependencies of housing datasets in multiple dimensions. Feature engineering, outlier identification, and normalization methods were adopted to improve data quality and the model’s performance. The experiments were done using the standard datasets from Kaggle and local real estate data, where the prediction accuracy over 92% with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 12.5% was achieved. Comparison results reveal that ensemble learning models are more powerful than traditional regression techniques in terms of their ability to generalize and be robust. This study paves the way for the evolution of intelligent property valuation systems that facilitate transparent, automated, and evidence-based decision-making in the real estate industry. Upcoming features are the integration of geospatial and temporal dimensions, enabling continuous and adaptive prediction models.

title: Machine Learning Straddle Strategy with Buffer-Based Execution: A Patient Trader Approach to Equity Trading
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico and Tecnológico de Monterrey - EGADE Business School

detail.title: Machine Learning Straddle Strategy with Buffer-Based Execution: A Patient Trader Approach to Equity Trading
detail.abstract: We introduce a buffer-based limit order execution framework for machine learning trading strategies. Our "straddle-then-reveal" approach operates on a two-day cycle: on day t, the trader enters simultaneous long and short positions at market open (Open_t); at day t's close, ML models—using features computed from historical data through day t—predict whether Close_{t+1} > Open_t; on day t+1, the "wrong" leg exits via patient limit orders placed at a buffer percentage from the intraday price extreme. Notably, anchoring the target to Open_t rather than Close_t proves essential: the alternative yields accuracy indistinguishable from random guessing, suggesting the intraday price path embeds predictive information about next-day movement. Testing three ML algorithms with standard and quantum-inspired feature selection across 48 global securities over 1,989 trading days (2018–2025), we find striking results. Models achieve classification accuracy near 70%, and the buffer mechanism translates this predictive power into realized profits: at the 10% buffer, average Sharpe ratios reach 14.86 with 85.5% win rates; at the conservative 30% buffer, Sharpe ratios remain strong at 7.26 with 65.6% win rates. The Sortino-to-Sharpe ratio ranges from 2.2× to 7.5× across configurations, confirming favorable return asymmetry. Robustness tests across five subperiods—including the COVID-19 crisis—confirm strategy stability. Slippage sensitivity analysis demonstrates profitability persists across realistic transaction cost scenarios. Our findings suggest that execution mechanism design can be as important as prediction accuracy for trading strategy performance.

title: Deep-injected straw incorporation enhances soil quality and buffers wheat yields against water deficit
affiliations: China Agricultural University, China Agricultural University, China Agricultural University, China Agricultural University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, China Agricultural University, China Agricultural University, China Agricultural University, China Agricultural University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and China Agricultural University

detail.title: Deep-injected straw incorporation enhances soil quality and buffers wheat yields against water deficit
detail.abstract: Intensive agricultural production has led to soil degradation and water scarcity, threatening global food security. Straw incorporation is widely considered for improving soil quality, yet its interactive effects with water availability on crop yield remain poorly understood. This study was conducted on a field site where straw treatments had been applied for two years. Building on this foundation, A two-year field was conducted to evaluate the integrated effects of five straw management practices—straw removal (SR), straw mulching (SM), straw incorporation into surface soil (SI), deep-ploughed straw incorporation (DP-SI), and deep-injected straw incorporation (DI-SI) and two irrigation strategies (conventional irrigation and water-saving irrigation) on soil quality, water use efficiency, and wheat yield in the North China Plain. On average, DI-SI increased SOC (25.2%) and available nutrients (NH4+, NO3-, and AP; 25.5%) while reducing bulk density (13.6%), resulting in a higher soil quality index (52.8%) than the other treatments. This advantage was strongest in the subsoil and remained consistent under both irrigation regimes. Under conventional irrigation, DI-SI increased wheat yield by 4.9%-12.3% compared to the other treatments, whereas under water-saving irrigation it also increased yield by 20.4% on average. SM achieved the highest water use efficiency due to reduced evapotranspiration under conventional irrigation. In contrast, under water-saving irrigation, DI-SI exhibited the highest water use efficiency, primarily attributed to its higher yield. Moreover, DI-SI exhibited a lower yield response factor to water deficit, indicating enhanced drought tolerance. This is due to the formation of subsurface straw clusters that act as water and nutrient reservoirs, improving subsoil structure, promoting deeper root growth, and facilitating crop access to deep soil resources. Our findings suggest that adopting DI-SI can contribute to sustainable agriculture and enhance crop yield particularly in water-limited scenarios, presenting a scalable, nature-based solution to address soil degradation, water shortages, and food insecurity.

title: The Effects of AI Assistance on Self-Promotion
affiliations: , Aarhus University - School of Business and Social Sciences, University of Aarhus - Department of Economics and Business Economics and Aarhus University

detail.title: The Effects of AI Assistance on Self-Promotion
detail.abstract: Persistent gender gaps in self-promotion contribute to unequal labor market outcomes. In this study, we investigate how AI-assisted writing tools shape self-promotion, and, as a secondary outcome, confidence and how these effects interact with gender. For this purpose, we conducted an online experiment in China in which participants wrote self-promotion texts, provided a numerical self-promotion score and stated their confidence about how they will perform in an upcoming math and logic test. We find suggestive evidence that AI assistance reduces numerical self-evaluations. Neither gender nor the interaction between gender and AI assistance is significantly related to self-promotion or confidence. We conduct a text analysis to investigate the mechanisms behind these results.

title: Ecce Homo Economicus: Conceiving Free Will with an Optimization-Oriented Mind
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Ecce Homo Economicus: Conceiving Free Will with an Optimization-Oriented Mind
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a minimal formalization of free will within standard utility maximization. In conventional economic models, behavior is uniquely determined once preferences and constraints are specified, except in cases of indifference that are typically treated as technical curiosities. This note instead interprets such indifference regions as the formal location of discretionary agency. Free will is defined as the size of the utility-maximizing set: when incentives select a single optimal action, behavior is fully determined, whereas when multiple actions are equally optimal, rational choice alone no longer dictates a unique outcome. The framework preserves fixed preferences, deterministic optimization, and orthodox rationality while allowing endogenous variation in behavior without randomness or preference instability. A single curvature condition governs the emergence and disappearance of discretionary space: strict concavity eliminates free will, while plateau regions of equal value generate it. The model thus recasts free will not as a departure from optimization but as a geometric property of choice environments, offering a tractable bridge between economic decision theory and broader discussions of agency.

title: The Geography of Inference: ZIP Codes as Geographic Proxy Variables in Algorithmic and Automated Decision Systems

detail.title: The Geography of Inference: ZIP Codes as Geographic Proxy Variables in Algorithmic and Automated Decision Systems

The analytical framework presented in this paper is model-agnostic and does not recommend or reference any SeraphicGuardian product or service. No financial relationship with any party influenced the analysis, findings, or conclusions of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a structural and governance analysis of statistical modeling practices using published literature, publicly available regulatory guidance, and illustrative numerical examples. No human subjects, patient data, clinical trials, or personal data were involved. Ethics approval is not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Automated decision systems increasingly influence consequential outcomes in areas such as credit underwriting, insurance pricing, and healthcare. In these systems, the choice of input variables can materially influence the relationships a model is able to learn and the outcomes it produces. Geographic identifiers such as ZIP codes frequently appear in applied analytics because many economic, environmental, and infrastructure conditions vary across locations. Although these identifiers were originally created for administrative purposes rather than statistical inference, they are often used in modeling pipelines to link individual-level records with neighborhood-level contextual information. Under certain conditions, geographic variables may absorb predictive weight associated with contextual characteristics that were never directly measured. When this occurs, they function as proxy variables, influencing predictions through associations with multiple underlying conditions that may not be captured by existing variable documentation or model specifications. This structural dynamic creates governance exposure that standard variable documentation practices may not be designed to detect. A model-agnostic analytical framework is presented for identifying and governing circumstances in which geographically defined inputs may function as proxy variables within automated decision systems. The analysis addresses statistical structure, the conditions under which feature selection decisions may produce disparate impact across protected populations, the structural mechanisms through which proxy discrimination and algorithmic bias may arise in both fully automated and algorithmically assisted decision-making, governance practices relevant to high-impact decision contexts, and practical review practices for documenting, validating, and monitoring such variables in regulated environments. The framework applies to systems in which algorithmic outputs determine outcomes directly and to systems in which algorithmic outputs inform decisions made by human reviewers, because the proxy mechanism operates at the point where geographic signal enters the model output rather than at the point where a final determination is made.

title: Turkey's FATF Grey-List Exit: An Empirical Assessment of AML/CFT Reforms, Regulatory Modernisation, and the Evolving Challenges of Cryptocurrency Compliance

detail.title: Turkey's FATF Grey-List Exit: An Empirical Assessment of AML/CFT Reforms, Regulatory Modernisation, and the Evolving Challenges of Cryptocurrency Compliance
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study evaluates Turkey’s AML/CFT reform programme during the FATF grey-list period (October 2021–June 2024), documenting the regulatory modernisation that led to successful grey-list exit and assessing the ongoing challenges posed by increasingly sophisticated cryptocurrency-based financial crime techniques that Turkey like all jurisdictions continues to confront.

Design/methodology/approach – Mixed-methods design combining analysis of FATF mutual evaluation reports, progress reviews, and plenary outcomes with Turkish legislative and regulatory instruments. Supplementary data from NSCTIP (Sonmez, 2024) provide empirical context on cryptocurrency compliance challenges. The study covers October 2021 through December 2024, encompassing the full grey-list period and six months of post-exit implementation.

Findings – Turkey achieved measurable progress across all FATF action plan items: VASP registration under Law 5549, enhanced STR filing (volume increased approximately fourfold during the grey-list period), beneficial ownership transparency improvements, MASAK resource expansion, and OFAC cooperation agreements. Grey-list exit reflects genuine institutional investment, not merely technical checkbox compliance. Remaining challenges are primarily attributable to the adaptive sophistication of transnational financial crime actors rather than regulatory gaps a challenge shared by all jurisdictions bordering sanctioned states.

Research limitations/implications – FATF assessment documents are the primary data source for reform evaluation; implementation effectiveness at the operational level is harder to measure from public data alone. The NSCTIP cryptocurrency data provide supplementary context but are author-developed. Post-exit assessment covers only six months.

Practical implications – Turkey’s reform trajectory offers a replicable model for other jurisdictions undergoing or anticipating FATF enhanced monitoring, particularly regarding VASP regulatory integration and inter-agency coordination.

Originality/value – The study provides the first detailed English-language assessment of Turkey’s grey-list reform programme from the dual perspective of a Turkish legal practitioner

title: Blockchain Analytics Effectiveness in Combating Financial Crime: An Empirical Assessment from the Builder's Perspective

detail.title: Blockchain Analytics Effectiveness in Combating Financial Crime: An Empirical Assessment from the Builder's Perspective
detail.abstract:
Blockchain analytics has become a cornerstone of cryptocurrency anti-money laundering (AML) and sanctions enforcement, yet empirical assessments of its actual effectiveness remain limited. This paper evaluates blockchain analytics effectiveness across three dimensions  detection capability, deterrence impact, and coverage gaps  using OFAC enforcement data (2018–2026), industry reporting from Chainalysis and Elliptic, and qualitative insights from the author's experience developing open-source AI-enhanced sanctions screening tools targeting the Turkey-Russia-Iran cryptocurrency corridor.

The findings reveal a critical paradox: while blockchain analytics enabled landmark enforcement actions, including the first-ever OFAC designation of Iran-linked crypto exchanges (January 2026), sanctions-linked transaction volumes surged by nearly $100 billion year-over-year in 2025 — driven by Russia's A7A5 stablecoin ($93.3 billion) and Iran's estimated $7.8–10 billion in annual crypto flows. Cross-chain laundering ($21.8 billion in 2025) and jurisdictional arbitrage through high-adoption corridors like Turkey consistently outpace analytical capabilities.

From the builder's perspective, this paper identifies three structural limitations: reliance on retrospective address attribution over predictive behavioral analysis, opacity of commercial platforms preventing independent verification, and absence of corridor-specific analytical frameworks. The paper proposes an AI-enhanced, open-source compliance model integrating machine learning-based predictive risk scoring with jurisdiction-aware analytical layers, and offers policy recommendations for OFAC, FinCEN, and virtual asset service providers.

title: DeFi Protocols as Sanctions Evasion Vectors: A Legal, Technical, and Policy Analysis of Decentralised Finance Exploitation by State Actors

detail.title: DeFi Protocols as Sanctions Evasion Vectors: A Legal, Technical, and Policy Analysis of Decentralised Finance Exploitation by State Actors
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines how sanctioned nation-state actors—North Korea, Russia, and Iran—exploit decentralised finance (DeFi) protocols for sanctions evasion, cryptocurrency laundering, and illicit value transfer. It analyses the technical characteristics that enable exploitation, documents specific campaign patterns, assesses regulatory responses including the Tornado Cash designation, and proposes detection frameworks.

Design/methodology/approach – Mixed-methods design combining technical analysis of DeFi protocol architecture (smart contract mechanics, Solidity-level vulnerability assessment) with empirical blockchain forensics from NSCTIP. The study tracks 2,340 wallet clusters with documented DeFi exploitation patterns across Ethereum, Tron, and seven bridge-connected chains. Supplementary data from OFAC designation documents, DOJ prosecution filings, and published blockchain analytics reports. Study period: January 2020–December 2024.

Findings – Four DeFi vulnerability categories are documented: mixing protocols (Tornado Cash processed an estimated $7+ billion before designation, with continued post-designation activity), DEXs (permissionless token swaps without KYC), lending platforms (collateralised dollar-equivalent borrowing without identity verification), and cross-chain bridges (inter-blockchain transfers that break single-chain forensic trails). DPRK's Lazarus Group has routed an estimated 30–40% of its $2+ billion in stolen cryptocurrency through DeFi protocols. The Tornado Cash designation (August 2022) established legal precedent but has not eliminated protocol usage. Ongoing litigation (Van Loon v. Treasury) contests the designation's scope.

Research limitations/implications – DeFi protocol interaction attribution is more complex than exchange-level attribution due to contract-level intermediation. Cross-chain tracking remains incomplete across all bridge protocols. Volume estimates for mixing service throughput carry significant uncertainty.

Practical implications – The detection framework provides protocol-specific screening indicators essential for any compliance programme processing DeFi-touched cryptocurrency flows.

Originality/value – The study combines Solidity-level technical analysis with empirical blockchain forensics and legal assessment, providing a multi-disciplinary perspective on DeFi exploitation that bridges the gap between smart contract engineering and sanctions compliance.

title: Cross-Chain Bridges and Mixers: Exploitation by Sanctioned Nation-State Actors for Cryptocurrency Laundering

detail.title: Cross-Chain Bridges and Mixers: Exploitation by Sanctioned Nation-State Actors for Cryptocurrency Laundering
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines how cross-chain bridges and mixing services have become critical laundering infrastructure for sanctioned nation-state actors, documenting specific exploitation campaigns, assessing regulatory responses, and proposing detection methodologies.

Design/methodology/approach – Empirical blockchain forensic analysis from NSCTIP tracking 3,100 wallet clusters with documented bridge/mixer exploitation patterns across nine blockchains. Campaign-level analysis of DPRK Lazarus Group operations (12 major theft-to-laundering chains traced), Russian post-sanctions bridge/mixer adoption, and Iranian mining-to-mixer patterns. Supplemented by OFAC designation analysis and published blockchain analytics reports. Study period: January 2020–December 2024.

Findings – DPRK’s Lazarus Group has routed an estimated $2+ billion in stolen cryptocurrency through bridge/mixer infrastructure since 2017, with processing speed accelerating from weeks to hours. Tornado Cash processed an estimated $7+ billion before its August 2022 OFAC designation; post-designation, usage decreased but did not cease NSCTIP documents continued deposits from sanctioned-actor wallets. Russian bridge/mixer adoption increased approximately threefold following February 2022 sanctions. The Tornado Cash and Blender.io designations established enforcement precedent but have not eliminated the infrastructure: new mixers emerge faster than they can be designated.

Research limitations/implications – Cross-chain tracing has inherent gaps (NSCTIP achieves 40–60% end-to-end success across bridges). Mixer throughput estimates carry significant uncertainty due to pooling mechanics. Attribution of specific mixer withdrawals to specific depositors is probabilistically bounded, not deterministic.

Practical implications – The detection framework provides bridge/mixer exposure indicators essential for compliance programmes processing multi-chain cryptocurrency flows.

Originality/value – The study provides campaign-level empirical analysis of nation-state bridge/mixer exploitation tracing specific theft-to-laundering chains with documented volumes and timing combined with detection methodologies grounded in the operational patterns these campaigns exhibit.

title: Institutional Land Ownership and Conservation Practice Adoption in the U.S. Midwest
affiliations: , Monash University and Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management

detail.title: Institutional Land Ownership and Conservation Practice Adoption in the U.S. Midwest
detail.abstract: We study how a firm's institutional ownership structure influences its adoption of environmentally beneficial innovations. This question is salient in the U.S. agricultural sector, where corporate structures like LLCs and trusts are becoming more prevalent. Nationally, institutional farmland ownership is growing and attracting new producers, yet its net impact on conservation remains ambiguous. Using representative panel data of landowners from Iowa—a state with surging institutional ownership from 9% to 38% between 1982 and 2022 —we analyze the adoption of no-till and cover crops, practices crucial for soil health and climate resilience. Employing a bivariate Tobit model with an instrumental variable of long-term capital gains tax liability to address endogeneity, results indicate institutional ownership significantly boosts conservation. It increases the likelihood and acreage of no-till adoption by 31.7% and 31.8%, and cover crops by 41.7% and 28.8%, respectively. Key drivers include professional management, access to information, and structured farm transitions.

title: Due to the link between temperatures and household energy demand for space heating and cooling, global warming can be expected to alter both the type of equipment chosen by U.S. households as well as how much energy is consumed in its use. Leveraging detailed household energy and demographic information to estimate a discrete-continuous household energy demand model, this paper estimates the difference in U.S. household energy outcomes from 1990-2023 between actual temperatures and a no global warming scenario. This paper finds global warming during this period induced three percent of U.S. households to switch to electric heating and four percent to central air conditioning. Overall, global warming is found to have reduced annual U.S. household energy consumption by 550 trillion BTUs by the end of the study period and household energy bills by $3.85 billion.
