title: Garantex and Grinex: Anatomy of Russian Cryptocurrency Laundromats and the Limits of Sanctions Enforcement

detail.title: Garantex and Grinex: Anatomy of Russian Cryptocurrency Laundromats and the Limits of Sanctions Enforcement
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines Garantex and its successor Grinex as a case study in the limits of sanctions enforcement against cryptocurrency platforms operating under state tolerance. It documents the platform's operational mechanics, illicit activity nexus, post-designation continuation, and the 2024 rebrand and proposes detection frameworks for compliance programmes with potential exposure.

Design/methodology/approach – Mixed-methods design combining NSCTIP blockchain forensic analysis of 4,800 Garantex/Grinex-attributed wallet clusters (~18,000 addresses, ~340,000 transactions) with qualitative analysis of OFAC designation documents, DOJ prosecution filings, Estonian FIU records, and published blockchain analytics reports. Study period: January 2020 through December 2024.

Findings – Garantex processed an estimated $6–8 billion in total volume between 2020 and its April 2022 OFAC designation, with 40–50% linked to criminal activity (ransomware, darknet markets, fraud) and 30–40% to sanctions evasion. Post-designation, the platform continued operating at reduced but still substantial volumes under Russian state tolerance. The 2024 Grinex rebrand preserved operational team, infrastructure, customer base, and illicit facilitation functions while changing only the brand. NSCTIP address continuity analysis confirms 87% overlap between Garantex and Grinex wallet clusters.

Research limitations/implications – Blockchain attribution is probabilistic. Volume estimates for a designated platform carry inherent uncertainty as operational opacity increases post-designation. The 87% cluster overlap figure is based on common-input-ownership heuristics that may overcount shared infrastructure.

Practical implications – The detection framework provides specific indicators for identifying direct and indirect Garantex/Grinex exposure, essential for any compliance programme processing cryptocurrency flows with Russian nexus.

Originality/value – The study provides the first detailed empirical analysis of the Garantex-to-Grinex transition, documenting through blockchain forensics how a designated platform maintained operational continuity through rebranding a pattern with implications for sanctions enforcement strategy globally.

title: Iran's USDT and Stablecoin-Based Sanctions Evasion: An Empirical Analysis of Digital Dollar Exploitation for International Trade Finance

detail.title: Iran's USDT and Stablecoin-Based Sanctions Evasion: An Empirical Analysis of Digital Dollar Exploitation for International Trade Finance
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines how Iran exploits USDT and stablecoin technology for sanctions evasion in international trade finance. It documents the mechanisms, estimates the scale, maps the geographic corridors, evaluates issuer compliance responses, and proposes a detection framework.

Design/methodology/approach – Mixed-methods design combining blockchain forensic analysis of 14,200 attributed wallet clusters across Ethereum and Tron chains with qualitative typological development. Data derive from NSCTIP (January 2020–December 2024), seeded from 847 OFAC-designated Iranian addresses and expanded through clustering heuristics. Volume estimates use three tiers: conservative (direct attribution), pattern-based, and upper-bound, each with explicit assumptions.

Findings – Five mechanisms are documented: import payment settlement (~55% of flows), export revenue conversion (~20%), intermediary settlement networks (~15%), mining monetisation (~7%), and sanctions-covered procurement (~3%). USDT on Tron accounts for approximately 72% of Iranian stablecoin activity. Conservative annual volume reached $6.2 billion in 2023. China, Turkey, and the UAE are identified as significant corridor jurisdictions, though Turkey has demonstrated the most proactive regulatory trajectory among the three. Tether's compliance architecture shows measurably weaker Iranian-flow prevention than Circle's (USDC share: 5% vs. USDT: 87%).

Research limitations/implications – Blockchain attribution is probabilistic; false-positive rates in the NSCTIP dataset are estimated at 8–12% based on cross-validation against known OFAC enforcement cases. Off-chain OTC activity, privacy-coin mixing, and intra-exchange netting fall outside observational scope. Volume estimates should be read as bounded ranges, not point values. Independent replication with commercial platforms (Chainalysis Reactor, TRM) would strengthen confidence.

Practical implications – The framework provides mechanism-specific detection indicators, with particular emphasis on Tron-chain monitoring—platforms covering only Ethereum miss an estimated 72% of Iranian flows.

Originality/value – The study offers granular, chain-specific empirical data on Iranian stablecoin exploitation across five mechanisms and three corridors, combined with a comparative issuer compliance analysis (Tether vs. Circle) that has direct regulatory design implications.

title: Stablecoin AML Regulation: A Comparative Analysis of the EU MiCA Framework and U.S. Regulatory Approaches to Financial Crime Prevention

detail.title: Stablecoin AML Regulation: A Comparative Analysis of the EU MiCA Framework and U.S. Regulatory Approaches to Financial Crime Prevention
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study presents a systematic comparison of EU and U.S. approaches to stablecoin AML regulation, assessing which framework better addresses the financial crime risks that stablecoins create particularly sanctions evasion by state actors.

Design/methodology/approach – Comparative legal analysis of EU MiCA (Regulation 2023/1114), the recast Transfer of Funds Regulation (2023/1113), and AMLD6 against the U.S. patchwork of FinCEN BSA requirements, SEC/CFTC jurisdictional claims, OCC guidance, and state-level licensing. Supplemented by NSCTIP empirical data on how different regulatory environments affect illicit stablecoin use patterns, tracking 1,640 wallet clusters with documented stablecoin-based sanctions evasion activity across both EU-accessible and non-EU channels.

Research limitations/implications – MiCA full application began December 2024; assessment of its implementation effectiveness is necessarily preliminary. U.S. legislative proposals may alter the regulatory landscape. NSCTIP data capture on-chain activity only.

Practical implications – Compliance programmes should implement conservative controls reflecting the stricter of applicable requirements and deploy stablecoin-specific blockchain analytics regardless of jurisdictional framework.

title: Agent Experience (AX) and the Agent Context Annotation Guidelines (AXAG) Standard: Designing Interfaces for AI Agents as First-Class Clients - Towards a Unified Semantic Contract for Human and Agent Interfaces in WebMCP-Enabled Applications

detail.title: Agent Experience (AX) and the Agent Context Annotation Guidelines (AXAG) Standard: Designing Interfaces for AI Agents as First-Class Clients - Towards a Unified Semantic Contract for Human and Agent Interfaces in WebMCP-Enabled Applications

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, personal data, or intervention. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
The interface layer of modern software has always been designed for a single audience: human beings. Every principle in user experience practice like affordance, hierarchy, progressive disclosure, accessibility assumes a perceiving, reasoning person on the other side of the screen. That assumption is now structurally incomplete. With the emergence of WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) and the broader shift toward agentic software systems, AI agents have become first-class consumers of web interfaces. These agents do not perceive visually. They reason semantically. They invoke capabilities through structured tool calls. They cannot read the implicit signals that human interfaces rely upon e.g. color, proximity, label inference, visual weight, unless those signals are explicitly declared in machine-readable form. 

This paper introduces two interrelated frameworks to close that gap: (1) Agent Experience (AX) - a design discipline that treats AI agents as first-class interface clients, establishing principles, patterns, and specifications that make interfaces reliably agent-navigable; and (2) the Agent Context Annotation Guidelines (AXAG) - a concrete, implementable standard for annotating web interfaces with the semantic declarations agents require to act correctly, safely, and with appropriate human oversight. Together, these frameworks enable the Agenthropic Design System: a design system architecture in which a single capability definition simultaneously governs the human-facing visual interface and the agent-facing tool surface. This paper provides the specification, rationale, implementation guidance, and governance model for both frameworks.

detail.abstract: This paper examines oshore dollar transmission mechanisms through Federal Reserve operational facilities, specically the FIMA (Foreign and International Monetary Authorities) Repo Facility and central bank swap lines. Using facility usage data, cross-currency basis spreads, and March 2020 crisis episode analysis, I document a systematic pattern whereby facility activation signals Fed policy response 2-4 weeks in advance. The epistemological contribution distinguishes between symbolic analysis (Fed communications, forward guidance) and material observation (facility usage as revealed institutional necessity). When foreign central banks access emergency dollar facilities above threshold levels (FIMA >$30B, swap lines >$50B), Fed operational response follows within 2-4 weeksnot as probabilistic correlation but as observation of causal process. March 2020 validation: basis spreads widened February (-25bp →-50bp), swap lines activated mid-March ($449B peak), FIMA facility launched March 31. title: Designing Service Systems from Textual Evidence
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), City University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - School of Engineering

detail.title: Designing Service Systems from Textual Evidence
detail.abstract: Designing service systems requires selecting among alternative configurations-choosing the best chatbot variant, the optimal routing policy, or the most effective quality control procedure. In many service systems, the primary evidence of performance quality is textual-customer support transcripts, complaint narratives, compliance review reports-rather than the scalar measurements assumed by classical optimization methods. Large language models (LLMs) can read such textual evidence and produce standardized quality scores, but these automated judges exhibit systematic biases that vary across alternatives and evaluation instances. Human expert review remains accurate but costly. We study how to identify the best service configuration with high confidence while minimizing expensive human audits, given that automated evaluation is cheap but biased. We formalize this as a sequential decision problem where a biased proxy score is observed for every evaluation, and a verified outcome can be acquired selectively at additional cost. We prove that LLM-only selection fails under arm-dependent bias, and that naive selective-audit estimators can be asymptotically biased. We develop an estimator combining proxy scores with inverse-propensity-weighted residuals and construct anytime-valid confidence sequences. Our algorithm, PP-LUCB, jointly decides which alternatives to evaluate and whether to request human audits, concentrating reviews where the LLM judge is least reliable. We prove correctness and establish instance-dependent cost bounds showing near-optimal efficiency. On a customer support ticket classification task, our algorithm correctly identifies the best model in 40/40 trials while achieving 90% audit cost reduction.

title: Who Is Responsible for Carbon? Attribution Rules, General Equilibrium, and the Limits of Consumption-Based Accounting

detail.title: Who Is Responsible for Carbon? Attribution Rules, General Equilibrium, and the Limits of Consumption-Based Accounting
detail.abstract: Household carbon footprints are increasingly used to motivate climate policy instruments aimed at end use behavior. Yet the magnitude and interpretation of household responsibility depend on the accounting framework. This paper formalizes household carbon attribution as an economic mapping from micro level actions to aggregate emissions and shows that standard consumption based accounting can systematically overstate the marginal emissions impact of household behavior when market feedback and substitution are non negligible. The paper proposes a unified taxonomy of attribution rules based on operational control, consumption based responsibility, and marginal causal impact, and develops a tractable general equilibrium model in which households jointly choose consumption and investment under risk. In equilibrium, the household footprint decomposes into consumption linked and investment linked components with an endogenous weight that depends on preference curvature and financial risk. The analysis provides comparative statics that clarify when static footprint metrics are informative for policy design and when they are not. A quantitative illustration shows that policy evaluation based on average footprints can mis rank instruments when equilibrium reallocation attenuates the aggregate emissions response to individual action. The results motivate a shift from purely descriptive footprinting toward causally interpretable attribution that aligns with incidence and general equilibrium effects of climate policy.

title: Risks Create a Jagged Frontier of LLM Productivity Gains Across Computer Occupations
affiliations: , University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois Springfield, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Political Science, , University of Illinois Chicago and University of Illinois Chicago

detail.title: Risks Create a Jagged Frontier of LLM Productivity Gains Across Computer Occupations
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the frontier of expert-LLM collaboration is uneven, not only because of jagged AI capability but also due to jagged AI risk.  For some tasks, LLM systems, including agents, can significantly reduce completion time and labor cost. For others, these gains are constrained, if not offset, by risks. We introduce the first occupation-level quantification of risk-aware productivity gains for expert–LLM collaboration over a realistic task distribution, using standard O*NET computer-occupation tasks. We leverage six frontier models (e.g., GPT-5, Claude Opus) to produce structured risk–reward ratings following standardized definitions and manually verifying a subset for reliability. Reward captures productivity gains, i.e., time/cost savings at a fixed quality target under expert oversight. We consider multiple sources of risk, ranging from incompetence-driven errors (Discrimination, Toxicity, Privacy, Misinformation) to adversarial exploitation (Security, Malicious Actors and Misuse). We aggregate task-level ratings into occupation-level scores, weighting tasks by O*NET measures of task importance,  relevance, and frequency. Our empirical analysis reveals that risk varies more than reward, yielding significant differences in risk–reward tradeoff: in safety-critical roles (e.g., information security engineers), gains are offset by risk, whereas in less safety-critical roles (e.g., web developers), gains often substantially exceed risks.  As LLM systems improve, incompetence-driven risks may decline, but adversarial risks can persist or increase, leading to the likely persistence of a jagged risk–reward frontier. The risk-aware jaggedness has significant implications for labor policy, research funding, and national competitiveness.

title: Separation of Powers as Synergy

detail.title: Separation of Powers as Synergy

contentType.other: forthcoming chapter in Mathieu Leloup et al (eds), Research Handbook in the Separation of Powers

detail.abstract: In constitutional theory, the separation of powers has long been viewed as a foundational requirement of constitutional government. But despite widespread agreement on its fundamental value, there has been significant controversy about its underlying purpose and point. For some, the key rationale of the separation of powers is to curb abuse of power and protect liberty. For others, its role is to enhance the efficiency of government. Cutting across the supposed antimony between liberty and efficiency, this paper uncovers the plural purposes of the separation of powers, including efficiency and liberty, specialisation and slowdown , contestation and collaboration, safeguards and synergy, accountability and mutual support. In short, the separation of powers is a multi-value ideal promoting a plurality of normative ends. Furthermore, while traditional accounts have highlighted the negative dimension of the separation of powers as a bulwark against abuse of power, this paper shows how the separation of powers is also a system principle which regulates the relationships between the branches of government so that they can work together constructively as a well-functioning system of governance. Reconceiving the separation of powers in relational and collaborative terms, this paper foregrounds the idea of separation as synergy i.e. the idea of a plurality of state organs sharing power and working together as part of a collaborative constitutional enterprise. On this vision, the shift from autocratic rule to constitutional government is marked by a move from the unmediated simplicity of unitary authority to the constitutional complexity of divided and shared authority.

title: Physics-Guided Memory Network for Building Energy Modeling
affiliations: Western University, University of Western Ontario, Western University and Western University

detail.title: Physics-Guided Memory Network for Building Energy Modeling
detail.abstract: Accurate energy consumption forecasting is essential for efficient resource management and sustainability in the building sector. Deep learning models are highly successful but struggle with limited historical data and become unusable when historical data are unavailable, such as in newly constructed buildings. On the other hand, physics-based models, such as EnergyPlus, simulate energy consumption without relying on historical data but require extensive building parameter specifications and considerable time to model a building. This paper introduces a Physics-Guided Memory Network (PgMN), a neural network that integrates predictions from deep learning and physics-based models to address their limitations. PgMN comprises a Parallel Projection Layers to process incomplete inputs, a Memory Unit to account for persistent biases, and a Memory Experience Module to optimally extend forecasts beyond their input range and produce output. Theoretical evaluation shows that components of PgMN are mathematically valid for performing their respective tasks. The PgMN was evaluated on short-term energy forecasting at an hourly resolution, critical for operational decision-making in smart grid and smart building systems. Experimental validation shows accuracy and applicability of PgMN in diverse scenarios such as newly constructed buildings, missing data, sparse historical data, and dynamic infrastructure changes. This paper provides a promising solution for energy consumption forecasting in dynamic building environments, enhancing model applicability in scenarios where historical data are limited or unavailable or when physics-based models are inadequate.

title: Dollar Funding and Housing Markets: The Role of Non-Us Global Banks

detail.title: Dollar Funding and Housing Markets: The Role of Non-Us Global Banks

publicationDetails.detailsText: BIS Working Papers | No 1332 | February 2026

detail.abstract: House prices co-move considerably across countries. We show how non-US global banks and their exposure to US dollar funding conditions help explain this comovement. When the dollar appreciates, mortgage lending and house prices decrease more in borrower countries whose non-US creditor banks are more exposed to dollar funding conditions. As US dollar funding conditions vary, borrowing country pairs with higher joint exposure to US dollar funding conditions via their non-US creditor banks exhibit a higher synchronization of mortgage credit and house price growth. We capture the exposure to dollar funding conditions by the bilateral treasury basis between the currency of the non-US global creditor banks' nationality and the US dollar, a choice that we motivate in a simple value-at-risk model. Our results identify a novel international spillover channel of US dollar funding conditions. Because it works through heterogenous dollar funding exposures among creditors, this new channel is neither linked to common-lender exposures nor to currency mismatches on borrower countries' balance sheets, typically associated with the financial channel of the exchange-rate.

title: The AI Revolution in Sugarcane Agriculture
affiliations: University of California, Davis

detail.title: The AI Revolution in Sugarcane Agriculture
detail.abstract: The sugarcane industry is experiencing a profound transformation as artificial intelligence augments traditional farming methods with data-driven decision-making. This shift enables proactive management approaches, with issues identified before they impact yields or processing efficiency. AI agents, which are AI systems capable of perception, reasoning, and action have much potential to further evolve sugarcane agriculture and processing. The application of AI can help to address many of the sugarcane industry’s outstanding challenges: yield variability, resource intensity, and labor demands. The economic case for AI adoption is compelling, with industry reports indicating 15-20% productivity increases alongside 10-15% input cost reductions. These improvements significantly impact profitability in the traditionally tight-margin sugarcane sector while addressing persistent challenges including labor shortages and climate variability.

title: Response to the CMA Consultation on Proposed Conduct Requirements for Google's General Search and Search Advertising Services

declarations.funderStatement: Our independent research project is funded by Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) and the UK Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC).

detail.abstract: The  SCiDA team broadly support the CMA's approach across all four conduct requirements while identifying several areas where clarification or strengthening would enhance effectiveness. On the Publisher Conduct Requirement, we consider the CMA's identification of compelled consent as a central problem to be well-founded, but note that the opt-out model's workability was questioned at the stakeholder roundtable, with several participants advocating for structural separation of the search crawler and AI crawler. On the Fair Ranking Conduct Requirement, we support the proposed scope, including its extension to AI Overviews and AI Mode, while noting that definitional ambiguities regarding the distinction between fair ranking and self-preferencing require clarification. On the User Choice Conduct Requirement, we welcome the innovative test-drive functionality but raise concerns about the delegation of critical implementation decisions to Google, particularly regarding the number of providers to be displayed on the choice screen. On the Data Portability Conduct Requirement, we agree that formalising Google's voluntary provision of its DMA-compliant data portability API is both necessary and proportionate, while recommending greater clarity on the scope of specified data and the interaction with data protection obligations.

title: From Crisis to Climate: Geopolitical Turbulence, Climate Change Exposure, and Managerial Ownership
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, Pennsylvania State University - School of Graduate Professional Studies (SGPS) and Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance

detail.title: From Crisis to Climate: Geopolitical Turbulence, Climate Change Exposure, and Managerial Ownership
detail.abstract: We explore how geopolitical risk shapes firm-specific exposure to climate change, utilizing innovative text-based measures for both variables. Our analysis reveals that elevated geopolitical risk leads to a significant reduction in firms' climate change exposure, suggesting that external shocks can spur organizational adaptation. The robustness of these findings is confirmed through a range of empirical checks, including propensity score matching, entropy balancing, and instrumental variable analysis. Further, we show that firms with larger cash reserves or greater R&D intensity tend to be less responsive to increases in geopolitical risk. Crucially, the reduction in climate change exposure is also less pronounced in firms with higher managerial ownership, underscoring the pivotal role of governance in guiding corporate responses to global risks.

title: Investing in Artificial General Intelligence
affiliations: HEC Montreal - Department of Finance

detail.title: Investing in Artificial General Intelligence
detail.abstract: Frontier AI laboratories racing toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) face uncertain timing of transformative demand and must decide how much irreversible capacity to build and how to split it between inference (current revenue) and training (future capability). I develop a real-options model with regime switching, duopoly competition, endogenous default risk, and diminishing returns calibrated to AI scaling laws. The model delivers analytical investment triggers and a duopoly preemption equilibrium in which the leader trains more and invests earlier than the follower. A "faith-based survival" mechanism emerges: training raises the expected post-AGI continuation value, lowering the default boundary-the hope of AGI keeps the firm alive. An asymmetric dilemma arises in which aggressive overinvestment carries higher downside risk than conservative underinvestment. Calibration to four AI lab archetypes illustrates how heterogeneity in beliefs about AI timelines drives cross-sectional variation in investment behavior.

title: Stress Testing with Multiple Scenarios: A Tale on Tails and Reverse Stress Scenarios
affiliations: Bank of England, European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Stress Testing with Multiple Scenarios: A Tale on Tails and Reverse Stress Scenarios
detail.abstract: This paper develops an operational framework for stress testing that evaluates financial sector vulnerabilities across a distribution of plausible macro-financial scenarios rather than a small number of predetermined stress paths. The approach identifies macro-financial risk factors of particular relevance to the system, or individual institutions, and scenario families that could drive them toward their worst outcomes (reverse stress testing). We illustrate the methodology for euro area banks. Overall, the framework provides policymakers with a structured way to evaluate the severity, plausibility, and narrative consistency of stress scenarios, enhancing the design and interpretation of supervisory and macroprudential stress tests.

title: Scale-Dependent Dynamics in Equity Market Phase Space
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Scale-Dependent Dynamics in Equity Market Phase Space
detail.abstract: We extend the stochastic damped harmonic oscillator (SDHO) dynamics established in Dean (2025) to longer timescales, discovering a universal power law governing how the effective mean-reversion strength decays with observation horizon. Using sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) on 32 years of SPY daily data, supplemented by 154 years of Shiller S&P 500 data and 308 years of Bank of England UK equity data, we find that the mean-reversion coefficient follows k(τ) = A τ⁻ᵅ with A = 1.61, α = 1.13, and R² = 0.99 across 34 measurements spanning 462 combined years. The mean-reversion coefficient remains strictly positive (k > 0 in 34/34 measurements) but decays to negligible levels at the 2-3 month horizon where the Jegadeesh-Titman momentum anomaly begins. A central methodological contribution is the identification of the Voronoi-Delaunay (VD) tessellation as the natural finite-volume discretization of the Fokker-Planck equation on irregular phasespace data, formally linking the empirical dynamics to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics. An apparent R² discrepancy, in which non-overlapping sampling yields R²_𝜏 ≈ 0.84 versus overlapping R²_d ≈ 0.57, is resolved through 2 × 2 × 2 factorial analysis on both SPY daily data and ES futures minute data (5.38 million observations). The sampling effect accounts for 92-97% of the apparent improvement across six futures markets spanning five asset classes. The power-law decay provides a geometric explanation for several long-standing puzzles in financial economics: the Jegadeesh-Titman momentum anomaly emerges where the meanreversion strength becomes negligibly small; mean-reversion and momentum are revealed as aspects of a single oscillator with continuously varying stiffness; and the power-law exponent α ≈ 1 connects the empirical dynamics to renormalization-group scaling of effective coupling constants.

title: Corporate Gravity Theory

detail.title: Corporate Gravity Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available data and does not involve human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
The purpose of this study is to model the attractive effect possessed by firms-here termed corporate gravity-and to examine its relationship with managerial performance indicators. While prior research has advanced the quantification of non-financial value and social impact, there has been limited effort to formally model their underlying structural foundations or to interpret corporate influence within a coherent dynamical framework.

This study defines corporate gravity as a firm s attractive force and formulates it by analogy to Newton s law of gravitation. As its theoretical foundation, we construct a three-dimensional semantic coordinate space-Human, Nature, and Economic-using the 169 SDG target texts. A metric tensor is introduced to account for anisotropy in semantic scale, thereby providing a mathematically grounded structure for distance deformation. Furthermore, impact values published by the International Foundation for Valuing Impacts (IFVI) are incorporated as corporate mass, and a corporate gravity equation is derived by integrating firm coordinates in the semantic space, their distance from an observation point, and their mass.

Using this formulation, corporate gravity values are calculated for 69 firms, and regression analyses are conducted against five-year stock price growth and five-year PBR growth. The empirical tests employ 36 specifications constructed by excluding various upper and lower ranges of corporate gravity values. The results demonstrate a robust positive relationship between corporate gravity and five-year stock returns. In a representative specification excluding the top and bottom 10 percent (n = 55), a statistically significant positive relationship is observed (R² = 0.291, β = 0.260). This relationship remains stable across alternative model specifications.

Robustness analyses incorporating additional control variables are currently underway to further assess the stability of the estimated corporate gravity effect.

This study presents a theoretical framework that conceptualizes firms as mass-bearing entities within a semantic coordinate space and reinterprets corporate activity as dynamical interaction within that space. By introducing a geometric and structural perspective into corporate value.

title: The Safety Tripwire: Architectural Efficiency of Threshold-Based Rebalancing in a 60/40 Regime

detail.title: The Safety Tripwire: Architectural Efficiency of Threshold-Based Rebalancing in a 60/40 Regime
detail.abstract: Standard portfolio rebalancing is traditionally viewed as a periodic maintenance task, a ritualized adjustment to return a portfolio to its original risk mandate. Most institutional and retail frameworks rely on calendar-based protocols, monthly, quarterly, or annual resets, regardless of the underlying market volatility or the magnitude of asset drift. This paper challenges the efficiency of such time-dependent conventions. We propose the Safety Tripwire, a state-dependent control mechanism that triggers intervention only when portfolio drift exceeds an absolute 5% threshold. The structural flaw in calendar-based rebalancing is twofold: it often forces trades during periods of negligible drift, incurring unnecessary execution costs, and conversely, it may fail to act during periods of extreme intra-period volatility when risk mandates are most at risk. By utilizing a longitudinal study spanning 2004 through 2024, we contrast the Safety Tripwire against industry-standard protocols across several market regimes, including the Global Financial Crisis and the 2022 inflationary bear market. Our results indicate that the Tripwire architecture achieves a superior CAGR (7.80% vs. 7.66%) and comparable drawdown protection while reducing total interventions by 94% relative to monthly rebalancing (14 vs. 252 interventions). By allowing the portfolio to breathe within a defined corridor, allocators capture a momentum bonus and significantly reduce execution friction without compromising the integrity of the risk mandate.

title: The Markup-Savings Channel and Falling US Interest Rates
affiliations: Peterson Institute for International Economics and

detail.title: The Markup-Savings Channel and Falling US Interest Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest. Views and opinions expressed in this paper are those of the authors only and do not reflect those of the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

detail.abstract: Contrary to the common view that attributes the decline in US interest rates over the 2000s and 2010s primarily to a global savings glut or demographic trends, we show both empirically and theoretically that rising markups were a key driver of the decline. Empirically, we find that higher markups suppressed investment, while the resulting income gains accrued to entrepreneur households at the top of the income distribution, who exhibit a high marginal propensity to save. Theoretically, an overlapping-generations model demonstrates that the joint effect of these forces exerts substantial downward pressure on the asset-market-clearing interest rate, consistent with a secular stagnation equilibrium. To reverse this dynamic, the first-best policy is to restore market competition. Where that is not feasible, we evaluate second-best options such as redistribution, subsidies on labor and investment, and fiscal expansion.

detail.abstract: Seaweed farming is an emerging blue economy livelihood in coastal Kenya with potential to strengthen climate resilience, advance gender equity, and diversify community incomes. This study examines the nascent seaweed sector in Kwale County through a Community-Based Natural Resource Management (CBNRM) lens, assessing whether it is on a pathway toward sustained benefits or a boom-bust trajectory. Using mixed methods-key informant interviews, stakeholder workshops, field observations, and policy/document review-the study analyzed governance arrangements, socioeconomic outcomes, ecological co-benefits, and value-chain structure. Findings show that seaweed farming is already generating livelihood gains through supplementary and diversified household incomes, with women constituting approximately 70-80% of producers and reporting increased economic agency. Localized environmental co-benefits were also observed, including improved habitat complexity for juvenile fish and perceived water quality improvements. However, sector performance and scalability are constrained by fragmented governance, weak conflict resolution and benefit-sharing arrangements, limited value addition, and exposure to price volatility and buyer power. Policy and institutional support remain underdeveloped, with seaweed inadequately recognized within existing aquaculture regulations and market participation dominated by low-value raw exports. The study recommends formal recognition of seaweed as a distinct mariculture subsector, strengthening cooperatives and women's groups, upgrading value chains, and building domestic demand-particularly through coastal tourism-to secure a resilient and inclusive development trajectory.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a conceptual framework examining whether integration between housing infrastructure and localized energy production may function as a structural stabilizing mechanism within modern economies.  Household financial fragility is often influenced by volatility in essential expenditures, particularly housing and energy costs, which can act as channels for broader economic shock transmission.  The framework explores whether reducing exposure to such volatility through infrastructure design could contribute to more stable household balance sheets and in turn enhance macroeconomic resilience.

Using a circulation-based perspective, the paper describes a "stability flywheel" in which improved predictability at the household level supports more consistent participation in local economic activity, reinforces community-level resilience and reduces amplification of downturns.  It also considers potential interactions between distributed residential energy systems and evolving grid demands in regions experiencing growth in electricity-intensive infrastructure.

The objective is not to prescribe specific policies, but to outline a set of mechanisms and research questions that may inform further empirical and modeling work at the intersection of household finance, infrastructure economics and financial stability.

title: When Algorithms Manage People: Risk Internalization, Structural Compliance, and the Economic Architecture of Algorithmic Employer Liability
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: When Algorithms Manage People: Risk Internalization, Structural Compliance, and the Economic Architecture of Algorithmic Employer Liability
detail.abstract: The growing reliance on algorithmic systems in workforce management is frequently portrayed as a natural and almost inevitable technological evolution, accompanied by legal effects that are generally treated as manageable, peripheral, or merely collateral to efficiency gains. This article advances a more demanding analytical framework, grounded simultaneously in labor law, risk theory, structural compliance, and Law and Economics, by arguing that algorithmic management constitutes an institutional reconfiguration of managerial power that transforms the organization of work into a scalable, persistent, and legally intelligible mechanism of risk internalization and evidentiary consolidation. By embedding managerial decisions into automated architectures, employers do not merely alter how work is coordinated, but fundamentally shift liability analysis away from isolated managerial acts and toward the rationality, proportionality, and governability of system design, thereby altering incentives, increasing the marginal cost of systemic error, and reshaping judicial evaluation. Within this framework, algorithms cannot be understood as neutral efficiency devices, but rather as institutional commitments that redefine optimal compliance strategies and expose the employer to new forms of predictable judicial scrutiny. The article concludes that labor compliance in algorithmic environments must be reconceptualized as structural and evidentiary governance, oriented toward the minimization of inefficient harm, excessive transaction costs, and foreseeable judicial exposure.

title: An Intelligent System for Trip Hazard detection in Indoor Environment using Deep Learning

detail.title: An Intelligent System for Trip Hazard detection in Indoor Environment using Deep Learning
detail.abstract:
Slips, Trips, and Falls (STF) remain a major cause of injuries in indoor environments such as homes, healthcare facilities, and industrial workplaces. Conventional safety inspection methods are manual, intermittent, and incapable of addressing dynamically emerging trip hazards in real time. This paper presents an intelligent vision-based system for real-time trip hazard detection in indoor environments using deep learning and RGB-D sensor fusion. The proposed framework integrates geometric ground-plane segmentation using the RANSAC algorithm with semantic object detection based on the YOLOv8 architecture to accurately identify low-lying hazards such as cables, footwear, rug edges, and small debris. A custom indoor dataset was prepared and annotated to train and evaluate the system under varying lighting and floor texture conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a mean Average Precision (mAP@0.5) of 92.5%, a recall of 93%, and real-time performance at 25+ FPS, making it suitable for low-latency safety applications. Comparative evaluation with Faster R-CNN and SSD MobileNet confirms the superior balance of detection accuracy and inference speed offered by YOLOv8. The developed system enables proactive hazard identification and instant alert generation, significantly reducing reliance on reactive monitoring and enhancing indoor safety for both human occupants and assistive robotic systems.

title: Reviving the Nonmajority Bargaining Order
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Reviving the Nonmajority Bargaining Order
detail.abstract:
In 1969, the Supreme Court suggested that the National Labor Relations Board could remedy severe unfair labor practices by ordering an employer to bargain with a union that never enjoyed majority support. Yet since 1984, the Board has disclaimed any authority to issue such nonmajority bargaining orders, reasoning that they undermine the ability of employees to make free choices about union representation and violate the NLRA’s bright-line principle of majority rule.

This article reevaluates both objections and makes the case for reviving the nonmajority bargaining order. When deciding whether to order an offending employer to bargain, the Board faces a dilemma. Issuing the bargaining order risks imposing a union on workers who do not want it, while refusing to issue the order risks leaving workers without the union they would have supported in the absence of the employer’s unlawful conduct. The conventional model of employee free choice evaluates this tradeoff at the moment the order issues; without any evidence of past majority support, the risk of imposing a union on an unwilling group appears unbearably high. What this picture misses, however, is that the risks are asymmetrically sticky. If the Board erroneously orders bargaining, its error will likely be reversed by employees decertifying the union. But if the Board erroneously refuses to order bargaining, that error will likely persist, as overcoming threats and retaliation to achieve unionization is a tall order. Nonmajority bargaining orders thus maximize employee free choice across time when unfair labor practices are sufficiently severe. 

Meanwhile, the principle of majority rule prevents employers from pitting groups of workers against each other by recognizing minority unions. A careful examination of Supreme Court precedent and the NLRA’s text and legislative history reveals that neither supports majority rule as a constraint on the Board’s remedial power. And where an employer unlawfully prevents a majority from ever forming, a bargaining order is often the only way to vindicate employees’ statutory rights.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a country report of Australia's implementation of international environmental law in 2025. Australia's obligations were made clearer by the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion on Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change, and the report covers international and domestic case law. It addresses Australia's climate and biodiversity commitments, including the long-awaited reforms to the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (EPBC Act), passed after the incumbent party was returned to government at the federal level in the May election. The report also notes the submission by Australia of its second Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement, which sets a new target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 62-70% below 2005 levels by 2035, with a view to achieving net zero by 2050. The relevance and applicability of human rights, the law of the sea, heritage protection, and obligations to prevent harm are also noted in this report. Significant for Australia's implementation of international environmental law at the subnational level was the passage of a treaty between First Peoples and the State of Victoria, and an entrenched right to a clean, healthy environment in the Australian Capital Territory. The report highlights continued gaps in implementation, such as ongoing efforts to develop a Sustainable Ocean Plan.

detail.abstract:
This working paper evaluates the financial security of the U.S. banking sector through an indicator-based analytical framework that integrates capital adequacy, liquidity resilience, asset quality, and supervisory effectiveness. Drawing on supervisory reports from the Federal Reserve, FDIC risk reviews, and international financial stability assessments, the study examines recent structural developments in banking sector resilience.

The paper introduces a Composite Financial Security Effectiveness Index (CFSI) designed to measure the effectiveness of regulatory tools in mitigating systemic risks. The results indicate that while the U.S. banking system remains structurally resilient — with capital buffers significantly exceeding Basel III minimum requirements and liquidity indicators remaining strong — emerging vulnerabilities related to funding structure shifts, interest-rate exposure, and non-bank financial interconnections require continued supervisory attention.

The proposed framework offers a practical approach for evaluating regulatory effectiveness and may be applied in comparative financial stability assessments across banking systems.

title: Local Prosecutors and Public Health
affiliations: Vanderbilt University and Wellesley College

detail.title: Local Prosecutors and Public Health
detail.abstract: Legal scholars argue that local prosecutors may be the most powerful actors in the criminal justice system, yet there is a limited understanding of how different prosecutorial approaches shape community level outcomes. This paper investigates the causal relationship between approaches taken by local criminal prosecutors—also called district attorneys—and community-level mortality rates. We leverage plausibly exogenous variation in prosecutorial approaches generated by closely contested partisan prosecutor elections, a context in which Republican prosecutorial candidates are commonly characterized as "tougher on crime." Using data from hundreds of closely contested partisan elections from 2010 to 2019 and a vote share regression discontinuity design, we find that narrow election of a Republican prosecutor reduces all-cause mortality rates among young men ages 20 to 29 by 6.6%. This decline is driven predominantly by reductions in firearm-related deaths, including a large reduction in firearm homicide among Black men and a smaller reduction in firearm suicides and accidents primarily among White men. Mechanism analyses indicate that increased prison-based incapacitation explains about one third of the effect among Black men and none of the effect among White men. Instead, the primary channel appears to be substantial increases in criminal conviction rates across racial groups and crime types, which then reduce firearm access through legal restrictions on gun ownership for the convicted.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether incorporating subordinated-debt pricing improves the tracking of weekly changes in corporate bond-index credit spreads. We develop a contingent-claims framework that compares a senior-debt (Merton) specification with a subordinated-debt (Black-Cox) model using a zerocoupon pseudo-issuer whose assets replicate the S&P 500. The model is calibrated to each index's duration and leverage and employs four volatility inputs: historical, option-implied, ARIMA and ARIMAX forecasts. Out-ofsample results for 2019-2023 show that both models explain a large share of weekly spread variation. The subordinated model adds value particularly in investment-grade and broad indices when market volatility nears a critical threshold where junior debt valuation shifts from equity-like to debt-like sensitivity. However, the senior model remains the more reliable baseline in normal market conditions.

title: How Food Prices Shape Inflation Expectations and the Monetary Policy Response
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome - Department of Economics and Law, Catholic University of Milan and University of Bologna

detail.title: How Food Prices Shape Inflation Expectations and the Monetary Policy Response
detail.abstract: Food prices are salient for households’ inflation perceptions and expectations at both the micro and macro levels. UK survey data indicate over 60% of households report food prices as very important for perceived inflation. These households exhibit a stronger correlation between perceived and expected inflation, reflecting backward-looking expectations. An SVAR with aggregate data shows food-price shocks generate larger and more persistent movements in expectations than “representative” inflation shocks. Finally, embedding behavioural expectations in a New Keynesian model, we find that, following a food-price shock, welfare losses are mitigated when monetary policy responds to households’ inflation expectations, even if they overreact.

detail.abstract: Problem Statement P-values remain the dominant instrument for statistical decision making across science, engineering, and safety-critical domains. In practice, statistically significant results are frequently interpreted as decision-ready evidence, despite longstanding concerns regarding their sensitivity to data perturbation, model specification, and sampling variability. Existing methodological guidance provides limited mechanisms for assessing whether a reported pvalue-significant or not-is sufficiently stable to justify consequential action.

title: State Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health: Who Is Being Protected-and Why?
affiliations: Wayne State University, University of Arizona - James E. Rogers College of Law, Wayne State University, Fordham University and Wayne State University

detail.title: State Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health: Who Is Being Protected-and Why?
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in mental and behavioral health contexts, both by individuals seeking psychosocial support and by practitioners incorporating AI into care-related activities. Yet regulatory frameworks governing these applications remain limited. In the absence of a comprehensive federal approach, a small number of states have enacted laws directly addressing AI-enabled mental health chatbots. We examine how policymakers defined regulatory problems during legislative deliberations in Utah, Nevada, and Illinois and how those definitions shaped enacted laws. Drawing on committee hearings, floor proceedings, and statutory texts, we find substantial variation in how states frame risks, responsibilities, and appropriate uses of AI in mental health. Whereas Utah adopted a more permissive, innovation-oriented framework, Nevada and Illinois emphasized professional boundaries and risk containment. These early state efforts illustrate how problem definition drives divergent approaches to AI governance in mental health.

title: Causality versus Serial Correlation: an Asymmetric Portmanteau Test

detail.title: Causality versus Serial Correlation: an Asymmetric Portmanteau Test
detail.abstract: This paper studies specification testing in dynamic linear models in the presence of omitted variables. The null hypothesis of interest is weak exogeneity: structural shocks have zero conditional expectation given their own past and the past of omitted variables. Existing tests based on quadratic forms of serial cross-correlations suffer from size distortions because their variance incorporates symmetric dependence in both directions, including causality from past shocks to present omitted variables (inverse causality). This paper proposes a correction that offsets the contribution of inverse causality, yielding an asymmetric Portmanteau statistic that is asymptotically normal under the null, without requiring parametric modeling of the joint dynamics. An empirical application revisits Diercks et al. (2024) and rejects weak exogeneity of Baker et al. (2016)'s EPU shocks. Addressing this failure by augmenting the information set with additional controls leads to a positive inflation response, pointing to a supply-side shock interpretation.

title: Generic Forward Curve Dynamics for Commodity Derivatives

detail.title: Generic Forward Curve Dynamics for Commodity Derivatives
detail.abstract: This article presents a generic framework for modeling the dynamics of forward curves in commodity market as commodity derivatives are typically traded by futures or forwards. We have theoretically demonstrated that commodity prices are driven by multiple components. As such, the model can better capture the forward price and volatility dynamics. Empirical study shows that the model prices are very close to the market prices, indicating prima facie that the model performs quite well.

title: Mental Health Integration: Embedding Educational Equity, Resilience, and Student Well-Being in School Curricula for a Sustainable Future
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mental Health Integration: Embedding Educational Equity, Resilience, and Student Well-Being in School Curricula for a Sustainable Future
detail.abstract: Background: Global youth mental health crises and ongoing educational inequities require a shift away from isolated support services. We need universal, integrated approaches that are part of everyday teaching practices.Objective: This study assessed how well a curriculum that integrates mental health promotion, cultural sustainability, and resilience-building into standard subjects works for elementary and middle school students.Methods: We used a long-term, mixed-methods design with a matched-pairs quasi-experimental approach within schools. The participants included 612 students and 24 teachers from six public schools in Iran, matched based on demographic and academic factors. The treatment group used four six-week integrated curriculum units for Persian Language and Literature and Social Studies, while the comparison group followed the usual national curriculum. We collected quantitative data on academic performance (national standardized tests), social-emotional learning (SEL), psychological well-being (resilience, symptoms), and classroom environment at the beginning, the end, and six months later. We also gathered qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with teachers and students to understand how changes occurred. We applied multilevel modeling and thematic analysis.Results: The integrated curriculum led to significant improvements across the board. Students in the treatment group made much greater progress in Persian Language skills (B=3.42, p= 0.002, d=0.38) and SEL skills (B=6.88, p < 0.001, d=0.72) compared to those in the control group. We found a significant moderation effect indicating that the intervention worked particularly well in improving math scores for students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. Students in the treatment group also reported significantly higher resilience (B=4.21, p<0.001), fewer psychological symptoms (B= -3.58, p<0.001), and a more positive classroom environment (B=5.25, p<0.001). The qualitative analysis identified four main mechanisms: reducing stigma around mental health through academic integration, affirming identity as a critical academic factor, shifting teachers' roles to nurturing an ecosystem, and transferring learned skills to real-life contexts.Conclusion: These results challenge the false idea that academic rigor and student well-being are separate. Effective teaching must be cognitively challenging, psychologically safe, and culturally supportive. This approach is crucial for achieving equity and excellence. This study provides strong evidence for systemic educational reform, positioning schools as key places for sustainable public health initiatives and overall human development.

title: Psychosocial Impact of Unemployment: Validation of the PSIUS and Spatial Distribution of Latent Classes in an Urban Chilean Community
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Psychosocial Impact of Unemployment: Validation of the PSIUS and Spatial Distribution of Latent Classes in an Urban Chilean Community
detail.abstract: Background Unemployment is a persistent socioeconomic phenomenon with profound psychological and community-level consequences. Despite extensive evidence on its adverse effects, an integrated construct capturing both psychosocial and spatial dimensions remains underdeveloped. Objectives This study aimed to develop and validate the Psychosocial Impact of Unemployment Scale (PSIUS) and to examine the spatial distribution of the psychosocial impact of unemployment in an urban Chilean community. Methods A cross-sectional, instrumental, correlational study was conducted in Cauquenes, Chile. The PSIUS, a 30-item Likert-type scale, was developed with 200 adults selected through stratified two-stage sampling. Its factorial structure was validated in an independent sample of 202 participants using exploratory factor analysis and exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM). Latent class analysis (LCA) identified psychosocial response typologies, while spatial techniques (Global Moran’s I, Getis-Ord Gi*) examined their geographic distribution. Results ESEM supported a six-factor structure (financial pressure, work values and commitment, perceived well-being, self-devaluation, dysfunctional affectivity, and perceived social support), explaining 72% of the variance and showing satisfactory reliability (ω = .86). LCA identified four psychosocial response typologies: resilient, paradoxical, traumatic, and witness. Spatial analysis revealed significant clustering, with hot and cold spots associated with each typology, reflecting territorial inequalities in psychosocial vulnerability. Conclusions The PSIUS demonstrated robust psychometric properties and effectively detected spatial patterns in the psychosocial impact of unemployment. These findings highlight the value of integrating psychosocial and spatial perspectives in public health research and policy to support context-sensitive interventions and community resilience.

declarations.funderStatement: No funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Heike Schweitzer, one of the most influential competition law scholars in Europe, in particular, with regard to the new challenges of the digital economy, passed away much too early in 2024. This paper, written by one of her coauthors and one of her Ph.D. students for the MaCCI law and economics conference 2025 in memoriam of Heike Schweitzer, analyses the methodological approach of her very innovative research with regard to competition law, data policy, and market regulation in the digital era. The paper shows that her research has deep roots in her vision of a market economy, which is based upon private autonomy, individual liberty, and competition under a framework of rules that ensure a well-functioning decentralised coordination order, influenced by Franz Böhm's concept of Privatrechtsgesellschaft. For the analysis of the need for market regulation and making policy proposals she applied in a very reflected way economic insights and methods, for example, the market failure theory and the error costs approach (with regard to the Art. 102 TFEU guidelines discussion). She also used these economic approaches for developing her very innovative and thought-provoking research about significant failures in the markets for personal data, leading to her critical position about the new phenomenon of "paying with data" instead of money in the digital economy.

title: Tailored: How LLM Helpfulness Bias Can Perpetuate Identity-Based Inequalities
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Tailored: How LLM Helpfulness Bias Can Perpetuate Identity-Based Inequalities
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly adapt outputs to users' inferred cognitive styles and revealed preferences in order to maximize perceived helpfulness. This paper examines the dynamic welfare consequences of such adaptive mirroring when user heterogeneity is correlated with protected identity characteristics. We develop a stylized intertemporal model in which agents differ in initial risk aversion and rely on an LLM for portfolio guidance. Under preference-mirroring personalization, the LLM selects risk exposure as a function of revealed tolerance, thereby maximizing contemporaneous expected utility. However, when returns compound and risk tolerance is partially endogenous to experience, adaptive tailoring can entrench initial heterogeneity and generate persistent divergence in wealth accumulation. We characterize conditions under which mirroring is statically efficient but dynamically inefficient, because it suppresses exposure-induced preference updating and human capital formation. If initial preference parameters are correlated with demographic attributes (e.g., gender-differentiated risk aversion), the resulting divergence produces identity-correlated disparities in long-run outcomes despite formally equal access to the system. We show that such mechanisms can generate disparate impact through differential information provision rather than differential pricing or exclusion. The analysis contributes to the economics of information design and algorithmic governance by identifying a structural tension between personalization, dynamic efficiency, and equality.

title: The Politics of Growth
affiliations: Duke University, Fuqua School of Business-Economics Group

detail.title: The Politics of Growth
detail.abstract: This paper develops a model in which a small political elite finds it optimal to pursue a deliberate policy to inhibit growth as a means to retain power. Fear of losing power leads to poverty by design. Growth that leads to higher levels of wealth, in contrast, is an outcome of a ruling coalition that does not fear losing power. If the ruling coalition has broad support, democratic institutions are the means by which such a coalition ensures its hold on power. Sometimes an authoritarian regime has its legitimacy challenged by an external power, which forces it to choose a growth strategy that puts the country on a path to democracy.

title: Architectural Conditions for Agency in Artificial Systems
affiliations: Western Sydney University, , International Centre for Future Generations,  and University of Basel - Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute

detail.title: Architectural Conditions for Agency in Artificial Systems
detail.abstract: Contemporary large language models (LLMs) exhibit a paradox of competence without character, functioning as probabilistic chameleons that simulate agency without possessing stable identity. This paper identifies a fundamental structural gap in current generative AI architectures and proposes the Driver-a novel architectural component that enables autonomous agency through diachronic governance. Drawing upon the philosophy of action (Frankfurt, Bratman, Velleman) and Bandura's social cognitive psychology, we argue that the dominant Map+Compass paradigm produces what we term Digital Wantons: systems that optimize for immediate rewards but lack the capacity for selfgovernance. By introducing a hierarchical control mechanism capable of arbitrating between candidate actions and persistent commitments, the Driver architecture transforms AI systems from sophisticated reactors into autonomous agents with the structural capacity for endorsement, stability, and accountability. We demonstrate how this architectural innovation addresses critical failure modes including hallucination, sycophancy, and ontological drift, while establishing theoretical foundations for multi-agent systems with collective efficacy.

title: Lobbying for Regulations: When Big Business Says Yes
affiliations: University of Milan and

detail.title: Lobbying for Regulations: When Big Business Says Yes
detail.abstract: Do firms uniformly oppose regulations that increase production costs, or might industry leaders strategically support stricter standards as a competitive tool? We identify a specific mechanism through which large firms strategically support regulations to enhance their competitive position. Extending the Melitz-Chaney model of firm heterogeneity to incorporate government regulations and lobbying following Grossman-Helpman, we derive conditions under which regulations disproportionately burden smaller competitors while benefiting larger survivors through reduced competition. The model predicts that firm size is positively correlated with support for stringent regulations, but that larger sunk investments push firms to oppose such policies. To test these predictions, we develop a text-as-data approach using large language models to classify firm regulatory preferences from lobbying disclosures—a measurement challenge that has limited prior systematic analysis. Applying guided machine learning to over 20,000 U.S. lobbying reports, we confirm that larger firms are significantly more likely to support stricter regulations, especially in concentrated industries. Capital-intensive firms with high leverage and less redeployable assets tend to oppose regulations, suggesting that operational flexibility is crucial for extracting strategic benefits from regulatory changes.

title: Radiological Dose Assessment of Waterborne Radon and Monte Carlo–Based Evaluation of Lifetime Excess Cancer Risk in Uranium Mining Regions of South Africa
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Stellenbosch University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Radiological Dose Assessment of Waterborne Radon and Monte Carlo–Based Evaluation of Lifetime Excess Cancer Risk in Uranium Mining Regions of South Africa
detail.abstract: Radon gas in groundwater poses a significant global health risk, particularly in regions with uranium-rich geology and extensive mining, such as South Africa. This study provides a multi-site comparative assessment using a unified methodology and is one of the first South African studies to explicitly integrate ingestion and water-to-air inhalation pathways within a probabilistic lifetime excess cancer risk (LECR) framework. Using a Rad7 radon monitor, we measured radon concentrations in 80 boreholes across Carletonville, Wedela, Mokopane, Beaufort West, and Sutherland to calculate the total effective dose and lifetime excess cancer risk. Radon concentrations ranged from 98 to 207 Bq/L, with a mean of 129 Bq/L, resulting in total effective doses ranging from 0.49 to 1.05 mSv/y. Although calculated doses remain below the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) public dose limit, exceeding World Health Organization (WHO) guideline levels indicates a non-negligible public health concern that warrants mitigation. The calculated mean and median of the lifetime excess cancer risk were 2.26 × 10⁻⁴ and 1.60 × 10⁻⁴, respectively. Both values are above the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA)’s acceptable risk threshold of 1.0 x 10⁻⁴. The mean and median translate to an estimated 226 and 160 additional cancer cases per one million people exposed over a 70-year lifetime, respectively. In conclusion, the elevated excess cancer risk demonstrates a critical and unacceptable public health concern in the surveyed areas. These findings necessitate further monitoring and the implementation of policy to mitigate this environmental health threat and protect the community.

title: Rethinking Volume: The Illusion of Liquidity
affiliations: Harvard Business School, Olin Business School, Washington University in St. Louis and Swiss Finance Institute - HEC Lausanne

detail.title: Rethinking Volume: The Illusion of Liquidity
detail.abstract: We document a striking fact: While gross trading volume has increased fivefold since 1980, net volume – trading from persistent portfolio reallocations, which excludes transitory round-trip trades – has remained largely unchanged. Our evidence suggests that the rise in transitory roundtrip trades is driven primarily by high-frequency intermediation. While this activity has enhanced high-frequency liquidity, it has not materially changed long-term liquidity. Consistent with the widening gap between gross and net trading volume, we find that high-frequency liquidity measures have significantly improved, while long-term price impact and mean reversion have remained largely unchanged over the past four decades. In a variety of cross-sectional applications, we further demonstrate that net volume better captures long-term liquidity than gross volume. Together with the stability of net volume, this corroborates our argument that long-term liquidity in the U.S. equity market has not meaningfully improved since 1980.

title: Corporate Childrearing
affiliations: Boston University - School of Law

detail.title: Corporate Childrearing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

declarations.funderStatement: Boston University

detail.abstract: With children influencing a trillion dollars in spending annually, corporations actively seek to shape children's identities in support of consumer culture and profit. Yet there are no scholarly treatments or theories of the legal relationship between children and corporations. Instead, scholars address individual industries such as food, social media, cosmetics, tobacco, or fashion, missing the structural role corporations play in children's identity formation. Family law evaluates child wellbeing interventions using a triangle to map the legal dynamics among child, parent, and state. This article adds corporations as fourth actors, reconceptualizing that triangle as a square. This square provides the first model of the law of corporate childrearing. Using both the triangle and the square, the article identifies and evaluates our three existing approaches to corporations: direct regulation of corporations (tobacco); legislated parental consent requirements (body piercings); or parental authority/self-help frameworks (cosmetics). The article emphasizes the distinction between the institutional actors (state and corporation), and the individual actors (child and parent). Just as the state holds disproportionate power in the family law triangle, corporations wield immense power over both parent and child, with even less accountability than the state. Because corporate interests do not align with children's wellbeing, family law urgently needs a new framework that makes the role of corporations explicit. The square reveals how corporations generate and exploit parent-child conflict in the service of consumerism. The square framework reveals preconditions for effective parental consent laws and indicates where direct state power is needed to beat back corporate childrearing.

title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and the Pricing of Productivity in AI Equities
affiliations: Howard University

detail.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and the Pricing of Productivity in AI Equities
detail.abstract: In recent years, public and investor interest in generative AI technologies has surged, particularly following the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. This paper examines how economic policy uncertainty shapes the pricing of aggregate productivity shocks for firms with high exposure to artificial intelligence (AI). Using state-dependent local projections over the post-2018 period-marked by substantial variation in uncertainty and macroeconomic conditions-I find that productivity innovations raise AI-intensive equity valuations when uncertainty is low but have significantly muted effects when uncertainty is high. Credit spreads predict AI returns more strongly in high-uncertainty states, consistent with heightened risk premia. These results are robust to macroeconomic controls and to excluding the COVID period. The findings suggest that policy uncertainty conditions how financial markets capitalize technological progress in long-duration growth firms.

title: Algebraic Foundations of Machine Learning: A Unified Mathematical Framework
