detail.title: Algebraic Foundations of Machine Learning: A Unified Mathematical Framework
detail.abstract: We present a unified algebraic framework for machine learning in which a "neural network" is formalized as a parameterized morphism in a structured category via the Para construction. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation, identified with cotangent pullbacks once a Euclidean (or bundle) duality choice is fixed. We then develop a hierarchy of algebraic constraints-group equivariance, algebra-valued features, tropical piecewise-linear geometry, operator-theoretic stability, attention as kernel learning, gauge equivariance on bundles, tensor-network compression, discrete semilattice learning, and singular learning theory. The guiding thesis is structure is prescriptive: algebraic constraints simultaneously (i) restrict admissible architectures, (ii) refine expressivity, and (iii) control generalization through compression in multiple senses (parameter reduction, low-rank factorization, description length, and effective Bayesian complexity via RLCT). We develop three areas with particular depth: operator networks, gauge equivariance, and tensor networks. For operator networks we provide explicit functional-analytic hypotheses, perturbation bounds, and finite-rank truncation theorems. For gauge equivariance we give a rigorous reformulation of gauge-equivariant operators as (connection, section) pairs, a proof that parallel-transport kernels are gauge-equivariant, a literature-supported density result for the discrete graph setting, and a precisely stated conjecture for compact manifolds. For tensor networks we derive a description-length generalization bound specialized to tensor-train compression.

title: Amplification Authority and Inferior Consensus in Evolutionary Systems
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Amplification Authority and Inferior Consensus in Evolutionary Systems
detail.abstract: This paper develops an evolutionary model in which institutions influence consensus formation by modifying amplification intensity rather than intrinsic payoffs. In nonlinear social environments governed by conformity and performative feedback, long-run outcomes depend on basin structure rather than value superiority alone. The analysis shows that inferior types can become consensus in decentralized systems due to tipping dynamics. It further demonstrates that institutional amplification can either eliminate or facilitate such inferior consensus by shifting equilibrium accessibility without altering underlying payoffs. The central contribution is to formalize amplification authority as equilibrium selection authority within evolutionary systems.

title: Healthcare Expenditure Rationing: Evidence from Tax Records
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics, University of Rome Tor Vergata and Universitas Mercatorum

detail.title: Healthcare Expenditure Rationing: Evidence from Tax Records
detail.abstract: We test the hypothesis of healthcare expenditure rationing on a unique database of more than 6 million tax records over 5 years We find that individuals in the lowest income tax bracket report around 1200 € lower health expenditure than those in the highest bracket after controlling for observable concurring factors. Fixed-effects estimates do not reject the healthcare rationing hypothesis showing a significant positive within-effect of income on health expenditure. Rationing is higher among the elders and healthcare expenditure income elasticities are up to three times higher in the lowest than in the highest income bracket. These findings suggest that richest taxpayers show a nearly inelastic spending pattern consistent with consumption saturation, while poorer taxpayers exhibit a steep response to income changes, indicating latent healthcare needs unmet due to budget constraints. Higher income individuals also report in their tax files higher average costs of medical intervention and drugs, reflecting both quantity and quality rationing.

title: Essential Levels of Care, Prevention and Inequality in Private Health Spending
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics, Departiment of Economics, Roma Tre University and Universitas Mercatorum

detail.title: Essential Levels of Care, Prevention and Inequality in Private Health Spending
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how regional differences in the effective implementation of Italy's Essential Levels of Care (Livelli Essenziali di Assistenza, LEA) relate to private health expenditure, using a large administrative dataset of more than 6.6 million taxpayer-year observations and exploiting substantial cross-regional variation in LEA quality. While higher public health standards might be expected to reduce the need for privately financed care, theory also allows for the opposite mechanism: well-functioning public systems may increase contacts with providers, detection of needs and care intensity, thereby stimulating complementary private spending. To test these competing hypotheses, we compare findings from pooled, fixed effects, and two-part models. Results show that higher regional LEA performance is systematically associated with lower individual out-of-pocket health expenditure. In pooled and fixed-effects linear models, a 1-point increase in the lagged LEA reduces annual private spending by approximately €0.4-0.8 per person. Two-part models yield even larger combined marginal effects, showing that LEA quality crowds out private spending along both the extensive margin (lower probability of any positive expenditure) and the intensive margin (lower conditional spending among users), with the effect being concentrated mainly on the prevention component. The evidence supports the crowding-out hypothesis and highlights the role of effective LEA implementation as a financial protection device in a decentralised universal healthcare system, which can be crucial to increase low-income households' access to care.

title: Innovation without Growth
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: Innovation without Growth
detail.abstract: Standard growth models treat innovation as one-dimensional: higher innovation effort implies faster frontier expansion and stronger long-run growth. This paper shows that this inference fails when innovation is multidimensional. Innovation effort can be directed either toward expanding the technological frontier or toward improving productivity relative to an existing frontier, but only the former sustains long-run growth. Shifts in private incentives can reallocate innovation toward activities with strong short-run payoffs but limited growth relevance. As a result, measured innovation and short-run productivity growth may rise even as long-run growth declines. This result does not rely on declining research productivity. Instead, it reflects an inference problem: aggregate innovation measures conflate activities with different growth implications and therefore cease to be sufficient statistics for growth. Crosscountry evidence is consistent with this compositional mechanism. The findings have implications for interpreting productivity dynamics and for the design of innovation policy.

title: Parent Perceptions of a Child Welfare-based Unconditional Cash Transfer Program: A Qualitative Study
affiliations: University of Delaware, School of Criminal Justice, Rutgers University, University of Washington, School of Criminal Justice, Rutgers University, University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania and Denver Health

detail.title: Parent Perceptions of a Child Welfare-based Unconditional Cash Transfer Program: A Qualitative Study
detail.abstract:
Background: Poverty-related needs are associated with child welfare involvement. Unconditional cash transfers are one mechanism to address these conditions, yet few child welfare systems have examined their impacts for parents and families. We conducted a qualitative study within a larger randomized controlled trial to assess the perceptions of and perceived impact of a child welfare-based unconditional cash transfer program.
 
Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 40 parents randomized to the trial’s treatment arm. The intervention consisted of $500 monthly unconditional cash transfers for 1 year. Interviews probed parental experiences with child welfare, experience in the cash transfer program, and the perceived impact of the intervention. Interviews were coded using an inductive and deductive approach to identify emergent themes.  

Results: Participants described the intervention as having positive impacts on their families, including improved ability to meet basic needs, investments in family health and child safety, and increased opportunities for parent-child bonding. Participants often reflected that earlier access to these benefits could have mitigated the circumstances that led to their child welfare referrals. Some participants expressed initial skepticism about the program due to fear of further family surveillance. Despite their reticence to engage with child welfare, participants universally expressed a positive opinion of the program.  

Conclusions: These findings suggest that unconditional cash transfers may be a promising intervention to mitigate child welfare involvement. Future research should explore the impacts of cash transfers programs on family perceptions of and trust in child welfare.

title: Robust Time-series Generation under Extreme Data Scarcity: An Engineering Benchmarking Study of Fuzzy and Lyapunov-regularized Adversarial Networks

detail.title: Robust Time-series Generation under Extreme Data Scarcity: An Engineering Benchmarking Study of Fuzzy and Lyapunov-regularized Adversarial Networks
detail.abstract:
Time-series generation under extreme data scarcity poses a fundamental challenge for machine learning systems deployed in decision-critical domains such as epidemiological monitoring, financial risk analysis, and engineering forecasting. While modern generative models perform well in data-rich settings, their reliability degrades sharply when available observations are severely limited, often leading to unstable training and poor temporal consistency. 
     This paper presents a stability-aware generative framework, referred to as FGAN, which integrates fuzzy regime modeling with Lyapunov-inspired regularization to improve robustness in ultra-scarce data regimes. Fuzzy memberships provide uncertainty-aware representations of partially observable temporal states, while the Lyapunov-based regularizer constrains generator sensitivity and suppresses unstable or chaotic dynamics during adversarial training. 
     A comprehensive empirical evaluation is conducted against seven state-of-the-art generative baselines across three real-world application domains: cholera surveillance, influenza-like illness monitoring, and financial volatility modeling. Experiments span multiple data availability levels and employ a unified set of evaluation metrics covering distributional fidelity, temporal structure preservation, forecasting utility, and privacy-related characteristics. 
     Results demonstrate that FGAN consistently outperforms competing methods across all scarcity levels, achieving substantial improvements in distributional accuracy and temporal coherence, while maintaining favorable performance–efficiency trade-offs. These findings indicate that stability-aware fuzzy–Lyapunov regularization offers a practical and effective foundation for reliable time-series generation in data-poor engineering applications.

title: Export Intensity & SMEs' Access to Bank Finance: Evidence from SAFE Database
affiliations: University of Glasgow - Adam Smith Business School, University of Glasgow, Faculty of Social Sciences, Department of Economics, Students, University of Glasgow and University of Glasgow - Department of Economics

detail.title: Export Intensity & SMEs' Access to Bank Finance: Evidence from SAFE Database
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the COVID-19 shock altered SMEs' financing conditions asymmetrically by international exposure. We use the ECB Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) for 2014-2022 to build firm-level measures of credit constraints based on loan application outcomes, and estimate a difference-indifferences specification interacting a post-COVID indicator with continuous export intensity. Export-intensive SMEs experience a disproportionate tightening of credit constraints after the pandemic onset, with effects concentrated in bank loans rather than credit lines. Measures of financing needs and application behavior show no differential increase in credit demand among exporters, supporting a credit-supply interpretation. The tightening is mainly explained by quantity rationing-exporters are more likely to receive smaller loan amounts than requested-consistent with banks scaling back exposures under elevated trade uncertainty. The findings highlight a financial amplification channel through which trade disruptions can impair SME activity even amid extensive policy support.

title: Handbook of Research on base of the Pyramid Entrepreneurship - Introduction
affiliations: and Suffolk University

detail.title: Handbook of Research on base of the Pyramid Entrepreneurship - Introduction
detail.abstract: This introductory chapter sets the stage for the Handbook's exploration of entrepreneurship at the Base of the Pyramid (BoP), a field that has evolved significantly since its emergence over two decades ago. We outline the unique characteristics of BoP entrepreneurship, including the profile of BoP entrepreneurs, the diversity of actors active at the BoP, the complexity of BoP contexts, and the innovative business models that arise in those contexts. We highlight how BoP entrepreneurship presents unique opportunity to challenge and enrich mainstream entrepreneurship theory and methodology, and management more generally. This introductory chapter also presents the structure of the Handbook, which is organized into three parts: (1) Understanding the Field: Theoretical and Empirical Perspectives, (2) Delving into the Setting: The BoP Context for Entrepreneurs and Its Varieties, and (3) Emerging Issues in BoP Entrepreneurship, and introduces each chapter one by one.

title: Optimal Incentives and the Price of Information in Sequential Production with Private Costs
affiliations: and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Optimal Incentives and the Price of Information in Sequential Production with Private Costs
detail.abstract: We characterize optimal investment-inducing mechanisms for sequential production processes with private costs and quantify the price of information relative to Winter (2006). In our model, a project consists of n tasks performed sequentially by n agents. Each agent decides whether to invest in her task, paying a privately known cost and guaranteeing success, or to shirk, in which case the task succeeds only probabilistically. The principal commits to a reward vector contingent on overall project success and seeks a mechanism that induces all agents to invest in the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium while minimizing total rewards uniformly over all admissible cost profiles. We first show that a natural extension of Winter's optimal mechanism under public costs fails to guarantee investment when costs are private and that simple "robust" uniform reward schemes are strictly suboptimal. We then fully characterize optimal investment-inducing mechanisms under private costs. For homogeneous costs, we derive a closed-form asymmetric reward vector that guarantees investment and minimizes total reward. For heterogeneous costs with a common non-investment success probability, the optimal mechanism is uniform across agents and depends only on the upper bounds of their cost supports. When task importance (non-investment success probabilities) is non-uniform, we obtain closed-form optimal rewards for any assignment of tasks and agents, and identify optimal task-agent matching. Finally, we introduce a notion of the price of information (PoI): the supremum over instances of the ratio between the optimal total reward under private costs and that under public costs. We establish that the PoI grows on the order of n/ log n in the homogeneouscost model, is exactly nr in the heterogeneous-cost model when cost supports are bounded by a factor r, and is unbounded when task importance varies sufficiently across tasks. We also extend the analysis to probability thresholds for project success, obtaining analogous results in a probability-constrained formulation.

title: How Much Financial Flexibility Is Optimal? A Closed-form Capital Structure Model for Investment-grade Firms
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: How Much Financial Flexibility Is Optimal? A Closed-form Capital Structure Model for Investment-grade Firms
detail.abstract: Investment-grade (IG) firms often manage capital structure by preserving financial flexibility and rating resilience rather than targeting a precise leverage ratio. I develop a tractable continuous-time model in which the key financing choice is contractual headroom: the firm selects a trigger threshold V g at which debt pricing steps up and reverts upon recovery. Optimal V g trades off tax benefits against expected trigger-based tightening costs and an issuance-time concession tied to headroom, yielding a closed-form interior solution. Implied leverage follows endogenously, and a simple Debt/EBITDA mapping expresses the policy in familiar covenant terms. Comparative statics provide clear predictions for how headroom and implied leverage vary with taxes, repricing severity, and debt-service burden.

title: Child Protection, Juvenile Justice, and Social Rehabilitation in Africa: Law, Policy, and Practice

detail.title: Child Protection, Juvenile Justice, and Social Rehabilitation in Africa: Law, Policy, and Practice
detail.abstract:
The paper provides a study on child protection, juvenile justice and social rehabilitation using data across Africa as the focal point. It explores the interconnected socio-legal system shaping the safety experience for young people, the effectiveness of reintegration, the extent of marginalisation and the frequency of recurring harm. The paper analyses the extent to which normative commitments through the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child and the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child are implemented, and addresses any gaps. The treaties have been ratified to a large extent, and there is evidence to show the permeation of child-focused legislation, yet the argument is based on constraints on the outcomes stemming from poorly resourced social welfare services, incompetency and limitation of specialised staff within, especially the police and courts, overreliance on the detention system, including that for minor offences and institutional mandates that are unfavourably fragmented.

The paper additionally discusses the effectiveness of diversion and restorative justice, thus, making sure it respects due process and alternatives to punitive justice with cultural sensitivity. It highlights programme access and availability disparities and the challenge of the lack of safeguards that protect victims from coercion and other threats. It discusses a paradigm shift from social rehabilitation rooted in individualism to the notion of social inclusion, where change is based on continuous education, family-based support systems, psychosocial and mental health services, and reintegration models that are community-based.   The paper draws the conclusion that reforms can only be sustainable through a robust rehabilitation infrastructure; this would imply that reforms are child-centred, dependent upon due process, enshrined in community service systems which are designed to bridge child protection and juvenile justice. It would imply that dignity and participation become the central focus in the reformation process, notwithstanding a workforce that is well-resourced and adequately trained. Without these changes, legal reform will only contribute to entrenching exclusion and do very little to advancing social cohesion and public safety.

title: Automated Routing, Patent Examiner Specialization and Quasi-random Assignment at the USPTO
affiliations: United States Patent and Trademark Office and EMLV

detail.title: Automated Routing, Patent Examiner Specialization and Quasi-random Assignment at the USPTO
detail.abstract: In October 2020, the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) introduced an automated process for routing new patent applications, in part to increase examiner specialization. In this research note, we first assess whether the USPTO achieved this objective using a difference-indifferences (DiD) research design on a sample of applications assigned to examiners between 2018 and 2021. The new routing system increased technical overlap between examiner work histories and newly assigned cases by nearly 57 percent, indicating a substantial increase in examiner specialization across the agency. In addition, we show that automated routinglargely unknown in the academic literature-effectively eliminated quasi-random assignment of applications to examiners. Given the importance of quasi-random assignment for empirical research, we discuss our findings within this context and their potential impact on future research.

title: Since the Bureau Acknowledges it Protects Competition in Future Markets, it must also Acknowledge that it Applies the Future Markets Model
affiliations: Bridgeline Solutions

detail.title: Since the Bureau Acknowledges it Protects Competition in Future Markets, it must also Acknowledge that it Applies the Future Markets Model
detail.abstract: In its draft Merger Enforcement Guidelines the Competition Bureau Canada acknowledges that when it protects competition to innovate it protects competition in Future Markets, markets for products at least some of which do not exist yet.  The Bureau has thus recognized, as the author had previously suggested it should, that it cannot directly protect competition to innovate (as the European Commission claims it can).  The Bureau should now take the next logical step and acknowledge that when it analyzes competition in Future Markets it applies the Future Markets Model.  It must apply the Model; its just a matter of logic.

title: Private Capital as a Network Phenomenon: A Graph-theoretic Analysis of Deal Flow, Contagion Risk, and Long-term Value at Rothschild & Co
affiliations: Universitas Tanjungpura

detail.title: Private Capital as a Network Phenomenon: A Graph-theoretic Analysis of Deal Flow, Contagion Risk, and Long-term Value at Rothschild & Co
detail.abstract:
BACKGROUND-Private capital markets or private equity, venture capital, and private debt, that are difficult to analyse because prices are hidden, assets are hard to sell quickly, and value depends on who you are connected to, not just what you own. Standard valuation tools like Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) and Net Asset Value (NAV) look at each firm in isolation and completely miss these relationship-driven dynamics, leaving investors and regulators unable to see risks building up across the network until it is too late.
OBJECTIVE-This study introduces the Illiquid Network Value with Contagion Risk (INVeCR) model with a new valuation framework that treats private capital as a network and prices assets based on how connected a firm is, how illiquid its network position makes it, and how financial distress can spread from firm to firm. Using two years of real transaction data from Rothschild & Co (2023-2024), the study provides the first real-world measurement of how network position adds to, or subtracts from a firm's value.
METHODS-A financial network was built from Rothschild & Co transaction records, mapping 120 funds across four entity types: General Partners (GPs), Limited Partners (LPs), Portfolio Companies, and Feeder Funds. For each firm, three connectivity measures were calculated: how central it is as a broker (betweenness centrality), how influential its connections are (eigenvector centrality), and how tightly clustered its neighbourhood is (clustering coefficient). These measures were used to adjust discount rates, estimate illiquidity costs, and simulate how financial distress would spread through the network under stress. Three hypotheses were tested and the model's valuations were compared against traditional DCF across 80 funds.
RESULTS-All three hypotheses were confirmed. Firms in central network positions earned nearly 20 percentage points more in annual returns than peripheral firms. Denser networks amplified financial distress almost one-for-one. Network-based illiquidity costs explained 88% of real-world pricing variation, far outperforming the standard fixed-discount approach. Against traditional DCF, INVeCR cut valuation errors by 67% and improved pricing accuracy by 50%. It also detected regime shifts 18 days earlier on average. The key finding: where a firm sits in the network matters as much as what it earns, with an information that conventional models ignore entirely.

detail.abstract:
The Global State of Open Banking and Open Finance Report examines the diverse regulatory and operational landscape for open banking and open finance across 95 jurisdictions. This comprehensive study provides an analysis of governance practices, highlights factors driving convergence or divergence among frameworks, and draws lessons from varying implementation strategies that are shaping the future of data sharing in financial services.

Conducted by the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAF) with the support of the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, this precedential offers critical insights for regulators, policymakers, and financial institutions worldwide, with particular attention to emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs).

title: The Efficiency Audit: Eliminating Performative Intermediaries in High-Stakes Deployments
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Efficiency Audit: Eliminating Performative Intermediaries in High-Stakes Deployments
detail.abstract:
This audit identifies a systemic waste pattern in corporate and government innovation spending termed the "Arbitrage of Ignorance." In this model, intermediary organizations—including accelerators, innovation labs, and traditional consultancies—capture an estimated $50–100B annually by monetizing process complexity rather than delivering measurable outcomes. By analyzing 47 major initiatives across 12 sectors, this research quantifies the operational and financial chasm between "Curriculum" approaches (education/awareness) and "Mechanism" approaches (infrastructure/access).

Core Findings:

  1. The Mechanism vs. Curriculum Principle: Data indicates that direct mechanism deployment achieves outcomes at 40–60% lower cost than education-first strategies. For example, M-KOPA solar infrastructure achieved a cost of $2.1M/MW compared to $15M/MW for training-focused programs—an 85% efficiency delta. The research concludes that access must precede education; training users for systems they cannot yet access constitutes structural waste.

  2. The Intermediary Tax: The average "innovation consultancy" engagement costs between $1.5M and $2.5M and extends project timelines by 8–12 months. Comparative analysis reveals that direct vendor procurement and internal mechanism design achieve identical outcomes at a 75–85% cost reduction. The signature of this waste is the delivery of "soft" assets—workshops, alignment sessions, and reports—rather than deployed products or legal instruments.

  3. Regulatory Friction and Architecture: In high-stakes sectors such as nuclear, defense, and healthcare, regulatory overhead accounts for 60–70% of deployment delays. The audit found that "Bypass Strategies"—utilizing alternative jurisdictions or pre-approved zones—reduce timelines by 50–65%. A critical strategic pivot is required: organizations must stop funding "navigators" of broken regulations and begin funding the architecture of regulatory reform.

The Solution Framework: The audit proposes a three-part protocol for capital efficiency:

  • Dismantle Hollow Structures: Institute a 90-day "tangible asset" requirement for all initiatives. Funding must be converted to milestone tranches tied to unit economics, terminating intermediaries that cannot demonstrate measurable deployment.

  • Architect Regulatory Bypasses: Prioritize deployment in permissive jurisdictions to gather empirical safety and operational data. This track record can then be leveraged to secure exemptions in restrictive markets and force policy reform.

  • Direct-Fund Mechanisms: Redirect capital from "capacity building" to infrastructure deployment. Measure success via cost-per-deployed-unit rather than activities completed or participants trained.

Projected Impact: Organizations implementing this framework consistently achieve a 40–60% reduction in innovation spending, 3–5x faster time-to-deployment, and a 70% increase in projects reaching full operational status.

Conclusion: The bottleneck to high-stakes innovation is not a scarcity of ideas or capital, but the presence of structural friction. Strategic operators must evolve from grant and program managers into mechanism architects: designing systems that eliminate intermediaries, bypass regulatory blockers, and enforce tangible outcomes. If a project does not result in a deployed asset, it is not innovation; it is curriculum.

title: Will the New European Fiscal Rules Raise the Debt-to-GDP Ratio? An Analysis of the Italian Case
affiliations: University Campus Bio-Medico

detail.title: Will the New European Fiscal Rules Raise the Debt-to-GDP Ratio? An Analysis of the Italian Case

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 243
publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The recent reform of the European fiscal governance framework has been portrayed as a break with the austerity logic of the past. Yet its core logic remains largely unchanged. This paper investigates the possible effects of the fiscal consolidations required under the new European fiscal rules on Italy's debt-to-GDP ratio. Drawing on the reference trajectory for net primary expenditure transmitted by the European Commission to Italy in June 2024, the analysis shows that the projected decline in the debt-to-GDP ratio relies on an assumption for which the Commission gives no justification: that the contractionary effects of fiscal consolidation on GDP are only temporary and fully dissipate three years after the adjustment period. Once this assumption is removed and the effects of consolidation are allowed to persistas suggested by empirical evidence on hysteresis-GDP growth weakens substantially, and the debt-to-GDP ratio may increase rather than decrease. The findings suggest that the new governance framework may lead to the pro-cyclical tightening, weaker growth and adverse debt dynamics that characterized earlier phases of EU fiscal governance.

title: Does Religiosity Make Communities More Economically Resilient? Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic
affiliations: and Baylor University - Institute for Studies of Religion

detail.title: Does Religiosity Make Communities More Economically Resilient? Evidence from the COVID-19 Pandemic
detail.abstract: We study whether religiosity is associated with greater economic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using county-level data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages and the Bureau of Economic Analysis from 2016 to 2024, together with the Religion Census in 2010 and 2020, we examine whether counties with larger pre-pandemic increases in Christian adherence experienced different post-pandemic trajectories in employment, wages, establishments, and real output. We find that counties with greater growth in religiosity between 2010 and 2020 exhibited significantly stronger resilience in employment, establishment counts, and real output during and after the pandemic, with weaker and less consistent effects for real wages. We complement these findings with cross-country evidence from the Gallup World Poll covering more than 140 countries, showing that countries with stronger pre-pandemic growth in religiosity also had more favorable post-pandemic trajectories in thriving, perceived social support, stress, and worry. The findings are consistent with the view that religiosity may operate as a distinct form of resilience capital during major shocks.

detail.abstract: This study examines the integration of satellite technology into community-based economic resilience strategies implemented at the Rukun Tetangga (RT) and Rukun Warga (RW) levels in Indonesia, particularly in the context of armed conflict risks, war and recurring natural disasters. As a disaster-prone and geopolitically strategic archipelagic state, Indonesia faces increasing challenges in sustaining inclusive economic development aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). While satellite technology has been widely applied in national-level disaster management and security systems, its localization at the neigh governance level remains underexplored. Using a qualitative research design grounded in the ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) framework and Design and Research (D&R) methodology, this study investigates how satellite-based data-such as early warning systems, geospatial monitoring, and disaster risk mapping-can be adapted to strengthen grassroots economic resilience. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, policy document analysis, and participatory observation involving RT/RW leaders, local government officials, disaster management agencies, and community economic actors. The findings demonstrate that satellite-enabled information enhances early response capacity, supports adaptive local economic planning, and improves coordination between community institutions and higher-level governance structures. However, challenges persist, including digital literacy gaps, data accessibility, and institutional fragmentation. This study contributes a novel model of satellite-integrated community economic resilience, offering policy-relevant insights for SDG localization, disaster risk reduction, and conflict-sensitive development in Indonesia and comparable Global South contexts.

title: Gender Role Attitudes and Marital Sorting: Implications for Household Inequality
affiliations: University of Essex,  and University of York

detail.title: Gender Role Attitudes and Marital Sorting: Implications for Household Inequality
detail.abstract: We study the role of gender role attitudes (GRA)—beliefs about appropriate roles for men and women—in marital sorting and intra-household allocations. Using the UK Household Longitudinal Study and a multidimensional matching model, we estimate the contribution of GRA to the joint marriage utility alongside age, education, BMI, height, health, personality traits, and risk preferences. We find that sorting on GRA is quantitatively important: its contribution to the joint utility is comparable in magnitude to that of education. We apply a decomposition that identifies three main indices underlying the joint utility, with GRA loading heavily on one of the dominant indices jointly with age and education. This GRA-related index strongly predicts subsequent allocations within marriage, including spouses’ shares of housework, childcare, earnings, and paid labor. These findings indicate that GRA are a central dimension of assortative matching and play a meaningful role in shaping intra-household behavior and gendered labor market outcomes.

title: Who Gets Publicly Guaranteed Loans? The Effect of Guarantee Fees on Loan Allocation and Pricing
affiliations: CUNEF Universidad and

detail.title: Who Gets Publicly Guaranteed Loans? The Effect of Guarantee Fees on Loan Allocation and Pricing
detail.abstract: We study how guarantee fees affect lending by exploiting the Belgian COVID-19 loan guarantee program, which charged lower fees to SMEs than to large firms. Using this size-based fee discontinuity in a regression discontinuity design, we show that large firms facing higher fees are more likely to obtain non-guaranteed loans that are cheaper than comparable guaranteed loans. Both banks and firms benefit from avoiding the fee: borrowers pay lower rates, and lenders retain part of the avoided fee as higher returns. Overall, fees discourage guaranteed lending and concentrate guaranteed loans among ex-ante riskier large firms, resulting in higher ex-post defaults.

detail.title: Household Infrastructure Stabilization as a Structural Economic Resilience Mechanism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The intent is to theorize about potential mechanisms for creating enduring economic channels of production and value within the context of residency and energy infrastructure.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a conceptual framework examining whether integration between housing infrastructure and localized energy production may function as a structural stabilizing mechanism within modern economies.  Household financial fragility is often influenced by volatility in essential expenditures, particularly housing and energy costs, which can act as channels for broader economic shock transmission.  The framework explores whether reducing exposure to such volatility through infrastructure design could contribute to more stable household balance sheets and, in turn, enhance macroeconomic resilience.  Using a circulation based perspective, the paper describes a "stability flywheel" in which improved predictability at the household level supports more consistent participation in local economic activity, reinforces community-level resilience and reduces amplification of downturns.  It also considers potential interactions between distributed residential energy systems and evolving grid demands in regions experiencing growth in electricity intensive infrastructure.

title: Timing of Environmental Regulation and the Adoption of Low-Pollution Technologies: An Experiment
affiliations: , University Jaume I, University of Kiel - Department of Economics and Bard College - Bard College Berlin

detail.title: Timing of Environmental Regulation and the Adoption of Low-Pollution Technologies: An Experiment
detail.abstract: We experimentally investigate how the timing of, and commitment to, an environmental regulation affects efficient technology adoption under emission taxes and tradable permits. An environmental regulator can either commit ex-ante to a specific policy level or ex-post to a rule on how to adjust the policy level after firms have decided whether or not to adopt an advanced low-emission technology. In a 2x2 design, we examine the performance of the four environmental policies (ex-ante vs. ex-post; tax vs. permits), all of which should theoretically lead to the social optimum. Indeed, we find that, in all scenarios, firms' adoption of advanced technology is close to the social optimum. Regarding static efficiency, the tax policy slightly outperforms the permit policy. However, the overall efficiency is very high in all treatments, suggesting that ex-post regulations do not necessarily hinder the adoption of low-polluting technologies.

title: Ancillary Probate: "There's No Place Like Home"
affiliations: Texas Tech University School of Law and Trinity University

detail.title: Ancillary Probate: "There's No Place Like Home"
detail.abstract:
Ancillary probate has become an increasingly common issue in agricultural law - and generally - as clients maintain assets, businesses, and agricultural operations in multiple jurisdictions. Although most practitioners are familiar with probate in general, the state‑specific nature of estates law creates significant variation in when and how ancillary probate must be pursued. This Article provides a practical, comprehensive primer for attorneys navigating these multi‑state matters, addressing when ancillary probate is necessary; how original probate choices influence later proceedings; the interaction between domiciliary law, situs rules, and jurisdiction; and the effects of property type, costs, ethics, and local practice requirements. The Article examines unique considerations for agricultural families and producers—who frequently own land, livestock, and equipment across state lines—and explores how federal agencies such as the USDA Farm Service Agency complicate interstate administration. It further analyzes the Uniform Probate Code’s framework for ancillary administration and reviews the divergent state‑specific approaches that either streamline or complicate the recognition of foreign probates. Ultimately, the Article equips practitioners with guidance for advising clients, avoiding unauthorized‑practice pitfalls, managing cost implications, and implementing planning strategies that can reduce or eliminate the need for ancillary proceedings in the future.

Publication Citation: Garrett Couts & Emily Daniel, Ancillary Probate There’s No Place Like Home, 29 DRAKE J. AGRIC. L. 299 (2024) (Copyright retained by Drake Journal of Agricultural Law)

title: Mission Possible: The Collection of High-Quality Data
affiliations: , , , , University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management and

detail.title: Mission Possible: The Collection of High-Quality Data
detail.abstract: Absent high-quality online data, research questions would be constrained conceptually and in study populations. To inform the debate about online data quality, this paper provides empirical evidence that compares data quality of responses from online participants, AI agents, and human subjects in the lab. Corresponding results reveal high data quality on some platforms, but not others. This paper also highlights a viable path for high-quality online data in an evolving landscape: use a two-stage recruitment method to broadly recruit online subjects in a baseline study and then limit recruitment for the main study to the resulting subset of "high quality" subjects.

title: Failures Of Rights Of First Refusal And Options And Their Perils For The Family Farm
affiliations: Texas Tech University School of Law

detail.title: Failures Of Rights Of First Refusal And Options And Their Perils For The Family Farm
detail.abstract:
Agricultural estates face unique challenges due to the critical role of real property in preserving agricultural operations across generations. 

This paper explores the limitations of relatively-common estate planning tools in the agricultural context, particularly Rights of First Refusal and Options to Purchase, and the detrimental outcomes which can occur when those tools are implemented under current provisions of Texas law.

One particularly destructive obstacle – the abuse of the "Power of Sale" in probate and estate administrations – is responsible for the loss of family farms and ranches across the State of Texas. Current Texas law enables executors and administrators, as fiduciaries, to exploit this power, often to the detriment of devisees, thereby fragmenting, or eliminating, family farms and ranches. Coupled with legal protections afforded to Bona Fide Purchasers (BFPs), even when conflicting interests are evident in probate records, this framework undermines the intent of decedents.

This paper calls for a reevaluation of the dignity and legal effect of probate records, arguing the law should affirm such records’ role in the chain of title and limit the ability of fiduciaries and purchasers to circumvent rightful inheritance claims. Without such reform, the foundational principles of estate law in Texas – and the future of generational agricultural land ownership – remain at risk in exchange for administrative convenience and expediency.

Publication: Garrett Couts, Failure of Rights Of First Refusal And Options And Their Perils For The Family Farm, 18 Est. Plan. & Comm. Prop. L. J. 49 (2025)

title: Compensation for Indirect Carbon Costs — Impacts on Electricity Efficiency, Production, and Emissions
affiliations: Statistics Norway, Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research and Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: Compensation for Indirect Carbon Costs — Impacts on Electricity Efficiency, Production, and Emissions
detail.abstract: The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) leads to higher electricity prices and thus higher costs for electricity-intensive industries in the EU, reducing their competitiveness compared to those in non-EU countries. This disparity may result in carbon leakage, where production shifts abroad, potentially increasing global emissions. To mitigate this, the EU introduced a compensation scheme in 2012, allowing member states to compensate affected industries for the higher electricity prices. This paper explores analytically and numerically the effects of this compensation scheme on production, electricity efficiency, and emissions. We find that while the EU ETS price signal reduces production and increases electricity efficiency, the compensation scheme can counteract these effects by boosting production and potentially reducing electricity efficiency. Additionally, conditional decarbonization or energy efficiency efforts may lead to socially inefficient investments and could have undesired impacts on electricity efficiency. These findings highlight the complex trade-offs in designing effective climate policies that balance environmental goals with industrial competitiveness.

title: Green Policies, Unequal Outcomes
affiliations: University of Oxford, Saïd Business School and University of Oxford - Said Business School and St. Edmund Hall

detail.title: Green Policies, Unequal Outcomes

declarations.funderStatement: Funding for this project was partly received from International Network for Sustainable Financial Policy Insights, Research, and Exchange (INSPIRE), which is an independent research network built to support the central banks and supervisors of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), under call for proposals on ‘Environment-related Financial Risks and Regulatory Capital Requirements’ jointly with the Sustainable Insurance Forum (SIF). Dimitrios Tsomocos also acknowledges funding received from GEOCEP.

detail.abstract: We study the distributional consequences of climate-focused financial regulation. We build a finite-horizon heterogeneous agent general equilibrium model with incomplete markets and endogenous climate damages to compare green capital requirements, which restrict credit to polluting firms, with carbon taxes. Green capital regulation lowers emissions but misallocates credit, reduces aggregate efficiency, and raises inequality primarily through depressed wages in the brown sector. Carbon taxes achieve larger emission reductions with smaller inequality costs, as tax revenues can be redistributed to workers. When economies are highly reliant on brown energy, capital requirements complement carbon taxes by curbing pollution externalities, while redistribution through taxes mitigates regressive effects. Empirical evidence from OECD data and voluntary bank credit contraction supports the model's mechanism: developed economies experience rising inequality when brown credit contracts. The results highlight a central policy trade-off: instruments that most effectively reduce climate damages tend to exacerbate inequality, making joint design of regulation and taxation essential.

title: Performance of Super Funds in Australia: The Contribution of Alternatives and Active Management
affiliations: Monash University - Monash Centre for Financial Studies and Monash University - Monash Centre for Financial Studies

detail.title: Performance of Super Funds in Australia: The Contribution of Alternatives and Active Management

declarations.ethicsApproval: The research was conducted with secondary data and, therefore, no ethical clearance was required.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the performance of Australia's largest superannuation funds by comparing their default MySuper products to custom public market equivalent (PME) benchmarks. Using two decades of monthly data and returns-based style analysis, we find that most funds generate statistically significant excess returns. This outperformance is robust across Sharpe, Sortino, and Omega ratios, as well as CAPM alphas, and holds under alternative benchmarking approaches. However, since 2021, excess performance has moderated. These findings contrast with international evidence questioning the value of active management in institutional portfolios. In the Australian context, large super funds have used diversified allocations, including unlisted assets, to improve member outcomes. Our results contribute new evidence on pension fund performance in a system characterised by long-term investment horizons and distinctive portfolio strategies.

title: Renewable Investment and Electricity Rationing: Evidence from South Africa
affiliations: Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg and

detail.title: Renewable Investment and Electricity Rationing: Evidence from South Africa
detail.abstract: Chronic electricity shortages constrain growth and welfare in many developing countries, where load shedding rations demand. Intermittent renewables can ease shortages, but their effects depend on how infeed timing aligns with scarcity. Using high-frequency data from South Africa and an instrumental-variables strategy, we estimate the effect of wind and solar generation on electricity rationing. On average, an additional MWh of wind generation reduces load shedding by 0.28 MWh, while an additional MWh of solar generation reduces it by 0.40 MWh. Wind provides a more robust reliability contribution across the day, including the evening peak, whereas solar benefits are concentrated in daylight hours. Our estimates permit a welfare-based evaluation of renewable investment. We show that the implied reliability benefits exceed benchmark investment costs by a wide margin and are complemented by sizeable climate and local air-pollution co-benefits.

title: A Comprehensive National Framework for Federal AI Adoption: Governance, Standards, and Implementation Pathways for Agentic and Generative Systems
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University

detail.title: A Comprehensive National Framework for Federal AI Adoption: Governance, Standards, and Implementation Pathways for Agentic and Generative Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: The United States federal government stands at a critical inflection point in artificial intelligence adoption, transitioning from experimental deployments to integration of autonomous systems across all agencies. This comprehensive paper presents a multi-layered national governance framework addressing the unique challenges posed by agentic AI-systems capable of autonomous decision-making, planning, and tool interaction without continuous human supervision. Building upon Executive Order 14110, OMB Memorandum M-25-21, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and international standards including ISO/IEC 42001, we conduct an exhaustive analysis of regulatory barriers, technical interoperability challenges, and organizational readiness gaps. Through systematic examination of government publications, industry whitepapers, academic research, and regulatory filings, we identify and categorize five primary barriers to federal AI adoption: regulatory mismatches, structural incompatibility, lack of regulatory clarity, direct hindrance mechanisms, and organizational factors. Our proposed framework integrates three pillars: (1) Technical standards harmonization incorporating ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, IEEE 7000, HL7 FHIR, and emerging agentic AI protocols; (2) A four-tier riskbased classification system aligned with the EU AI Act and tailored for U.S. federal requirements; (3) Administrative flexibility mechanisms including regulatory sandboxes, conditional approvals, and graduated compliance enforcement. We provide detailed implementation roadmaps across four phases (immediate, shortterm, medium-term, and long-term), sector-specific pathways for healthcare, financial services, transportation, defense, and federal operations, and numerous TikZ diagrams for policy visualization. Key contributions include: (a) A comprehensive synthesis of agentic AI governance requirements for federal adoption; (b) A comparative analysis of international AI governance frameworks; (c) Technical specifications for AI interoperability across federal domains; (d) Workforce development frameworks addressing multiple competency areas; (e) Economic impact projections estimating significant annual productivity gains through responsible AI adoption. This framework provides policymakers, agency leaders, and industry stakeholders with actionable pathways to accelerate responsible AI innovation while maintaining public trust, safety, and U.S. global competitiveness in the agentic AI era.

title: Uncertainty Matters: How Does Uncertainty Affect Firms' Behavior in High Inflation?
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and Sabanci University

detail.title: Uncertainty Matters: How Does Uncertainty Affect Firms' Behavior in High Inflation?
detail.abstract: This paper studies how uncertainty shapes firms' inflation expectations and real decisions, and how these effects vary across inflation regimes. Using a uniquely rich combination of monthly survey and administrative data from Türkiye, we show that a rise in uncertainty leads firms to significantly increase their inflation expectations while becoming more pessimistic about future sales and employment. Crucially, these expectations translate into tangible actions: firms facing heightened uncertainty reduce their sales and purchases, shrink the number of trading partners, and cut back on new hires. Idiosyncratic uncertainty shocks have much larger effects on firm outcomes than aggregate uncertainty shocks. Moreover, the impact of uncertainty is substantially magnified by the macroeconomic environment: the effect of a firmlevel uncertainty shock on inflation expectations is more than four times stronger during periods of high inflation. Our results highlight that in volatile economies, uncertainty can act as a potent accelerant, deanchoring expectations and depressing real activity, suggesting that policies aimed at reducing uncertainty are a critical component of macroeconomic stabilization.

title: Board Governance of Occupational Licensing and Labor Market Outcomes in Eye Care Occupations
affiliations: Illinois Institute of Technology - Stuart School of Business, IIT

detail.title: Board Governance of Occupational Licensing and Labor Market Outcomes in Eye Care Occupations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

contentType.other: Under review for journal of regulatory economics

detail.abstract: In this study, the author is trying to analyze the labor market influence of occupational licensing on two occupations in the eye care industry: opticians and optometrists. Opticians and Optometrists are often considered as lower-level and higher-level eye-care occupations, in that they are complements to and substitutes for one another in providing eye-care services. With occupational licensing requirements in place for both occupations, the statutes and regulations determine who can do what tasks to which extent for the practitioners, and the board for each state would implement such regulations. The author is trying to use the board compositions for the optician occupation as a proxy for the optometrists' control over opticians to see how different levels of regulations can have differential influence on wages for both opticians and optometrists. Using two different samples from ACS and CPS, combined with a novel dataset on board composition and statutory licensing requirements for the 22 states regulating opticians from 2000-2024, this study finds that non-independent board composition is positively associated with wages for both opticians and optometrists-particularly larger for optometristswhile being negatively associated with optician employment, and showing limited nonsignificant associations with hours worked. These findings suggest that who governs professional regulation may matter as much as, or more than, how stringent formal requirements are, contributing to ongoing discussions about healthcare regulation and workforce organization.

title: Dynamic Pricing under Information Frictions: Evidence from Firm-level Subjective Expectations
affiliations: and National Bank of Belgium

detail.title: Dynamic Pricing under Information Frictions: Evidence from Firm-level Subjective Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper develops and implements a structural method to quantify how forwardlooking firms are and estimate their effective discount factor from the dynamic passthrough of production-cost shocks into prices. We propose a model featuring real, nominal, and information frictions, and demonstrate how incomplete information distorts the pricing behavior to appear as if firms were myopic, anchoring current prices to past decisions, and underreacting to idiosyncratic cost shocks. Using a unique monthly micro-dataset for the Belgian manufacturing sector that links firm-level prices and costs to survey-based expectations, we find a significant contemporaneous pass-through but a muted response to expected future cost growth. The implied monthly discount factor is about 0.8. These results are consistent with an essentially static pricing behavior, with firms responding strongly as cost shocks materialize. Our micro-estimates imply a "hybrid" Phillips curve with high aggregate discounting and persistence, which can explain the hump-shaped response of inflation to shocks and its long and variable lags.

title: Opportunity Lost

detail.title: Opportunity Lost
detail.abstract:
The purpose of this article is to provide the appropriate policy framework to view the turmoil within which the US economy exists after the start of the second Trump administration utilizing tariffs with no comprehension of their long-term impacts.  By highlighting the current economic events and comparing the conditions with the fundamental principles of free trade, the article seeks to provide a convincing case for the complete rejection of isolationist and mercantilist tools. 

The article demonstrates that free trade between global states leads to increased competition and more efficient production.  When the principles of free trade are properly implemented, consumers in the marketplace enjoy a greater variety of better-quality goods at a lower price which is a win for the consumer.  The concept of economic advantage leads to specialization in free trade economies, where a country only produces goods that they are efficient at producing resulting in higher levels of output in quantity and quality.  When the principles of free trade are abandoned in favor of mercantilist and nationalist policies, other nations that relied on established free trade agreements seek other trading partners.  The resulting impact to the transitioning economy away from free trade is chaotic at best and harmful for all of the economic participants.  The first year of the second Trump administration can be best described as chaotic and detrimentally harmful to the United States’ interests and trading partners with no long-term plan for economic revitalization and prosperity.

The article presents a concrete plan for Trade Law & Development to rectify the shortcomings in the current administration’s trade policy by addressing the following topics:  The fundamental differences between free trade and mercantilism.   A comparison between present-day Trade Law & Development policy in the United States and the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act to show the negative consequences of utilizing tariffs to shape trade policy.  The benefits that were offered by the Trans-Pacific Partnership to its sponsoring members and the opportunity lost by the United States’ withdrawal.  The attacks levied against free trade principles by special interest groups benefit an economy in the short-term only.  Pursuit of free-trade principles as part of a long-term Trade Law & Development policy requires an effective education and marketing plan to obtain popular support.  Illustrating the certitude of the foregoing statements by examining the failure of former US Senator, Joe Manchin, to embrace free trade and its negative effects on his constituents and his political career.  In the final section of the article, a blueprint for a long-term Trade Law & Development policy on behalf of the United States is presented to accomplish sustained economic growth for the country once the Trump administration ends.

title: Credibility Cycles

detail.title: Credibility Cycles
detail.abstract: I model the strategic interactions between the manager of a firm and an outside investor in a dynamic cheap talk game with two-sided asymmetric information. Each period, the investor selectively discloses his information to influence the manager's capital investment decision. While the manager knows that she can learn from the investor's disclosures, she also knows that the investor is trying to manipulate her; in equilibrium, the investor's incentives to mislead the manager constrain the credibility of his disclosures, leading to a mutually-deleterious loss of information. My model has implications for short-termism, management guidance, and investor credibility over the business cycle.

title: More Than Just Money: Fraud Aversion and Portfolio Choice
affiliations: Claremont McKenna College and Claremont McKenna College

detail.title: More Than Just Money: Fraud Aversion and Portfolio Choice

declarations.ethicsApproval: IRB approval
declarations.funderStatement: Lowe Institute

detail.abstract: Standard models assume the source of financial loss does not affect investor utility. We challenge this assumption by showing that losses due to fraud are perceived as more distressing than equivalent losses caused by poor performance or external shocks-a phenomenon we term fraud aversion. We formalize this by nesting the seminal framework of Guiso et al. (2008) within a utility model incorporating nonpecuniary disutility from deception. Using survey evidence, we calibrate this model to quantify its impact on equity participation. Our estimations imply that a typical investor requires an equity risk premium of about 15% to participate in the stock market. In a multi-asset setting, we show that fraud aversion generates underdiversication. These findings provide a behavioral microfoundation for governance preferences in ESG investing and suggest that the demand for high-quality, independent audits is driven partly by the psychological costs of nancial misconduct.

title: Universities and Pro-government Mobilization in Autocratic Regimes
affiliations: Boston College and Boston College

detail.title: Universities and Pro-government Mobilization in Autocratic Regimes
detail.abstract: Universities are widely viewed as hotbeds of dissent and anti-government protest. This study complements and complicates this understanding by showing that, in autocratic regimes, universities also function as vehicles of pro-government mobilization. Authoritarian governments cultivate regime-affiliated student organizations and align incentives, particularly through public-sector career opportunities, to organize and sustain state-led participation on campuses. We show this argument through a mixed-methods approach. First, we conduct the first cross-national, subnational analysis of pro-government mobilization across 93 autocratic regimes from 2003 to 2019, using grid-cell and country-level data. Areas with more universities consistently experience higher levels of pro-government mobilization, a relationship that remains robust across alternative model specifications. Second, comparative case studies of China, Russia, and Iran illustrate the mechanisms through which autocratic regimes cultivate campus-based mobilization. Our findings highlight the often-overlooked mobilizational role of universities in authoritarian contexts, adding a new dimension to research that has primarily portrayed campuses as sites of dissent.

title: Asymmetries of Convergence: A Structural Audit of Central-Eastern European Growth Models (2010-2024)
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS)

detail.title: Asymmetries of Convergence: A Structural Audit of Central-Eastern European Growth Models (2010-2024)
detail.abstract: This paper examines macroeconomic developments in Czechia, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia (the Visegrád Four, V4) over 2010–2024. The region converged toward EU-27 living standards, supported by broad labour-market activation. As labour slack diminished, cross-country differences in growth drivers became more visible. First, productivity fundamentals differ: economies with stronger R&D effort and absorptive capacity are associated with more sustained TFP gains as labour contributions fade. Second, inflation, exchange rates and component deflators diverged across countries and, in some cases, created wedges between nominal expenditure shares and real volumes. Third, fiscal space differs across countries as interest burdens and budget composition vary, with implications for maintaining spending on health, education and social protection. Slovakia stands out for a comparatively strong expansion in social protection and lower inequality within the V4. Overall, Czechia and Poland appear better positioned for a knowledge-intensive phase of convergence. Hungary, having recorded the largest gains in labour-force participation, faces a more demanding adjustment as the scope for further labour-input-led growth narrows, amid higher interest burdens and signs of allocative frictions.

title: Competition in Health Insurance Markets
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University and Kellogg School of Management, Northweste

detail.title: Competition in Health Insurance Markets

declarations.funderStatement: There was no funding support for this research.

detail.abstract: The United States relies primarily on private health insurance markets, yet these markets are highly concentrated and becoming more so over time. We document concentration across commercial, Medicare Advantage, and Medicaid markets. We then examine how asymmetric information — particularly adverse selection — interacts with market power to shape premiums, plan design, and consumer welfare. Empirical evidence confirms that insurer consolidation raises premiums. We discuss how antitrust enforcement, risk adjustment, regulation, and informational interventions shape competition and consumer welfare in these markets.

title: The Attention Factor: The Speculative Risk You May Already Own

detail.title: The Attention Factor: The Speculative Risk You May Already Own
detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency and equity markets have become linked-and the linkage is intensifying. Bitcoin now shares roughly a quarter of its return variation with world equities during periods of elevated speculative participation, while gold shares near zero. An asset with no shared business fundamentals-cash flows, earnings, or production linkages has developed meaningful co-movement with equity markets. For allocators, understanding this linkage is not a crypto question-it is a portfolio risk question. We therefore test whether the linkage is entirely explained by shared exposure to economy-wide conditions-global market returns and risk appetite shifts. It is not. After removing these systematic channels, a residual connectedness survives-but not uniformly. The residual is largest for firms whose revenues depend mechanically on speculative participation (DraftKings, Robinhood, Coinbase) and for sentiment-driven strategies (BUZZ Social Sentiment ETF). For institutionally priced benchmarks like the Nasdaq-100 and AI stocks, residual connectedness drops to the level explained by shared market exposure alone-despite their popularity. This pattern suggests a common cause. Our hypothesis: the linkage transmits through shared marginal investors. A speculative cohort-retail traders active across crypto exchanges, zero-day options, sports betting, and commission-free brokerages-sets prices in multiple markets simultaneously. When this cohort's sentiment shifts, it creates correlated movements across every venue they participate in. Crypto, having no fundamental equity linkage, serves as the cleanest signal of this transmission. We interpret this transmission as an Attention factor-capital-backed collective conviction expressed by a speculative cohort active across multiple markets. The key finding is not binary. Every equity investor carries some speculative sentiment exposure through the market itself-crypto co-moves with world equities broadly, meaning this channel is already embedded in market returns. What varies is how much additional connectedness specific equities carry beyond this market-level dose. Thematic growth funds, small-cap indices, and social-sentiment strategies concentrate it. The relevant question for allocators is not whether to add crypto, but how much speculative sentiment exposure already exists in the portfolio-and where on the spectrum their holdings sit.

title: Persuasion in the Political Marketplace: How Firms Snitch on Rivals to Encourage Regulatory Enforcement
affiliations: IE University,  and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

detail.title: Persuasion in the Political Marketplace: How Firms Snitch on Rivals to Encourage Regulatory Enforcement
detail.abstract: We study an important, but largely overlooked, non-market strategy used by firms in the enforcement stage of policy: "snitching", i.e. providing intelligence about potential violations of their rivals in an attempt to persuade regulators to fine them. Building on political marketplace theory, we develop and test a theoretical model of how firms use snitching during regulatory enforcement. We show that in equilibrium, firms snitch when the rival's violations are likely to cause significant harm to the population. We then derive several boundary conditions outlining when firms will engage in more or less snitching. We find support for our theory in panel data on enforcement actions by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for more than 8,000 facilities over 12 years.

title: Bilateral Bargaining Design

detail.title: Bilateral Bargaining Design
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the relation between the Myerson-Satterthwaite theorem and the Coase theorem in bilateral trade with private information. It argues that the inefficiency identified by the Myerson-Satterthwaite theorem does not stem from private information per se, but from a deterministic allocation rule that centralizes authority over surplus division. Such centralization generates a strategic externality that underlies the impossibility result. The paper constructs a mechanism that separates information communication from surplus determination by conveying derived information while preserving decentralized price negotiation. The mechanism achieves incentive compatibility without outside subsidies and implements ex post efficient meeting assignments. The analysis reconciles Coasean bargaining with private information and expands the domain of mechanism design to institutional environments with decentralized authority and probabilistic indeterminacy within a Bayesian framework.

title: Banks and Culture
affiliations: University of Essex - Essex Business School and University of Roma, Tor Vergata

detail.title: Banks and Culture
detail.abstract: The institutional model of banks-whether shareholder-focused or stakeholderoriented-shapes their role in fostering local economic growth and wealth creation. Our research offers new evidence that stakeholder-oriented banks also contribute to the development of tangible cultural capital within communities. Conversely, commercial and savings banks do not exhibit a similar influence.

title: Copula Density Estimation in Factor Models
affiliations: , Brunel University London and Brunel University London

detail.title: Copula Density Estimation in Factor Models
detail.abstract: This paper investigates risk premium estimation in a one-factor asset pricing model using a copula-based likelihood framework. While traditional methods, such as Fama-MacBeth or Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR), rely on linear covariance structures, the copula framework allows for a flexible representation of dependence in the residuals, including tail dependence. In particular, the multivariate copula density likelihood recovers cross-sectional Generalized Least Squares (GLS) estimates, while the univariate copula likelihood recovers Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimates under standard assumptions of homoskedasticity and no cross-sectional correlation. Differences arise under non-Gaussian specifications, where the copula framework changes the weighting of observations through the residual distribution.

title: Socio-economic determinants of Health Literacy among blood donors: A cross-sectional study in Italy
affiliations: University of the Republic of San Marino and University of Urbino Carlo Bo

detail.title: Socio-economic determinants of Health Literacy among blood donors: A cross-sectional study in Italy
detail.abstract: As a life-sustaining procedure and an integral part of the health system, blood donation relies heavily on Health Literacy (HL) to empower individuals to critically assess health information. This study primarily aimed to assess HL levels among blood donors and compare them with the general population, specifically focusing on 471 donors aged 18 and over affiliated with AVIS within a local health authority in the Marche Region. Using the HLS-EU-Q16 tool administered via a web-based interview method, the 16 items were aggregated into a General HL Index standardized on a scale from 0 to 50. Statistical analysis, including independent t-tests and multinomial logistic regression, was conducted to explore associations with sociodemographic factors. The results revealed a mean HL score for blood donors of 30.29 ± 7.11. Notably, 36% of donors demonstrated adequate HL (sufficient or excellent), a significantly higher share than the 25% observed in the general Italian population. Higher HL levels were significantly associated with higher education, economic status, and better self-perceived health, while the risk of inadequate HL increased among those with chronic diseases. In conclusion, blood donors possess HL levels superior to the national average, suggesting that improving HL could serve as a strategic lever to enhance the donor base and the social impact of donor associations.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives

declarations.ethicsApproval: IRB human subjects approval was received for this project.

detail.abstract:
We use novel data from a survey of nearly 750 corporate executives to study the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on productivity and the workforce. We document substantial heterogeneity in AI adoption across firms, with more than half having already invested, though many smaller firms are only beginning to do so. Labor productivity gains are positive, vary across sectors, and are expected to strengthen in 2026, with the largest effects concentrated in high-skill services and finance. These gains are not primarily driven by firms' capital deepening but instead reflect increases in revenue-based total factor productivity, closely associated with innovation-and demand-oriented channels. We document a productivity paradox, in which perceived productivity gains are larger than measured productivity gains, likely reflecting a delay in revenue realizations. In labor markets, we find little evidence of near-term aggregate employment declines due to AI, though larger companies anticipate AI-driven workforce reductions, while smaller firms expect modest gains. We also find evidence of compositional reallocation of labor both within and across firms, with routine clerical roles declining and a relative demand for skilled technical roles increasing. We develop an index that ranks job functions most negatively affected by AI.

title: An Examination of the Intermediate Macroeconomics: Results from a Survey of U.S. Institutions

detail.title: An Examination of the Intermediate Macroeconomics: Results from a Survey of U.S. Institutions
detail.abstract: Intermediate macroeconomics (macro) is a core requirement in the undergraduate economics major, serving as a terminal macro course for many students while preparing others for advanced electives and, in some cases, graduate study. Yet systematic evidence on how intermediate macro is taught across U.S. institutions remains limited, an issue that is particularly acute given the diversity of theoretical approaches and the gap between undergraduate coverage and the research frontier. This paper reports results from a national survey of instructors who have recently taught intermediate macro at U.S. institutions awarding bachelor's degrees in economics. The survey instrument was designed to capture multiple facets of course design, curricular context, and instructor characteristics and perceptions. Responses about content reveal that the course typically includes a version of the short-run IS/LM (or IS/MP) model while only slightly over one-tenth of instructors (11.1%) teach a fully micro-founded macro model. The treatment of long-run growth is dominated by a version of the Solow model that incorporates technological progress (71.6%) with slightly less than half of instructors (48.4%) covering some endogenous growth theory. While almost all instructors indicate their intermediate macro course requires prerequisite introductory coursework in macro, formal mathematics prerequisites were less common (e.g. Calculus I is required by 37.2% of respondents). Over three quarters of the responding instructors (76.6%) identified as male and most (84.2%) are in traditional tenure-track or tenured positions. Instructors report high autonomy over content, strong support for integrating real-world examples and data, and high satisfaction teaching the course. Open-ended responses emphasize tensions in framing the course amid limited disciplinary consensus and competing course objectives.
